docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This practical lab combines the skills learned throughout the Users and Groups module.

You will perform common Linux administration tasks including:

  • Creating users
  • Creating groups
  • Managing group membership
  • Setting passwords
  • Reviewing account information
  • Managing account access
  • Testing permissions

The scenario is based on a common real-world administration task: preparing a Linux server for a new team.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are a Linux administrator managing a development server.

A new development team requires access.

The requirements are:

  • Create a development group
  • Create user accounts
  • Assign users to the correct groups
  • Configure passwords
  • Verify access
  • Remove access when required

docs.title: Lab Environment
docs.text:
Before starting, check your current account:

whoami

Check your permissions:

id

Confirm you can use sudo:

sudo -v

docs.title: Task 1 - Create the Development Group
docs.text:
Create a group called:

developers

Command:

sudo groupadd developers

Verify:

getent group developers

Expected output:

developers:x:1001:

docs.title: Task 2 - Create User Accounts
docs.text:
Create two users:

alice
bob

Create their home directories:

sudo useradd -m alice
sudo useradd -m bob

Verify:

id alice
id bob

docs.title: Task 3 - Set User Passwords
docs.text:
Set passwords:

sudo passwd alice
sudo passwd bob

Confirm the accounts exist:

cat /etc/passwd | grep -E "alice|bob"

docs.title: Task 4 - Add Users to the Development Group
docs.text:
Add both users to the developers group:

sudo usermod -aG developers alice
sudo usermod -aG developers bob

Verify:

groups alice
groups bob

Expected:

alice : alice developers

bob : bob developers

docs.title: Task 5 - Create a Shared Development Directory
docs.text:
Create:

sudo mkdir /development

Assign ownership to the developers group:

sudo chown root:developers /development

Set permissions:

sudo chmod 770 /development

Check:

ls -ld /development

Expected:

drwxrwx--- root developers /development

docs.title: Task 6 - Test User Access
docs.text:
Switch to the alice account:

su - alice

Check identity:

whoami

Try creating a file:

touch /development/alice-test.txt

List the directory:

ls -l /development

Exit:

exit

docs.title: Task 7 - Review Account Information
docs.text:
Check users:

id alice
id bob

Review groups:

getent group developers

Review password status:

sudo passwd -S alice

docs.title: Task 8 - Configure Administrative Access
docs.text:
Add alice to the sudo group:

sudo usermod -aG sudo alice

Verify:

groups alice

The output should include:

sudo

docs.title: Task 9 - Test sudo Access
docs.text:
Switch to alice:

su - alice

Run:

sudo whoami

Expected:

root

Exit:

exit

docs.title: Task 10 - Disable an Account
docs.text:
Temporarily disable bob:

sudo passwd -l bob

Check status:

sudo passwd -S bob

Unlock:

sudo passwd -u bob

docs.title: Task 11 - Remove Test Accounts
docs.text:
Remove users:

sudo userdel -r alice
sudo userdel -r bob

Remove group:

sudo groupdel developers

Verify:

getent group developers

No output should be returned.

docs.title: Problem 1
docs.text:
A user cannot access:

/development

Check:

id username

Possible causes:

  • User not in the correct group
  • Incorrect permissions
  • Incorrect ownership

docs.title: Problem 2
docs.text:
A user cannot run sudo commands.

Check:

groups username

Possible causes:

  • User not in sudo group
  • Incorrect sudo configuration

docs.title: Knowledge Check
docs.text:
1. Which command creates a Linux user?
  2. Which command creates a group?
  3. How do you add a user to an existing group?
  4. What command displays user IDs and groups?
  5. Why is chmod 770 used for shared directories?
  6. Why should administrators use sudo instead of logging in as root?

docs.text:

✓ Created groups

✓ Managed group membership

✓ Configured shared directory access

✓ Tested permissions

✓ Configured sudo access

✓ Managed account security

✓ Removed accounts safely

docs.title: Lesson 01 - Understanding Linux Processes
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 01 – Command Line Fundamentals - Module 02 – Linux Filesystem Administration - Module 03 – Users and Groups

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A Linux system is made up of many running processes.

Every command you execute, every application you start, and every system service running in the background is a process.

Understanding processes is a fundamental Linux administration skill because it allows administrators to:

  • Monitor system activity
  • Identify resource usage
  • Troubleshoot problems
  • Stop unwanted applications
  • Investigate service failures

docs.title: What is a Process?
docs.text:
A process is a running instance of a program.

When a program is stored on disk, it is simply a file.

When that program is started, Linux loads it into memory and creates a process.

Example:

Program:

/usr/bin/nginx

Running process:

nginx process

docs.title: A program is:
docs.text:
• A file stored on disk
  • Contains instructions for the computer

docs.title: A process is:
docs.text:
• A running copy of a program
  • Uses CPU and memory resources
  • Has a unique identifier

Example:

Program:

/usr/bin/nginx

Running process:

nginx PID 1234

docs.title: Process IDs (PID)
docs.text:
Every running process in Linux receives a unique number called a:

Process ID (PID)

The PID allows administrators to identify and manage individual processes.

Example:

PID Command 1 systemd 550 sshd 1200 nginx 2500 bash

No two running processes have the same PID.

docs.title: The Init Process
docs.text:
The first process started by the Linux kernel is:

PID 1

On modern Linux systems this is normally:

systemd

Check PID 1:

ps -p 1

Example output:

PID TTY      TIME CMD
1   ?        00:00:02 systemd

The PID 1 process is responsible for:

  • Starting system services
  • Managing background services
  • Handling system startup
  • Replacing failed processes

docs.title: Parent and Child Processes
docs.text:
Processes can create other processes.

The process that creates another process is called the:

Parent Process

The new process is called the:

Child Process

Example:

systemd
 |
 ├── sshd
 |    |
 |    └── bash
 |
 └── cron

In this example:

  • systemd is the parent of sshd
  • sshd is the parent of bash

docs.title: Viewing Processes
docs.text:
The ps command displays running processes.

Basic usage:

ps

Example:

PID TTY          TIME CMD
2301 pts/0    00:00:00 bash
2450 pts/0    00:00:00 ps

By default, ps only shows processes from your current terminal.

docs.title: Viewing All Processes
docs.text:
To view all running processes:

ps aux

Example:

USER       PID %CPU %MEM COMMAND

root         1  0.0  0.5 /sbin/init
root       500  0.1  1.2 sshd
james     2200  0.0  0.3 bash

Information shown:

Column Meaning USER Owner of process PID Process ID %CPU CPU usage %MEM Memory usage COMMAND Program running

docs.title: Viewing Process Relationships
docs.text:
The pstree command displays processes in a tree format.

Example:

pstree

Output:

systemd
├─sshd
│ └─bash
├─cron
└─nginx

This makes parent and child relationships easier to understand.

docs.title: Searching for Processes
docs.text:
The pgrep command searches for processes by name.

Example:

pgrep ssh

Output:

500

This returns the PID of matching processes.

docs.title: Monitoring Processes
docs.text:
The top command provides a live view of system activity.

Run:

top

Example:

PID USER      %CPU %MEM COMMAND

1200 root      5.0  2.1 nginx
2200 james     1.0  0.5 bash

Useful information:

  • CPU usage
  • Memory usage
  • Running processes
  • System load

Exit top:

q

docs.title: Background Processes
docs.text:
Linux can run commands in the background.

Example:

sleep 300 &

The & symbol runs the command in the background.

Example output:

[1] 3456

Where:

3456 = Process ID

docs.text:
Run:

Record:

PID:

docs.text:

Identify:

docs.title: Lesson 02 - Managing Linux Processes
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes

Difficulty: Beginner to Intermediate

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Linux systems run many processes at the same time.

Administrators need to understand how to:

  • View running processes
  • Identify resource usage
  • Find specific processes
  • Run commands in the background
  • Control and stop processes safely

Process management is an important skill for troubleshooting performance issues and maintaining system stability.

docs.title: Viewing Processes
docs.text: Linux provides several commands for viewing running processes.

docs.title: ps Command
docs.text:
The ps command displays information about running processes.

Basic usage:

ps

Example output:

PID TTY          TIME CMD
1234 pts/0    00:00:00 bash
5678 pts/0    00:00:01 ps

Information shown:

Column Meaning PID Process ID TTY Terminal TIME CPU time used CMD Command

docs.title: Viewing All Processes
docs.text:
To view all running processes:

ps aux

Example:

USER       PID %CPU %MEM COMMAND
root         1  0.0  1.2 systemd
james     1234  0.1  0.5 bash

Important columns:

Column Meaning USER Process owner PID Process ID %CPU CPU usage %MEM Memory usage COMMAND Running command

docs.title: Using pgrep
docs.text:
The pgrep command searches for processes by name.

Example:

pgrep ssh

Output:

742

This returns the process ID.

docs.title: Using ps with grep
docs.text:
Example:

ps aux | grep ssh

This searches the process list.

Example output:

root 742 0.0 sshd

docs.title: Process Information
docs.text:
To view details about a process:

ps -fp PID

Example:

ps -fp 742

Output:

UID   PID  PPID CMD
root  742    1  sshd

Information:

Field Meaning PID Process ID PPID Parent Process ID CMD Command

docs.title: Parent and Child Processes
docs.text:
Processes can create other processes.

Example:

systemd
 |
 ├── sshd
 |    |
 |    └── bash
 |
 └── cron

View process relationships:

pstree

This shows the hierarchy of processes.

docs.title: Background Processes
docs.text:
Commands normally run in the foreground.

Example:

sleep 60

The terminal waits until the command finishes.

To run a command in the background:

sleep 300 &

Example output:

[1] 12345

The number returned is the process ID.

docs.title: Viewing Background Jobs
docs.text:
Show running background jobs:

jobs

Example:

[1]+ Running sleep 300 &

docs.title: Bringing Jobs to the Foreground
docs.text:
Move a background job back:

fg

Example:

fg %1

docs.title: Sending Processes to the Background
docs.text:
A running command can be moved into the background.

Press:

CTRL + Z

Then:

bg

Example:

sleep 300

CTRL + Z

bg

docs.title: Process Signals
docs.text:
Linux controls processes using signals.

Common signals:

Signal Number Purpose SIGHUP 1 Reload configuration SIGTERM 15 Graceful shutdown SIGKILL 9 Force termination

docs.title: Using kill
docs.text:
Terminate a process:

kill PID

Example:

kill 12345

This sends:

SIGTERM

docs.title: Force Stopping Processes
docs.text:
If a process does not stop:

kill -9 PID

Example:

kill -9 12345

SIGKILL immediately stops the process.

Use carefully because the application cannot clean up.

docs.title: Using pkill
docs.text:
Kill processes by name:

pkill process_name

Example:

pkill sleep

docs.title: top
docs.text:
The top command provides real-time process monitoring.

Run:

top

Shows:

  • CPU usage
  • Memory usage
  • Running processes
  • System load

docs.title: htop
docs.text:
If installed:

htop

Provides an interactive interface.

Install:

sudo apt install htop

docs.title: Process Priority
docs.text:
Linux allows processes to have different priorities.

Priority is controlled using:

nice
renice

View priority:

ps -el

docs.title: Starting a Process with Priority
docs.text:
Example:

nice -n 10 command

Higher nice values mean lower priority.

docs.title: Changing Process Priority
docs.text:
Example:

renice 10 -p PID

docs.title: Task 1 - View Processes
docs.text:
Run:

ps aux

Identify:

  • Your shell process
  • System processes
  • Running applications

docs.title: Task 2 - Monitor the System
docs.text:
Run:

top

Record:

Highest CPU process:

Highest memory process:

docs.title: Task 3 - Create a Background Process
docs.text:
Run:

sleep 300 &

Find it:

ps aux | grep sleep

Stop it:

kill PID

docs.title: Task 4 - Explore Process Tree
docs.text:
Run:

pstree

Identify:

  • Parent processes
  • Child processes

docs.text:

  2. Which command shows all running processes?

  3. What command displays a process tree?

  7. Which command provides live process monitoring?

docs.text:

✓ How to view Linux processes ✓ How to find specific processes ✓ How parent and child processes work ✓ How to run background jobs ✓ How to stop processes safely ✓ How to monitor system activity ✓ How Linux signals control processes

docs.title: Lesson 03 - Systemd and Service Management
docs.text:
You will learn:

  • What systemd is
  • How services are managed
  • Starting and stopping services

docs.title: Lesson 03 - Systemd and Service Management
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 04 – Processes and Services - Lesson 01 – Understanding Linux Processes - Lesson 02 – Managing Linux Processes

Difficulty: Beginner to Intermediate

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Modern Linux systems use systemd to manage system startup, background services and system processes.

Services such as web servers, databases, SSH access and monitoring tools are controlled by systemd.

Understanding systemd is an essential Linux administration skill because it allows administrators to:

  • Start and stop services
  • Enable services at boot
  • Check service status
  • Investigate failures
  • Review service logs

docs.title: What is systemd?
docs.text:
systemd is the service manager used by most modern Linux distributions.

Examples:

  • Ubuntu
  • Debian
  • Rocky Linux
  • Fedora
  • Red Hat Enterprise Linux

systemd is responsible for:

  • Starting services during boot
  • Managing running services
  • Monitoring service health
  • Handling dependencies
  • Recording service events

The systemd process normally runs as:

PID 1

Check:

ps -p 1

Example:

PID TTY      TIME CMD
1   ?        00:00:03 systemd

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
A service is a background process that provides functionality to the system.

Examples:

Service Purpose ssh Remote administration nginx Web server cron Scheduled tasks docker Container management networking Network management

Services normally run without user interaction.

docs.title: Service Units
docs.text:
systemd manages services using unit files.

Common unit types:

docs.text:

  • Troubleshoot problems
  • Investigate service failures
  • Monitor system activity
  • Identify security events
  • Understand system behaviour

Modern Linux systems use systemd-journald to collect and manage system logs.

The main tool used to view these logs is:

journalctl
Linux Logging

Linux records information about:

System startup
Running services
User activity
Hardware events
Application messages
Security events

Examples of logs:

Log Type    Example
Authentication  SSH login attempts
System  Kernel messages
Services    Service startup failures
Applications    Application errors
Traditional Log Files

Historically, Linux stored logs in:

/var/log

View the directory:

ls /var/log

Common log files:

File    Purpose
auth.log    Authentication events
syslog  General system messages
kern.log    Kernel messages
dpkg.log    Package management events

Example:

cat /var/log/syslog
systemd Journal

Modern Linux distributions use the systemd journal.

The journal collects messages from:

The kernel
System services
Applications
User sessions

The journal is managed by:

systemd-journald

Check the service:

systemctl status systemd-journald
Viewing Logs with journalctl

The basic command:

journalctl

displays the system journal.

Example:

Jul 31 10:15:01 server systemd[1]: Started SSH service.
Jul 31 10:15:02 server sshd[500]: Accepted password login.
Viewing Recent Logs

Show the latest log entries:

journalctl -n

Example:

journalctl -n 50

This displays the last 50 entries.

Following Live Logs

Similar to tail -f:

journalctl -f

This displays new log entries as they appear.

Useful when:

Starting services
Testing changes
Troubleshooting problems

Exit using:

CTRL + C
Viewing Logs for a Service

To view logs for a specific service:

journalctl -u service_name

Example:

journalctl -u ssh

This shows only SSH service logs.

Viewing Recent Service Failures

Show recent errors:

journalctl -p err

Example output:

Failed to start nginx.service

Priority levels include:

Level   Meaning
emerg   System unusable
alert   Immediate action required
crit    Critical error
err Error
warning Warning
info    Information
debug   Debug messages
Viewing Logs Since Boot

View logs from the current boot:

journalctl -b

This is useful after:

System crashes
Unexpected reboots
Startup problems
Previous Boot Logs

View logs from the previous boot:

journalctl -b -1

Useful when investigating:

Failed boots
System crashes
Hardware problems
Kernel Messages

The kernel produces important system messages.

View kernel messages:

dmesg

Examples:

Hardware detection
Driver messages
Disk errors
Network events

Example:

dmesg | less
Filtering Logs by Time

View logs after a specific time:

journalctl --since "1 hour ago"

Example:

journalctl --since today

View logs before a specific time:

journalctl --until "10:00"
Searching Logs

Use standard Linux tools with journalctl.

Example:

journalctl | grep ssh

Search for errors:

journalctl | grep error
Checking Service Failures

When a service fails:

First check status:

systemctl status service_name

Then check logs:

journalctl -u service_name

Example:

systemctl status nginx

journalctl -u nginx

Troubleshooting approach:

Check service status
Review logs
Identify the error
Correct the issue
Restart the service
Log Storage

The systemd journal can store logs:

Temporary:

/run/log/journal

Persistent:

/var/log/journal

Check journal storage:

journalctl --disk-usage
Managing Journal Size

View journal usage:

journalctl --disk-usage

Clean old logs:

sudo journalctl --vacuum-time=7d

This removes logs older than 7 days.

  • Search for available software
  • Install applications
  • Verify installed packages
  • Remove software
  • Understand package dependencies
  • Troubleshoot installation problems

docs.title: Finding Available Software
docs.text:
Before installing software, administrators normally search available packages.

Package managers search configured software repositories.

docs.title: Searching Packages with APT
docs.text:
Debian and Ubuntu systems use apt.

Search for a package:

apt search package_name

Example:

apt search nginx

Example output:

nginx - high performance web server
nginx-common - small, powerful web server

The search results provide:

  • Package name
  • Description
  • Available version

docs.title: Searching Packages with DNF
docs.text:
Red Hat-based systems use dnf.

Search for a package:

dnf search package_name

Example:

dnf search nginx

docs.title: Installing Software
docs.text: Package managers download software from repositories and install all required dependencies.

docs.title: Installing Software with APT
docs.text:
Install a package:

sudo apt install package_name

Example:

sudo apt install nginx

APT will:

  1. Check package availability
  2. Download required files
  3. Install dependencies
  4. Configure the application
  5. Register the package

docs.title: Installing Software with DNF
docs.text:
Install a package:

sudo dnf install package_name

Example:

sudo dnf install nginx

docs.title: Understanding Dependencies
docs.text:
Applications often require additional software to run.

Example:

nginx

requires:

├── libraries
├── configuration files
└── supporting packages

The package manager automatically identifies and installs dependencies.

docs.title: Viewing Package Information
docs.text: Before installing software, administrators may want more information.

docs.title: APT Package Information
docs.text:
View package details:

apt show package_name

Example:

apt show nginx

Information displayed:

  • Package version
  • Description
  • Dependencies
  • Package size
  • Repository source

docs.title: DNF Package Information
docs.text:
View package details:

dnf info package_name

Example:

dnf info nginx

docs.title: Checking Installed Software
docs.text: Administrators often need to confirm whether software is installed.

docs.title: Debian / Ubuntu
docs.text:
List installed packages:

dpkg -l

Search installed packages:

dpkg -l | grep package_name

Example:

dpkg -l | grep nginx

docs.title: Red Hat / Rocky Linux
docs.text:
List installed packages:

rpm -qa

Search installed packages:

rpm -qa | grep package_name

docs.title: Removing Software
docs.text: Software can be removed when it is no longer required.

docs.title: Removing Packages with APT
docs.text:
Remove a package:

sudo apt remove package_name

Example:

sudo apt remove nginx

Remove package and configuration files:

sudo apt purge package_name

Example:

sudo apt purge nginx

docs.title: Removing Packages with DNF
docs.text:
Remove a package:

sudo dnf remove package_name

Example:

sudo dnf remove nginx

docs.title: Cleaning Unused Packages
docs.text:
Over time, systems may contain unused dependencies.

Debian / Ubuntu:

sudo apt autoremove

This removes packages no longer required.

docs.title: Installing Local Package Files
docs.text:
Sometimes software is provided as a downloaded package file.

Examples:

application.deb
application.rpm

docs.title: Installing DEB Files
docs.text:
Using dpkg:

sudo dpkg -i package.deb

If dependencies are missing:

sudo apt install -f

docs.title: Installing RPM Files
docs.text:
Using rpm:

sudo rpm -ivh package.rpm

docs.title: Package Installation Troubleshooting
docs.text: Common installation problems include:

docs.title: Package Not Found
docs.text:
Example:

Unable to locate package

Possible causes:

  • Repository information is outdated
  • Package name is incorrect
  • Repository is unavailable

Solution:

sudo apt update

docs.title: Dependency Problems
docs.text:
Example:

Unmet dependencies

Solution:

sudo apt --fix-broken install

docs.title: Permission Errors
docs.text:
Example:

Permission denied

Solution:

Use administrative privileges:

sudo command

apt search nginx

Record:

Package found:
Description:

docs.text:

apt show nginx

Record:

Version:
Dependencies:

docs.title: Task 3 - Install Software
docs.text:
Install nginx:

sudo apt install nginx

Verify:

dpkg -l | grep nginx

docs.title: Task 4 - Remove Software
docs.text:
Remove nginx:

sudo apt remove nginx

Confirm:

dpkg -l | grep nginx

docs.title: Lesson 03 - Updating Linux Systems
docs.text:
You will learn:

  • Updating package information
  • Installing system updates
  • Security updates
  • Upgrade strategies
  • Maintenance practices

docs.title: Lesson 03 - Updating Linux Systems
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 05 – Package Management - Lesson 01 – Understanding Linux Package Managers - Lesson 02 – Installing Software Packages

Difficulty: Beginner to Intermediate

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Keeping Linux systems updated is an essential administration task.

Updates provide:

  • Security fixes
  • Bug fixes
  • Performance improvements
  • New features
  • Software stability improvements

Linux administrators must understand how to safely update systems while reducing the risk of service disruption.

This lesson covers updating Linux systems using common package management tools.

docs.title: Why Update Linux Systems?
docs.text:
Regular updates help maintain:

  • System security
  • Application reliability
  • Hardware compatibility
  • Performance
  • Vendor support

Unpatched systems may contain:

  • Security vulnerabilities
  • Software bugs
  • Outdated components
  • Unsupported versions

docs.title: Package Updates vs Distribution Upgrades
docs.text: There are different types of updates.

docs.title: Package Update
docs.text:
Updates installed software packages.

Example:

nginx version 1.24
        |
        v
nginx version 1.26

Usually includes:

  • Bug fixes
  • Security patches
  • Minor improvements

docs.title: Distribution Upgrade
docs.text:
Moves the operating system to a newer release.

Example:

Ubuntu 24.04 LTS

        |

Ubuntu 26.04 LTS

Distribution upgrades require more planning because they can affect:

  • Applications
  • Configuration files
  • Services
  • Hardware compatibility

docs.title: Updating Debian and Ubuntu Systems
docs.text:
Debian-based systems use:

apt

The update process normally has two stages:

  1. Refresh package information
  2. Install available updates

docs.title: Updating Package Information
docs.text:
Run:

sudo apt update

This downloads the latest package information from repositories.

Example:

Hit:1 http://archive.ubuntu.com
Get:2 security updates
Reading package lists...

This does not install updates.

It only checks what updates are available.

docs.title: Installing Updates
docs.text:
Install available updates:

sudo apt upgrade

The system will:

  • Download updated packages
  • Install new versions
  • Keep existing configuration

Example:

20 packages can be upgraded.

docs.title: Full Upgrade
docs.text:
For more complex updates:

sudo apt full-upgrade

This allows:

  • Installing new dependencies
  • Removing conflicting packages
  • Updating core components

Use carefully on production systems.

docs.title: Checking Available Updates
docs.text:
View available upgrades:

apt list --upgradable

Example:

nginx
openssl
curl

docs.title: Removing Unused Packages After Updates
docs.text:
Old dependencies may no longer be required.

Remove unused packages:

sudo apt autoremove

Clean downloaded package files:

sudo apt clean

docs.title: Updating Red Hat and Rocky Linux Systems
docs.text:
Red Hat-based systems use:

dnf

docs.title: Checking Available Updates
docs.text:
Run:

dnf check-update

This checks repositories for available updates.

docs.title: Installing Updates
docs.text:
Update the system:

sudo dnf upgrade

or:

sudo dnf update

Both commands update installed packages.

docs.title: Viewing Update History
docs.text: Package managers keep records of changes.

docs.title: Debian / Ubuntu
docs.text:
View package logs:

cat /var/log/apt/history.log

docs.title: Red Hat / Rocky Linux
docs.text:
View DNF history:

dnf history

Example:

ID   Command
1    Install nginx
2    Upgrade packages

docs.title: Security Updates
docs.text:
Security updates are especially important.

They fix vulnerabilities in:

  • Operating system components
  • Libraries
  • Applications
  • Services

docs.title: Checking Security Updates on Ubuntu
docs.text:
Install update tools:

sudo apt install unattended-upgrades

Enable automatic security updates:

sudo dpkg-reconfigure unattended-upgrades

docs.title: Update Planning
docs.text: Before updating production systems:

docs.title: Check Current State
docs.text:
Review:

  • Running services
  • Disk space
  • System health
  • Current versions

Commands:

systemctl --failed

df -h

docs.title: Backup Important Data
docs.text:
Before major updates:

  • Backup configuration files
  • Backup application data
  • Confirm recovery procedures

docs.title: Test Updates
docs.text:
Where possible:

  1. Test updates in development
  2. Review changes
  3. Schedule maintenance window
  4. Apply updates

docs.title: Reboot Requirements
docs.text:
Some updates require a reboot.

Common examples:

  • Kernel updates
  • Hardware drivers
  • Core system libraries

Check if reboot is required:

ls /var/run/reboot-required

docs.title: Repository Errors
docs.text:
Example:

Failed to fetch package information

Possible causes:

  • Network problems
  • Repository unavailable
  • Incorrect configuration

docs.title: Locked Package Database
docs.text:
Example:

Could not get lock

Another package process may be running.

Check:

ps aux | grep apt

docs.title: Broken Packages
docs.text:
Repair:

sudo apt --fix-broken install

docs.title: Task 1 - Check Available Updates
docs.text:
Run:

sudo apt update

Then:

apt list --upgradable

Record:

Available updates:

docs.title: Task 2 - Update Installed Packages
docs.text:
Run:

sudo apt upgrade

Record:

Packages updated:

docs.title: Task 3 - Review Update History
docs.text:
Run:

cat /var/log/apt/history.log

Identify:

  • Installed packages
  • Updated packages
  • Dates

docs.title: Task 4 - Check System Health
docs.text:
Run:

systemctl --failed

and:

df -h

Record:

Failed services:

Disk usage:

docs.title: Knowledge Check
docs.text:
1. What command refreshes APT package information?
  2. What command installs available Ubuntu updates?
  3. What is the difference between a package update and distribution upgrade?
  4. Why are security updates important?
  5. What command shows available Ubuntu updates?
  6. What command shows DNF update history?
  7. Why should updates be tested before production systems?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson you learned:

✓ Why Linux systems need regular updates ✓ The difference between updates and upgrades ✓ How to update Debian and Ubuntu systems ✓ How to update Red Hat-based systems ✓ How to review update history ✓ How to troubleshoot update problems ✓ How administrators safely manage system updates

docs.title: Lesson 04 - Software Repositories
docs.text:
You will learn:

  • How Linux repositories work
  • Repository configuration
  • Package sources
  • Trusted software sources
  • Managing repository settings

docs.title: Lesson 04 - Software Repositories
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 05 – Package Management - Lesson 01 – Understanding Linux Package Managers - Lesson 02 – Installing Software Packages - Lesson 03 – Updating Linux Systems

Difficulty: Beginner to Intermediate

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Linux package managers rely on software repositories to locate and download software packages.

Repositories provide a controlled source of software that has been tested and packaged for a specific Linux distribution.

Understanding repositories is important for Linux administrators because they control:

  • Where software is downloaded from
  • Which software versions are available
  • How systems receive updates
  • Which software sources are trusted

docs.title: What is a Software Repository?
docs.text:
A software repository is a server location that stores software packages and related information.

A repository contains:

  • Software packages
  • Package versions
  • Dependency information
  • Security updates
  • Package metadata

Example:

Linux System

      |
      |
 Package Manager

      |
      |
 Software Repository

      |
      |
 Package Download

docs.title: Why Use Repositories?
docs.text: Repositories provide several benefits:

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Packages are usually:

  • Signed by trusted providers
  • Verified before installation
  • Maintained with security updates

docs.title: Dependency Management
docs.text:
Repositories provide required supporting software.

Example:

Application

requires:

Library A
Library B
Configuration Package

The package manager automatically downloads dependencies.

docs.title: Software Updates
docs.text:
Repositories allow administrators to:

  • Receive security fixes
  • Update applications
  • Maintain supported versions

docs.title: Repository Components
docs.text: A repository normally contains:

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
The actual software files.

Example:

nginx.deb

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
Information about packages:

  • Name
  • Version
  • Description
  • Dependencies
  • Available updates

docs.title: Digital Signatures
docs.text:
Used to verify:

  • Package authenticity
  • Repository trust
  • Package integrity

docs.title: Debian and Ubuntu Repositories
docs.text:
Debian-based systems use:

apt

Repository configuration is stored in:

/etc/apt/sources.list

Additional repositories:

/etc/apt/sources.list.d/

docs.title: Viewing APT Repository Configuration
docs.text:
View configured repositories:

cat /etc/apt/sources.list

Example:

deb http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu noble main

docs.title: Updating Repository Information
docs.text:
After changing repository settings:

Run:

sudo apt update

This downloads the latest repository information.

docs.title: APT Repository Format
docs.text:
A repository entry contains several parts:

Example:

deb http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu noble main

Breakdown:

Section Meaning deb Package type URL Repository location noble Distribution release main Repository component

docs.title: Repository Components in Ubuntu
docs.text:
Ubuntu repositories are divided into sections.

Common components:

Component Purpose main Officially supported software universe Community maintained software restricted Proprietary drivers multiverse Software with licensing restrictions

docs.title: Adding Software Repositories
docs.text:
Sometimes software is not available in the default repositories.

Administrators may add additional repositories.

Examples:

  • Vendor repositories
  • Internal company repositories
  • Third-party software sources

Before adding repositories, consider:

  • Is the source trusted?
  • Is it maintained?
  • Does it provide security updates?
  • Is it required?

docs.title: Personal Package Archives (PPA)
docs.text:
Ubuntu supports additional repositories called:

PPA - Personal Package Archive

Example:

sudo add-apt-repository ppa:name/repository

Update package information:

sudo apt update

docs.title: Removing Repositories
docs.text:
Repositories can be removed when no longer required.

Example:

sudo add-apt-repository --remove ppa:name/repository

Then update:

sudo apt update

docs.title: Red Hat and Rocky Linux Repositories
docs.text:
Red Hat-based systems use:

dnf

Repository configuration is stored in:

/etc/yum.repos.d/

docs.title: Viewing DNF Repositories
docs.text:
List enabled repositories:

dnf repolist

Example:

repo id
baseos
appstream

docs.title: Repository Configuration Files
docs.text:
Example:

/etc/yum.repos.d/example.repo

A repository file contains:

  • Repository name
  • Repository URL
  • Enabled status
  • Security settings

docs.title: Trusted Software Sources
docs.text:
Linux administrators should evaluate software sources carefully.

Good sources include:

  • Official distribution repositories
  • Vendor maintained repositories
  • Internal company repositories

Avoid:

  • Unknown download sites
  • Unmaintained repositories
  • Unsupported packages

docs.title: Repository Not Found
docs.text:
Example:

Unable to locate package

Possible causes:

  • Repository missing
  • Incorrect repository configuration
  • Package unavailable

Check:

apt update

docs.title: Repository Key Errors
docs.text:
Example:

NO_PUBKEY

Possible cause:

  • Missing signing key

Solution:

  • Install the correct trusted key
  • Verify the repository source

docs.title: Failed Repository Connection
docs.text:
Possible causes:

  • Network issues
  • Incorrect URL
  • Repository outage

Test:

ping repository-server

docs.title: Task 1 - View APT Repositories
docs.text:
Run:

cat /etc/apt/sources.list

Record:

Repository sources:

docs.title: Task 2 - Update Repository Information
docs.text:
Run:

sudo apt update

Record:

Successful repositories:

docs.title: Task 3 - View Available Software
docs.text:
Search for nginx:

apt search nginx

Record:

Repository providing package:

docs.title: Task 4 - View DNF Repositories (Optional)
docs.text:
On Red Hat-based systems:

dnf repolist

Record:

Enabled repositories:

docs.text:

  2. Why do Linux systems use repositories?
  3. Where are Ubuntu repository settings stored?
  4. What command refreshes APT repository information?
  5. What command lists DNF repositories?
  6. Why should administrators only use trusted repositories?
  7. What is a PPA?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson you learned:

✓ What Linux software repositories are ✓ How package managers use repositories ✓ How Debian and Ubuntu repositories work ✓ How Red Hat repositories work ✓ How to view repository configuration ✓ How to troubleshoot repository problems ✓ Why trusted software sources are important

Recommended distributions:

Run:

cat /etc/os-release

Record:

Distribution:

Version:

Package manager:

Search for nginx:

apt search nginx

Red Hat / Rocky:

Package found:

Description:

apt show nginx

Package version:

Dependencies:

Description:

docs.text:
Install a software package.

Install nginx:

Debian / Ubuntu:

sudo apt install nginx

Red Hat / Rocky:

Verify installation:

Debian / Ubuntu:

dpkg -l | grep nginx

Red Hat / Rocky:

rpm -qa | grep nginx

Record:

Installation successful:

Version installed:

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Understand installed software management.

Debian / Ubuntu:

dpkg -l

Red Hat / Rocky:

rpm -qa

Find:

  • Installed applications
  • Package versions
  • Package status

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Safely remove installed software.

Remove nginx:

Debian / Ubuntu:

sudo apt remove nginx

Red Hat / Rocky:

sudo dnf remove nginx

Verify removal:

dpkg -l | grep nginx

or:

rpm -qa | grep nginx

Record:

Package removed:

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Refresh available package information.

Debian / Ubuntu:

sudo apt update

Review:

  • Repository connections
  • Available updates
  • Package information

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Apply available updates.

Debian / Ubuntu:

sudo apt upgrade

Red Hat / Rocky:

sudo dnf upgrade

Record:

Packages updated:

Reboot required:

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Investigate package changes.

Debian / Ubuntu:

cat /var/log/apt/history.log

Red Hat / Rocky:

dnf history

Identify:

  • Installed packages
  • Removed packages
  • Updates performed

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Review configured software sources.

Debian / Ubuntu:

cat /etc/apt/sources.list

Red Hat / Rocky:

dnf repolist

Record:

Configured repositories:

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
A user reports:

"The application cannot be installed because the package cannot be found."

Investigate the issue.

docs.text:

sudo apt update

Check for:

  • Repository errors

docs.text:
Example:

apt search application_name

Confirm:

  • Package name

docs.text:
Check for running package processes:

ps aux | grep apt

docs.text:
If required:

sudo apt --fix-broken install

docs.text:

docs.title: Module 06 - Networking
docs.text:

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Networking is a core Linux administration skill.

Linux systems rarely operate in isolation. Servers, applications, cloud platforms, containers, and users all depend on reliable network communication.

A Linux administrator needs to understand how systems communicate, how networks are configured, and how to troubleshoot connectivity problems.

This module introduces the networking concepts and practical tools required to support Linux systems in modern infrastructure environments.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this module you will understand:

  • How computer networks operate
  • How Linux systems communicate across networks
  • The role of network interfaces
  • MAC addresses and IP addresses
  • IPv4 addressing and subnetting
  • Routing and default gateways
  • DNS and name resolution
  • Network troubleshooting techniques
  • Linux networking commands and tools

  • Troubleshooting connectivity issues
  • Validating DNS resolution
  • Checking network services
  • Documenting technical investigations

docs.title: Module 07 - Storage
docs.text:
You will learn:

  • Disk management
  • Linux filesystems
  • Mounting storage
  • Partitioning
  • Logical Volume Management (LVM)
  • Storage troubleshooting

docs.title: Lesson 01 - Networking Fundamentals
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 01 – Command Line Fundamentals

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Networking is a fundamental skill for Linux administrators, cloud engineers, and DevOps professionals.

Linux systems rely heavily on networking to communicate with other systems, access services, transfer data, and support applications.

Understanding networking fundamentals allows administrators to:

  • Understand how systems communicate
  • Troubleshoot connectivity issues
  • Configure Linux network settings
  • Support servers and cloud environments
  • Work with containers and distributed systems

This lesson introduces the basic concepts required before learning IP addressing, subnetting, and network troubleshooting.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this lesson you will understand:

  • What a network is
  • How devices communicate
  • The purpose of IP addresses
  • The role of MAC addresses
  • The difference between local and remote networks
  • The purpose of gateways
  • How DNS works
  • What ports and protocols are
  • Basic Linux networking commands

docs.title: What Is a Network?
docs.text:
A network is a collection of connected devices that can communicate and exchange information.

Examples of networked devices:

  • Computers
  • Servers
  • Routers
  • Switches
  • Mobile devices
  • IoT devices
  • Cloud infrastructure

A simple network:

Computer
    |
 Switch
    |
 Router
    |
 Internet

Networks allow systems to share:

  • Data
  • Applications
  • Services
  • Internet access
  • Storage

docs.title: Types of Networks
docs.text: Networks can be classified by their size and purpose.

docs.title: Local Area Network (LAN)
docs.text:
A Local Area Network connects devices within a small geographical area.

Examples:

  • Home networks
  • Office networks
  • Data centre networks

Example:

Laptop
   |
 Switch
   |
Server

A LAN allows devices to communicate directly with each other.

docs.title: Wide Area Network (WAN)
docs.text:
A Wide Area Network connects networks across larger distances.

Examples:

  • Company sites connected together
  • Internet connections
  • Cloud networks

Example:

Office Network

      |
      |

   Internet

      |
      |

 Cloud Network

The internet is the largest example of a WAN.

docs.title: How Devices Communicate
docs.text:
Devices communicate using agreed rules called protocols.

Communication requires:

  • A source device
  • A destination device
  • An addressing system
  • A communication protocol

Example:

Linux Server

192.168.1.50

        |
        |
      Network
        |
        |

Database Server

192.168.1.100

The devices use addresses to identify where data should be sent.

docs.title: IP Addresses
docs.text:
An IP address identifies a device on a network.

Example:

192.168.1.50

IP addresses allow systems to:

  • Send data to the correct device
  • Identify network locations
  • Communicate across networks

IPv4 addresses contain four numbers separated by periods.

Example:

192 . 168 . 1 . 50

Each section is called an octet.

Each octet has a range of:

0 - 255

IP addressing and subnetting are covered in detail in:

Lesson 02 - IP Addressing and Subnetting

docs.title: MAC Addresses
docs.text:
A MAC address identifies a physical network interface.

Example:

00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E

MAC addresses:

  • Are assigned to network hardware
  • Are used by switches
  • Operate at Layer 2 of the OSI model

Example:

Computer

MAC Address

      |

Network Switch

      |

Router

A switch uses MAC addresses to deliver traffic inside a local network.

docs.title: Routers and Default Gateways
docs.text:
A router connects different networks together.

Example:

Home Network

192.168.1.0/24

        |

     Router

        |

     Internet

The router acts as the default gateway.

The default gateway is where a device sends traffic that is not on the local network.

Example:

Linux Server

192.168.1.50


Default Gateway

192.168.1.1

Traffic to another local device stays on the LAN.

Traffic to the internet goes through the gateway.

docs.title: DNS
docs.text:
DNS stands for Domain Name System.

DNS converts human-readable names into IP addresses.

Humans use:

www.example.com

Computers use:

93.184.216.34

DNS allows users and applications to access services without remembering IP addresses.

Common DNS servers:

Provider Address Google DNS 8.8.8.8 Cloudflare DNS 1.1.1.1

docs.title: Ports and Services
docs.text:
A server can run multiple network services at the same time.

Ports identify individual services.

Example:

192.168.1.50:22

This means:

  • IP address: 192.168.1.50
  • Port: 22

Common ports:

Port Protocol Purpose 22 SSH Remote administration 53 DNS Name resolution 80 HTTP Web traffic 443 HTTPS Secure web traffic 3306 MySQL Database 5432 PostgreSQL Database

docs.title: Network Protocols
docs.text: Protocols define how devices communicate.

docs.title: TCP
docs.text:
Transmission Control Protocol.

TCP provides:

  • Reliable communication
  • Error checking
  • Ordered delivery
  • Connection management

Common TCP services:

  • SSH
  • HTTPS
  • Databases

docs.title: UDP
docs.text:
User Datagram Protocol.

UDP provides:

  • Faster communication
  • Lower overhead
  • No guaranteed delivery

Common UDP services:

  • DNS queries
  • Video streaming
  • Voice communication

docs.title: Linux Networking Commands
docs.text: Linux provides several commands for viewing and troubleshooting networking.

docs.title: View Network Interfaces
docs.text:
The ip address command displays network interfaces and IP addresses.

ip address

Example output:

eth0

inet 192.168.1.50/24

docs.title: View Routing Information
docs.text:
The routing table shows where traffic is sent.

ip route

Example:

default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0

docs.title: Test Connectivity
docs.text:
The ping command tests whether another device can be reached.

ping 8.8.8.8

Example uses:

  • Testing network connectivity
  • Checking if a host responds

docs.title: DNS Lookup
docs.text:
The nslookup command checks DNS resolution.

nslookup google.com

Example:

Name:

google.com

Address:

142.250.x.x

docs.title: View Network Connections
docs.text:
The ss command shows network sockets and listening services.

ss -tulnp

This can show:

  • Open ports
  • Running network services
  • Listening applications

docs.title: Practical Lab
docs.text:
The objective of this lab is to explore basic networking information on a Linux system.

Tasks:

  • Identify network interfaces
  • View IP addresses
  • View routing information
  • Test connectivity
  • Check network services

docs.title: Lab 1 - View Network Interfaces
docs.text:
Run:

ip address

Identify:

  • Network interface name
  • IP address
  • MAC address

docs.title: Lab 2 - View Routing Information
docs.text:
Run:

ip route

Identify:

  • Default gateway
  • Network routes
  • Active interface

docs.title: Lab 3 - Test Connectivity
docs.text:
Test internet connectivity:

ping 8.8.8.8

Test DNS:

ping google.com

docs.title: Lab 4 - View Network Services
docs.text:
Run:

ss -tulnp

Identify:

  • Listening services
  • Open ports
  • Running applications

docs.title: Lab Challenge
docs.text:
A Linux server cannot access a website.

Describe the troubleshooting process:

  1. Check the network interface
  2. Confirm the IP address
  3. Check the default gateway
  4. Test network connectivity
  5. Test DNS resolution
  6. Check listening services
  7. Check firewall rules

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson you learned:

  • What networks are
  • How devices communicate
  • The purpose of IP addresses
  • The role of MAC addresses
  • How routers and gateways work
  • How DNS translates names into addresses
  • How ports identify services
  • Basic Linux networking commands

The next lesson covers:

Lesson 02 - IP Addressing and Subnetting

docs.title: Lesson 02 - IP Addressing and Subnetting
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 06 – Networking Fundamentals

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
IP addressing is a fundamental networking skill for Linux administrators.

Every device connected to a network requires an address so that systems can communicate with each other.

Understanding IP addressing allows administrators to:

  • Identify devices on a network
  • Understand network ranges
  • Configure Linux network settings
  • Troubleshoot connectivity problems
  • Support cloud and enterprise environments

This lesson introduces IPv4 addressing, subnet masks, CIDR notation, and network gateways.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this lesson you will understand:

  • What an IP address is
  • How IPv4 addresses are structured
  • The difference between private and public addresses
  • The purpose of subnet masks
  • How CIDR notation works
  • How networks and hosts are identified
  • The purpose of default gateways
  • How to view IP configuration on Linux

docs.title: What Is an IP Address?
docs.text:
An IP address is a unique identifier assigned to a device on a network.

IP addresses allow systems to:

  • Communicate with other devices
  • Send and receive network traffic
  • Access services
  • Connect to other networks

Example:

192.168.1.50

An IPv4 address contains four numbers separated by periods.

Example:

192 . 168 . 1 . 50

Each section is called an octet.

Each octet has a range of:

0 - 255

docs.title: IPv4 Address Structure
docs.text:
An IPv4 address contains two sections:

  • Network portion
  • Host portion

Example:

192.168.1.50/24

The /24 represents the subnet size.

The address contains:

Network:
192.168.1.0

Host:
50

The network portion identifies the network.

The host portion identifies the individual device.

docs.title: Private IP Addresses
docs.text:
Private IP addresses are used inside internal networks.

They are not directly accessible from the internet.

Common private address ranges:

Range Usage 10.0.0.0/8 Large private networks 172.16.0.0/12 Medium private networks 192.168.0.0/16 Home and small business networks

Examples:

192.168.1.50

10.0.0.25

172.16.5.10

Common environments using private addresses:

  • Home networks
  • Enterprise networks
  • Cloud virtual networks
  • Container networks

docs.title: Public IP Addresses
docs.text:
Public IP addresses are used for communication across the internet.

Examples:

8.8.8.8

1.1.1.1

Public IP addresses are used by:

  • Websites
  • Public cloud services
  • Internet-facing applications

Internet Service Providers assign public addresses to customers.

docs.title: Static and Dynamic IP Addresses
docs.text: IP addresses can be assigned in two ways.

docs.title: Static IP Address
docs.text:
A static IP address is manually configured.

Common uses:

  • Servers
  • Network equipment
  • Infrastructure services

Example:

Linux Server

192.168.1.50

Advantages:

  • Address remains consistent
  • Easier administration
  • Suitable for services

docs.title: Dynamic IP Address
docs.text:
A dynamic IP address is automatically assigned using DHCP.

Common uses:

  • Workstations
  • Laptops
  • Mobile devices

Example:

Laptop

192.168.1.120

Advantages:

  • Automatic configuration
  • Easier management

docs.title: Subnet Masks
docs.text:
A subnet mask determines which part of an IP address identifies the network and which part identifies the host.

Example:

IP Address:

192.168.1.50


Subnet Mask:

255.255.255.0

CIDR notation:

192.168.1.50/24

The /24 means:

  • 24 bits identify the network
  • 8 bits identify hosts

docs.title: Common CIDR Notation
docs.text: CIDR Subnet Mask Available Hosts /24 255.255.255.0 254 /16 255.255.0.0 65,534 /8 255.0.0.0 16 million

docs.title: Network Address
docs.text:
The network address identifies the network itself.

Example:

192.168.1.0/24

Network address:

192.168.1.0

This address cannot be assigned to a device.

docs.title: Broadcast Address
docs.text:
The broadcast address is used to communicate with all devices on the network.

Example:

192.168.1.255

This address is reserved for network broadcasts.

docs.title: Default Gateway
docs.text:
A default gateway allows devices to communicate with other networks.

Usually this is a router.

Example:

Linux Server

192.168.1.50

        |
        |

Router

192.168.1.1

        |
        |

Internet

The Linux system sends traffic outside its local network through the default gateway.

docs.title: Viewing Network Configuration on Linux
docs.text:
Display IP address information:

ip address

Example:

eth0

inet 192.168.1.50/24

View routing information:

ip route

Example:

default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0

docs.title: Practical Lab
docs.text:
The objective of this lab is to identify and understand IP addressing on a Linux system.

Tasks include:

  • Identify IP addresses
  • Identify network information
  • Understand subnet sizes
  • Identify default gateways

docs.title: Lab 1 - View IP Address Information
docs.text:
Run:

ip address

Identify:

  • Network interface
  • IP address
  • MAC address
  • CIDR prefix

Example:

192.168.1.50/24

docs.title: Lab 2 - View Routing Information
docs.text:
Run:

ip route

Identify:

  • Default gateway
  • Network routes
  • Active interface

docs.title: Lab 3 - Calculate Network Information
docs.text:
Using:

192.168.1.50/24

Identify:

Network:

192.168.1.0

Broadcast:

192.168.1.255

Available hosts:

192.168.1.1 - 192.168.1.254

docs.title: Lab Challenge
docs.text:
A Linux server has the following configuration:

IP Address:

192.168.10.25/24


Gateway:

192.168.10.1

Answer:

  1. What is the network address?
  2. What is the broadcast address?
  3. Can the server communicate with:
192.168.10.50
  1. Can the server communicate with:
192.168.20.50

Explain why.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson you learned:

  • How IPv4 addresses work
  • How private and public addresses differ
  • How subnet masks define networks
  • How CIDR notation works
  • How default gateways provide external connectivity
  • How to view Linux network configuration

IP addressing knowledge is essential for Linux administration, cloud platforms, containers, and enterprise networking.

docs.title: Lesson 03 - Network Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 06 Lesson 01 – Networking Fundamentals - Module 06 Lesson 02 – IP Addressing and Subnetting

Difficulty: Beginner to Intermediate

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Network troubleshooting is an essential skill for Linux administrators.

When users report connectivity problems, administrators need a structured approach to identify the cause and resolve the issue.

Network problems can occur at different layers:

  • Network interface
  • IP configuration
  • Routing
  • DNS resolution
  • Firewall rules
  • Application services

This lesson introduces a practical troubleshooting methodology and the Linux tools used to diagnose network problems.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this lesson you will understand:

  • How to troubleshoot Linux network problems
  • How to check network interfaces
  • How to verify IP configuration
  • How to analyse routing information
  • How to test connectivity
  • How DNS affects network communication
  • How to identify network services
  • How to collect troubleshooting evidence

docs.title: A Structured Troubleshooting Approach
docs.text:
Network troubleshooting should follow a logical process.

A common approach:

Identify Problem
        |
        v
Check Interface
        |
        v
Verify IP Configuration
        |
        v
Check Routing
        |
        v
Test Connectivity
        |
        v
Check DNS
        |
        v
Check Services
        |
        v
Document Resolution

Always collect evidence before making changes.

docs.title: Step 1 - Check Network Interfaces
docs.text:
The first step is confirming that the Linux system has an active network connection.

Use:

ip address

Example:

eth0

state UP

inet 192.168.1.50/24

Check:

  • Interface exists
  • Interface is enabled
  • IP address is assigned
  • Correct network is configured

docs.title: Network Interface Status
docs.text:
View interface status:

ip link

Example:

eth0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP>

Common states:

State Meaning UP Interface active DOWN Interface disabled UNKNOWN Status unavailable

docs.title: Step 2 - Verify IP Configuration
docs.text:
A system requires a valid IP address to communicate.

View configuration:

ip address

Check:

  • IP address
  • Subnet prefix
  • Network interface

Example:

192.168.1.50/24

Common problems:

  • Missing IP address
  • Incorrect subnet
  • Wrong interface configuration

docs.title: Step 3 - Check Routing
docs.text:
Routing determines where network traffic is sent.

View routes:

ip route

Example:

default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0

This shows:

  • Default gateway
  • Network route
  • Active interface

Routing problems can cause:

  • Internet access failures
  • Remote connection failures
  • Application communication issues

docs.title: Step 4 - Test Connectivity
docs.text:
The ping command tests network communication.

Test a local device:

ping 192.168.1.1

Test external connectivity:

ping 8.8.8.8

Example output:

64 bytes from 8.8.8.8:
time=12 ms

Successful responses indicate:

  • Network path exists
  • Device is reachable

docs.title: Understanding Ping Results
docs.text:
Successful response:

64 bytes from 8.8.8.8:
time=12 ms

Indicates:

  • Host responded
  • Network communication works

Packet loss example:

100% packet loss

Possible causes:

  • Network failure
  • Incorrect routing
  • Firewall blocking traffic
  • Remote host unavailable

docs.title: Step 5 - Troubleshoot DNS
docs.text:
A system may have network connectivity but still fail to access services if DNS is not working.

DNS converts names into IP addresses.

Example:

google.com

        |

        v

142.250.x.x

Check DNS resolution:

nslookup google.com

or:

dig google.com

docs.title: DNS Configuration
docs.text:
View configured DNS servers:

cat /etc/resolv.conf

Example:

nameserver 192.168.1.1

Check:

  • DNS server availability
  • Correct DNS configuration
  • Name resolution success

docs.title: Step 6 - Check Listening Services
docs.text:
Applications provide services through network ports.

View listening services:

ss -tuln

Example:

LISTEN 0.0.0.0:22

This indicates:

  • SSH service
  • Port 22 listening

docs.title: Common Network Ports
docs.text: Port Service 22 SSH 53 DNS 80 HTTP 443 HTTPS 3306 MySQL 5432 PostgreSQL

docs.title: Step 7 - Check Firewall Configuration
docs.text:
Firewalls control network traffic.

Common Linux firewall technologies:

  • nftables
  • iptables
  • ufw
  • firewalld

Check firewall status:

sudo ufw status

Review nftables rules:

sudo nft list ruleset

Firewall problems can cause:

  • Blocked connections
  • Unreachable services
  • Failed remote access

docs.title: Useful Network Troubleshooting Commands
docs.text: Command Purpose ip address View interfaces and addresses ip route View routing information ping Test connectivity traceroute Show network path nslookup Test DNS dig Detailed DNS queries ss View listening services curl Test application connectivity

docs.title: Practical Lab
docs.text:
The objective of this lab is to troubleshoot common Linux network issues.

Tasks include:

  • Checking network interfaces
  • Reviewing IP configuration
  • Testing connectivity
  • Checking DNS
  • Identifying services

docs.title: Lab 1 - Check Network Interfaces
docs.text:
Run:

ip link

Record:

  • Available interfaces
  • Interface status

docs.title: Lab 2 - Check IP Configuration
docs.text:
Run:

ip address

Record:

  • IP address
  • Subnet
  • Interface name

docs.title: Lab 3 - Check Routing
docs.text:
Run:

ip route

Identify:

  • Default gateway
  • Network routes

docs.title: Lab 4 - Test Connectivity
docs.text:
Test the gateway:

ping <gateway-address>

Test internet connectivity:

ping 8.8.8.8

Record:

  • Success or failure
  • Packet loss
  • Response time

docs.title: Lab 5 - Test DNS
docs.text:
Run:

nslookup google.com

Identify:

  • DNS server
  • Returned IP address

docs.title: Lab 6 - Check Running Services
docs.text:
Run:

ss -tuln

Identify:

  • Listening ports
  • Available services

docs.title: Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
A user reports:

"The application server cannot connect to the database."

You have been asked to investigate.

docs.title: Investigation Steps
docs.text:
Check network configuration:

ip address

Check routing:

ip route

Test connectivity:

ping database-server

Test DNS:

nslookup database-server

Check services:

ss -tuln

docs.title: Troubleshooting Report
docs.text: Document:

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Describe the reported issue.

docs.title: Evidence Collected
docs.text:
Include:

  • Commands executed
  • Output observed
  • Errors identified

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
Examples:

  • Incorrect IP address
  • Missing route
  • DNS failure
  • Firewall rule
  • Service unavailable

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
Document:

  • Changes made
  • Tests performed
  • Final outcome

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson you learned:

  • A structured approach to network troubleshooting
  • How to inspect Linux network interfaces
  • How to verify IP configuration
  • How to analyse routing
  • How to troubleshoot DNS
  • How to identify network services
  • How to document technical issues

Network troubleshooting is a core Linux administration skill used in enterprise systems, cloud environments, containers, and production platforms.

docs.title: Lesson 04 - Networking Administration Lab
docs.text:
Estimated time: 2–3 hours

Prerequisites: - Module 06 Lesson 01 – Networking Fundamentals - Module 06 Lesson 02 – IP Addressing and Subnetting - Module 06 Lesson 03 – Network Troubleshooting

Difficulty: Beginner to Intermediate

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This practical lab combines the networking concepts covered throughout Module 06.

The objective is to practise the skills required by Linux administrators when configuring, validating, and troubleshooting network connectivity.

You will investigate a Linux system, collect network information, test communication, and document your findings.

docs.title: Lab Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this lab you will be able to:

  • Identify Linux network interfaces
  • Review IP addressing information
  • Understand routing configuration
  • Test network connectivity
  • Troubleshoot DNS resolution
  • Identify running network services
  • Document network troubleshooting activities

docs.title: Lab Environment
docs.text:
You will need:

  • A Linux system
  • Network connectivity
  • Terminal access
  • Basic command-line knowledge

Example environment:

Linux Server

        |
        |

Network Switch

        |
        |

Router

        |
        |

Internet

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Identify the network interfaces available on the Linux system.

Run:

ip link

Example output:

1: lo:
2: eth0:

Record:

  • Interface names
  • Interface status
  • Available network adapters

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Identify the IP addresses assigned to the system.

Run:

ip address

Example:

eth0

inet 192.168.1.50/24

Record:

Item Value Interface IP Address CIDR Prefix MAC Address

docs.title: Task 3 - Identify Network Details
docs.text:
Using the IP address discovered, identify:

Example:

IP Address:

192.168.1.50/24

Network address:

192.168.1.0

Broadcast address:

192.168.1.255

Available host range:

192.168.1.1 - 192.168.1.254

Record your results:

Item Value Network Address Broadcast Address Host Range

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Identify how traffic leaves the local network.

Run:

ip route

Example:

default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0

Record:

Item Value Default Gateway Interface

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Confirm communication with the local gateway.

Run:

ping <gateway-address>

Example:

ping 192.168.1.1

Record:

  • Packets sent
  • Packets received
  • Response time

Example:

Packets transmitted: 4
Packets received: 4
Packet loss: 0%

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Verify access outside the local network.

Run:

ping 8.8.8.8

Record:

  • Successful response
  • Packet loss
  • Latency

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Verify that DNS is working.

Run:

nslookup google.com

Example:

Name:

google.com


Address:

142.x.x.x

Record:

Item Value DNS Server Resolved Address

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Identify services running on the Linux system.

Run:

ss -tuln

Example:

LISTEN 0 128 0.0.0.0:22

Record:

Port Service

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Test communication with a service.

Example HTTP test:

curl http://localhost

Example SSH test:

ssh localhost

Record:

  • Service tested
  • Result
  • Any errors

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
A Linux server cannot access an external website.

You have been asked to investigate.

docs.title: Step 1 - Check Interface
docs.text:
Run:

ip link

Question:

Is the network interface active?

docs.title: Step 2 - Check IP Address
docs.text:
Run:

ip address

Question:

Does the system have a valid IP address?

docs.title: Step 3 - Check Route
docs.text:
Run:

ip route

Question:

Is a default gateway configured?

docs.title: Step 4 - Test Gateway
docs.text:
Run:

ping <gateway-address>

Question:

Can the server communicate locally?

docs.title: Step 5 - Test External IP
docs.text:
Run:

ping 8.8.8.8

Question:

Does external connectivity work?

docs.title: Step 6 - Test DNS
docs.text:
Run:

nslookup google.com

Question:

Can the system resolve names?

docs.title: Module 07 - Storage Management
docs.text:

Prerequisites: - Module 01 – Command Line Fundamentals - Module 02 – Filesystem Fundamentals - Module 06 – Networking Fundamentals

Difficulty: Beginner

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Storage management is a fundamental skill for Linux administrators.

Linux systems rely on storage for:

  • Operating system files
  • Application data
  • User data
  • Logs
  • Databases
  • Virtual machines
  • Container workloads

Understanding how Linux manages storage allows administrators to:

  • Identify disks and devices
  • Create and manage partitions
  • Understand filesystems
  • Mount storage devices
  • Monitor disk usage
  • Troubleshoot storage problems

This module introduces the core storage concepts required for Linux administration, cloud platforms, and DevOps environments.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this module you will understand:

  • How Linux represents storage devices
  • The difference between disks and partitions
  • How filesystems work
  • The purpose of mount points
  • How to view disk usage
  • How to create and manage filesystems
  • How Linux mounts storage automatically
  • How to troubleshoot common storage issues

docs.title: Lesson 01 - Storage Fundamentals
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 01 – Command Line Fundamentals - Module 02 – Filesystem Fundamentals

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Storage management is a fundamental skill for Linux administrators.

Every Linux system requires storage to hold:

  • The operating system
  • Applications
  • Configuration files
  • User data
  • Logs
  • Databases
  • Container data

Understanding how Linux manages storage allows administrators to identify disks, understand storage layouts, and troubleshoot storage problems.

This lesson introduces the basic concepts of Linux storage, including disks, block devices, partitions, and storage layouts.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this lesson you will understand:

  • What storage devices are
  • How Linux represents storage devices
  • The difference between disks and partitions
  • What block devices are
  • The purpose of /dev
  • Common storage technologies
  • The difference between HDD and SSD storage
  • How to identify storage devices on Linux

docs.title: What Is Storage?
docs.text:
Storage is hardware or software used to save data permanently.

Unlike memory (RAM), storage retains data when the system is powered off.

Examples of storage devices:

  • Hard disk drives (HDD)
  • Solid state drives (SSD)
  • USB drives
  • Network storage
  • Cloud storage

A Linux server may use storage for:

  • The operating system
  • Application data
  • Databases
  • Virtual machines
  • Container images

docs.title: Storage Devices in Linux
docs.text:
Linux represents storage devices as files inside the /dev directory.

The /dev directory contains device files that represent hardware.

Example:

/dev/sda

This usually represents the first disk detected by Linux.

Other examples:

/dev/sdb
/dev/nvme0n1
/dev/mmcblk0

docs.title: SATA and SCSI Devices
docs.text:
Traditional disks are usually named:

/dev/sda
/dev/sdb
/dev/sdc

Example:

/dev/sda

First disk in the system

Partitions are numbered:

/dev/sda1
/dev/sda2
/dev/sda3

Example:

/dev/sda

    |
    |
    +-- /dev/sda1
    |
    +-- /dev/sda2

docs.title: NVMe Devices
docs.text:
Modern SSDs often use NVMe naming.

Example:

/dev/nvme0n1

Partitions are shown as:

/dev/nvme0n1p1
/dev/nvme0n1p2

Example:

/dev/nvme0n1

        |
        |

/dev/nvme0n1p1

        |

/dev/nvme0n1p2

docs.title: Block Devices
docs.text:
Linux storage devices are usually block devices.

A block device stores and retrieves data in fixed-size blocks.

Examples:

  • Hard drives
  • SSDs
  • USB storage devices
  • Virtual disks

Linux identifies block devices using the lsblk command.

Example:

lsblk

Example output:

NAME        SIZE TYPE
sda         100G disk
├─sda1       1G part
└─sda2      99G part

This shows:

  • Physical disk
  • Partitions
  • Storage sizes

docs.title: Disks and Partitions
docs.text:
A disk is the physical storage device.

A partition is a logical section of a disk.

Example:

Physical Disk

/dev/sda

        |
        |

Partitions

/dev/sda1
/dev/sda2
/dev/sda3

Partitions allow a single disk to be divided into separate areas.

Common uses:

  • Separate operating system files
  • Separate user data
  • Separate application storage

docs.title: Hard Disk Drive (HDD)
docs.text:
HDDs use spinning magnetic disks.

Advantages:

  • Low cost
  • Large capacities
  • Good for bulk storage

Disadvantages:

  • Slower performance
  • Moving parts
  • Higher power usage

Common uses:

  • File servers
  • Backup storage
  • Archives

docs.title: Solid State Drive (SSD)
docs.text:
SSDs use flash memory.

Advantages:

  • Faster performance
  • No moving parts
  • Lower power usage

Disadvantages:

  • Higher cost per GB
  • Limited write endurance

Common uses:

  • Operating systems
  • Databases
  • Virtual machines
  • Cloud servers

docs.title: Local Storage Layout
docs.text:
A typical Linux system may look like:

Disk

/dev/sda

 |

Partitions

 |

Filesystem

 |

Directories

 |

/data
/home
/var

The filesystem provides the structure used to store files and directories.

docs.title: Viewing Storage Devices on Linux
docs.text: Linux provides several commands to inspect storage.

docs.title: List Block Devices
docs.text:
The lsblk command displays disks and partitions.

lsblk

Example:

NAME        SIZE TYPE
nvme0n1     500G disk
├─nvme0n1p1 512M part
└─nvme0n1p2 499G part

docs.title: Display Disk Information
docs.text:
The fdisk command can display partition information.

sudo fdisk -l

Example:

Disk /dev/sda: 100 GiB

docs.title: Display Filesystem Information
docs.text:
The blkid command shows filesystem details.

blkid

Example:

/dev/sda1: UUID="1234-abcd" TYPE="ext4"

docs.title: Storage Information Workflow
docs.text: A common administrator workflow:

docs.title: Step 1 - Identify Disks
docs.text: lsblk

docs.title: Step 2 - Check Partitions
docs.text: sudo fdisk -l

docs.title: Step 3 - Identify Filesystems

docs.title: Step 4 - Check Usage

Lesson 02 - Partitions and Filesystems

docs.title: Lesson 02 - Partitions and Filesystems
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 07 – Storage Management - Lesson 01 – Storage Fundamentals

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Partitions and filesystems are essential parts of Linux storage management.

A disk provides physical storage, but before Linux can store files on that disk it normally requires:

  • A partition layout
  • A filesystem
  • A mount point

Understanding partitions and filesystems allows administrators to prepare new storage devices, manage server storage, and troubleshoot storage issues.

This lesson introduces partition tables, partition management, filesystem types, and creating filesystems on Linux.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this lesson you will understand:

  • What disk partitions are
  • The difference between MBR and GPT partition tables
  • How Linux identifies partitions
  • Common Linux filesystem types
  • How to create filesystems
  • How to inspect filesystem information
  • How to safely prepare storage devices

docs.title: What Is a Partition?
docs.text:
A partition is a logical section of a physical storage device.

A single disk can contain multiple partitions.

Example:

Physical Disk

/dev/sda

        |
        |

+----------------+
| /dev/sda1      |
| Operating      |
| System         |
+----------------+

+----------------+
| /dev/sda2      |
| Data           |
+----------------+

Partitions allow administrators to separate different types of data.

Common uses:

  • Operating system files
  • User data
  • Application storage
  • Database storage
  • Swap space

docs.title: Partition Tables
docs.text:
Before partitions can be created, a disk requires a partition table.

The partition table stores information about:

  • Partition locations
  • Partition sizes
  • Partition types

The two common partition table formats are:

  • MBR
  • GPT

docs.title: MBR Partition Table
docs.text:
MBR stands for Master Boot Record.

MBR is an older partitioning system.

Limitations:

  • Maximum disk size around 2 TB
  • Maximum of four primary partitions

Example:

/dev/sda

MBR

 |
 |
 +-- Partition 1
 |
 +-- Partition 2
 |
 +-- Partition 3
 |
 +-- Partition 4

MBR is still supported but is less common on modern systems.

docs.title: GPT Partition Table
docs.text:
GPT stands for GUID Partition Table.

GPT is the modern replacement for MBR.

Advantages:

  • Supports very large disks
  • Supports many partitions
  • More reliable partition information
  • Works with modern UEFI systems

Example:

/dev/nvme0n1

GPT

 |
 |
 +-- Partition 1
 |
 +-- Partition 2
 |
 +-- Partition 3

Modern Linux installations normally use GPT.

docs.title: Viewing Partition Information
docs.text: Linux provides several commands to inspect disks and partitions.

docs.title: lsblk
docs.text:
The lsblk command displays block devices.

lsblk

Example:

NAME        SIZE TYPE
sda         100G disk
├─sda1       20G part
└─sda2       80G part

This shows:

  • Disk name
  • Partition names
  • Sizes
  • Device types

docs.title: fdisk
docs.text:
The fdisk command manages disk partitions.

Display partition information:

sudo fdisk -l

Example:

Disk /dev/sda: 100 GiB

Device      Size
/dev/sda1   20G
/dev/sda2   80G

docs.title: Creating Partitions
docs.text:
The fdisk utility can create partitions.

Example:

sudo fdisk /dev/sdb

Common options inside fdisk:

Option Purpose n Create new partition d Delete partition p Display partition table w Write changes q Quit without saving

Example workflow:

Open disk

Create partition

Review changes

Write changes

docs.title: Filesystems
docs.text:
A filesystem controls how data is stored and organised on a disk.

Without a filesystem, Linux cannot store normal files and directories.

A filesystem provides:

  • File organisation
  • Permissions
  • Metadata
  • Storage allocation

Example:

Disk

 |

Partition

 |

Filesystem

 |

Files and Directories

docs.title: ext4
docs.text:
ext4 is the most common Linux filesystem.

Features:

  • Reliable
  • Good performance
  • Supports large files
  • Widely supported

Example:

/dev/sda1

Filesystem:

ext4

docs.title: XFS
docs.text:
XFS is commonly used in enterprise environments.

Features:

  • High performance
  • Good for large filesystems
  • Common on servers

Example uses:

  • Database servers
  • Large storage systems

docs.title: Btrfs
docs.text:
Btrfs is a modern filesystem with advanced features.

Features:

  • Snapshots
  • Compression
  • Storage management features

docs.title: Creating a Filesystem
docs.text:
The mkfs command creates a filesystem.

Example:

sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1

This creates an ext4 filesystem on the partition.

Warning:

Creating a filesystem will erase existing data.

docs.title: Checking Filesystem Information
docs.text:
The blkid command displays filesystem information.

blkid

Example:

/dev/sdb1

UUID="abcd-1234"

TYPE="ext4"

Information displayed:

  • Device name
  • UUID
  • Filesystem type

docs.title: UUIDs
docs.text:
A UUID is a unique identifier assigned to a filesystem.

Example:

UUID="7f3a9d2e-1234"

Linux uses UUIDs because device names can change.

Example:

/dev/sda1

could become:

/dev/sdb1

The UUID remains the same.

UUIDs are commonly used in:

  • /etc/fstab
  • Automated mounts
  • Server configurations

docs.title: Filesystem Check
docs.text:
Linux provides tools to check filesystem health.

For ext filesystems:

sudo fsck /dev/sdb1

fsck checks and repairs filesystem problems.

Important:

Do not run filesystem repairs on mounted filesystems.

docs.text:

Tasks:

docs.text:

Identify:

  • Partition table type
  • Partition layout

docs.title: Lab 3 - View Filesystem Information
docs.text:

Identify:

docs.text:
