docs.text:
In this lesson you learned:

  • What disk partitions are
  • The difference between MBR and GPT
  • How Linux identifies partitions
  • What filesystems do
  • Common Linux filesystem types
  • How to create filesystems
  • How UUIDs identify storage

The next lesson covers:

Lesson 03 - Mount Points

docs.title: Lesson 03 - Mount Points
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 07 – Storage Management - Lesson 01 – Storage Fundamentals - Lesson 02 – Partitions and Filesystems

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A filesystem must be attached to the Linux directory structure before it can be used.

This process is called mounting.

Mount points allow Linux administrators to connect storage devices to directories, making the data available to users and applications.

Understanding mount points is essential for managing:

  • Additional disks
  • Application storage
  • Database storage
  • Backup locations
  • Cloud attached storage

This lesson introduces mounting filesystems, persistent mounts, and the /etc/fstab configuration file.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this lesson you will understand:

  • What a mount point is
  • How Linux mounts filesystems
  • The difference between temporary and permanent mounts
  • How to mount and unmount storage
  • How UUIDs are used
  • How /etc/fstab works
  • How to troubleshoot mount problems

docs.title: What Is a Mount Point?
docs.text:
A mount point is a directory where a filesystem is attached.

Linux uses a single directory tree.

Unlike Windows, which uses drive letters:

C:
D:
E:

Linux attaches storage into directories.

Example:

Filesystem

/dev/sdb1

        |

        |

Mount Point

/data

        |

        |

Files

/data/application.log

The filesystem contents become available inside the mount point directory.

docs.title: Linux Directory Structure
docs.text:
Common mount locations include:

Directory Purpose / Root filesystem /home User data /var Application data and logs /opt Optional software /data Additional storage /mnt Temporary mounts

docs.title: Viewing Mounted Filesystems
docs.text:
The mount command displays mounted filesystems.

mount

Example:

/dev/sda2 on / type ext4

/dev/sdb1 on /data type ext4

This shows:

  • Device name
  • Mount location
  • Filesystem type

docs.title: Using the df Command
docs.text:
The df command also shows mounted filesystems.

df -h

Example:

Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Mounted on

/dev/sda2       100G   40G   60G /

/dev/sdb1       500G  100G  400G /data

docs.title: Creating a Mount Point
docs.text:
Before mounting storage, the directory must exist.

Example:

sudo mkdir /data

The directory can then be used as a mount point.

docs.title: Temporary Mounts
docs.text:
A filesystem can be mounted manually.

Example:

sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /data

This attaches:

/dev/sdb1

to

/data

The storage is immediately available.

docs.title: Checking a Mount
docs.text:
After mounting:

df -h

Example:

/dev/sdb1

Mounted on:

/data

Files can now be stored in:

/data

docs.title: Unmounting Filesystems
docs.text:
A filesystem can be detached using umount.

Example:

sudo umount /data

The filesystem is removed from the directory tree.

Important:

A filesystem cannot usually be unmounted while it is being used.

docs.title: Finding What Is Using a Mount
docs.text:
If unmounting fails:

lsof /data

Example:

process1

application.log

/data

This shows which processes are accessing the filesystem.

docs.title: Persistent Mounts
docs.text:
Manual mounts are temporary.

After a reboot:

Mounted filesystem

        |

        |

System restart

        |

        |

Mount removed

To automatically mount storage, Linux uses:

/etc/fstab

docs.title: The /etc/fstab File
docs.text:
The filesystem table controls automatic mounting.

View the file:

cat /etc/fstab

Example:

UUID=1234-abcd /data ext4 defaults 0 2

Each field has a purpose:

Field Purpose UUID Filesystem identifier Mount point Directory location Filesystem type ext4, xfs etc Options Mount settings Dump Backup setting Pass Filesystem check order

docs.title: Using UUIDs
docs.text:
Linux recommends using UUIDs instead of device names.

Example:

Device name:

/dev/sdb1

UUID:

UUID=7f3a9d2e-1234

The UUID remains consistent even if device names change.

docs.title: Finding UUID Values
docs.text:
Use:

blkid

Example:

/dev/sdb1

UUID="7f3a9d2e-1234"

TYPE="ext4"

docs.title: Testing /etc/fstab
docs.text:
After editing /etc/fstab, test the configuration.

Run:

sudo mount -a

If there are no errors, the configuration is valid.

docs.title: Incorrect UUID
docs.text:
Symptoms:

  • System fails to mount storage
  • Mount errors during boot

Check:

blkid

Compare with:

cat /etc/fstab

docs.title: Missing Mount Directory
docs.text:
Example:

/data

does not exist.

Create it:

sudo mkdir /data

docs.title: Filesystem Type Incorrect
docs.text:
Example:

TYPE=xfs

but the filesystem is actually:

ext4

Check:

blkid

docs.title: Filesystem In Use
docs.text:
Unmount fails because processes are using it.

Check:

lsof /data

docs.title: Practical Lab
docs.text:
The objective of this lab is to mount and manage storage.

Tasks:

  • Create a mount point
  • Mount a filesystem
  • Verify the mount
  • Configure persistent mounting

docs.title: Lab 1 - Create a Mount Point
docs.text:
Create a directory:

sudo mkdir /data

docs.title: Lab 2 - Mount Storage
docs.text:
Example:

sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /data

Verify:

docs.title: Lab 3 - Identify UUID
docs.text:
Run:

Record the UUID value.

docs.title: Lab 4 - Configure Persistent Mounting
docs.text:
Edit:

sudo nano /etc/fstab

Add:

UUID=<filesystem-uuid> /data ext4 defaults 0 2

Test:

sudo mount -a

docs.title: Lab Challenge
docs.text:

After reboot the directory is empty.

Explain:

  1. Why did this happen?
  2. Which file controls automatic mounts?
  3. How would you make the mount persistent?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson you learned:

  • What mount points are
  • How Linux attaches filesystems
  • How to mount storage manually
  • How to unmount filesystems
  • How UUIDs identify storage
  • How /etc/fstab provides persistent mounts
  • How to troubleshoot mount problems

Lesson 04 - Disk Usage and Monitoring

docs.title: Lesson 04 - Disk Usage and Monitoring
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 07 – Storage Management - Lesson 01 – Storage Fundamentals - Lesson 02 – Partitions and Filesystems - Lesson 03 – Mount Points

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Monitoring storage usage is an essential task for Linux administrators.

A full filesystem can cause serious problems including:

  • Applications failing
  • Services stopping
  • Databases becoming unavailable
  • Log files failing to write
  • System instability

Linux provides several tools to monitor storage usage, identify large files, and troubleshoot storage problems.

This lesson introduces disk usage commands, inode management, and storage troubleshooting techniques.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this lesson you will understand:

  • How to check filesystem usage
  • How to check directory sizes
  • How to find large files
  • What inodes are
  • How to monitor storage growth
  • How to troubleshoot full disks
  • Common storage problems on Linux

docs.title: Checking Disk Space
docs.text:
The df command displays filesystem usage.

Example:

df -h

The -h option displays sizes in a human-readable format.

Example output:

Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on

/dev/sda2       100G   45G   50G  48% /

Information shown:

Column Meaning Filesystem Storage device Size Total capacity Used Space consumed Avail Available space Use% Percentage used Mounted on Mount location

docs.title: Checking Specific Filesystems
docs.text:
A specific filesystem can be checked by providing the mount point.

Example:

df -h /

Example:

Filesystem

/dev/sda2

Mounted on:

/

docs.title: Finding Large Directories
docs.text:
The du command displays directory usage.

Example:

du -h /var

Example output:

500M    /var/log
2G      /var/lib

The du command is useful for finding where storage is being used.

docs.title: Summary Directory Sizes
docs.text:
The -s option displays a summary.

Example:

du -sh /var/*

Example:

500M /var/log

2G   /var/lib

100M /var/cache

This helps identify large directories.

docs.title: Finding Large Files
docs.text:
Large files can consume storage quickly.

The find command can locate large files.

Example:

find / -type f -size +1G

This searches for files larger than 1GB.

Example output:

/var/log/application.log

docs.title: Sorting Disk Usage
docs.text:
The output from du can be sorted.

Example:

du -sh /var/* | sort -h

Example:

100M /var/cache

500M /var/log

2G /var/lib

This displays directories from smallest to largest.

docs.title: Log Files and Storage
docs.text:
Log files are a common cause of storage growth.

Common log locations:

/var/log

Examples:

/var/log/syslog

/var/log/auth.log

/var/log/journal

Large logs may indicate:

  • Application problems
  • Security events
  • Misconfigured services

docs.title: Inodes
docs.text:
An inode stores information about files.

An inode contains:

  • File permissions
  • Ownership
  • File size
  • File timestamps
  • File location information

Every file requires an inode.

A filesystem can run out of inodes even when free disk space exists.

docs.title: Checking Inode Usage
docs.text:
Use:

df -i

Example:

Filesystem     Inodes  IUsed  IFree IUse%

/dev/sda2      655360 10000 645360 2%

The IUse% column shows inode usage.

docs.title: Common Inode Problems
docs.text:
A filesystem may have free space:

Disk usage:

50%

but no available inodes:

Inode usage:

100%

Symptoms:

  • Cannot create files
  • Applications fail
  • Errors saying "No space left on device"

docs.title: Monitoring Storage Growth
docs.text:
Regular monitoring helps identify storage problems before failures occur.

Important metrics:

  • Filesystem usage
  • Available capacity
  • Inode usage
  • Large files
  • Log growth

Example:

df -h

Run regularly to check storage status.

docs.title: Linux Storage Troubleshooting
docs.text: A common troubleshooting workflow:

docs.title: Step 1 - Check Disk Space
docs.text:
df -h

Identify full filesystems.

docs.title: Step 2 - Find Large Directories
docs.text:
du -sh /*

Identify where space is being used.

docs.title: Step 3 - Find Large Files
docs.text:
find / -type f -size +1G

Locate large files.

docs.title: Step 4 - Check Logs
docs.text:
du -sh /var/log/*

Look for excessive log growth.

docs.title: Step 5 - Check Inodes
docs.text:
df -i

Confirm inode availability.

docs.title: Filesystem Full
docs.text:
Symptoms:

  • Applications fail
  • Cannot create files
  • Services stop

Solution:

  • Remove unnecessary files
  • Archive old data
  • Increase storage capacity

docs.title: Large Log Files
docs.text:
Symptoms:

  • /var/log grows rapidly

Solution:

  • Review logs
  • Configure log rotation
  • Investigate application errors

docs.title: Deleted Files Still Using Space
docs.text:
A deleted file can continue using disk space if a process still has it open.

Check:

lsof | grep deleted

Solution:

Restart the process holding the file.

docs.title: Practical Lab
docs.text:
The objective of this lab is to monitor storage usage and troubleshoot disk problems.

Tasks:

  • Check filesystem usage
  • Identify large directories
  • Find large files
  • Check inode usage

docs.title: Lab 1 - Check Disk Usage
docs.text:
Run:

df -h

Identify:

  • Filesystem capacity
  • Used space
  • Available space

docs.title: Lab 2 - Find Large Directories
docs.text:
Run:

du -sh /*

Identify:

  • Largest directories
  • Potential storage issues

docs.title: Lab 3 - Check Inodes
docs.text:
Run:

df -i

Identify:

  • Total inodes
  • Used inodes
  • Available inodes

docs.title: Lab Challenge
docs.text:
A Linux server reports:

No space left on device

However:

df -h

shows:

50% used

Explain:

  1. What could cause this problem?
  2. Which command would confirm the issue?
  3. How would you resolve it?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson you learned:

  • How to monitor disk usage
  • How to use df
  • How to use du
  • How to find large files
  • What inodes are
  • How to troubleshoot storage problems

Lesson 05 - Storage Lab

docs.title: Lesson 05 - Storage Lab
docs.text:
Estimated time: 90–120 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 07 – Storage Management - Lesson 01 – Storage Fundamentals - Lesson 02 – Partitions and Filesystems - Lesson 03 – Mount Points - Lesson 04 – Disk Usage and Monitoring

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This practical lab combines the storage concepts covered throughout this module.

The objective is to safely identify storage devices, create partitions, create filesystems, mount storage, and monitor disk usage.

Storage management is a critical Linux administration skill used in:

  • Servers
  • Cloud environments
  • Virtual machines
  • Containers
  • Database systems

docs.title: Lab Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this lab you will:

  • Identify storage devices
  • Inspect existing disk layouts
  • Create a partition
  • Create a filesystem
  • Mount storage
  • Configure persistent mounting
  • Verify storage usage
  • Troubleshoot storage problems

docs.title: Lab Environment
docs.text:
This lab requires:

  • A Linux system
  • A test disk or virtual disk
  • Administrator privileges

Example test device:

/dev/sdb

Warning:

Do not use a production disk.

The commands in this lab may erase data on the selected device.

docs.title: Lab 1 - Identify Storage Devices
docs.text:
Before modifying storage, identify available disks.

Run:

lsblk

Example:

NAME        SIZE TYPE

sda         100G disk
├─sda1       1G part
└─sda2      99G part

sdb          50G disk

Identify:

  • Existing system disk
  • New storage disk
  • Available capacity

docs.title: Lab 2 - Inspect Disk Information
docs.text:
Display detailed partition information.

Run:

sudo fdisk -l

Identify:

  • Disk device name
  • Disk size
  • Partition table type

Example:

Disk /dev/sdb: 50 GiB

Partition table:

gpt

docs.title: Lab 3 - Create a Partition
docs.text:
Open the disk using fdisk.

Example:

sudo fdisk /dev/sdb

Inside fdisk:

Create a new partition:

n

Display the partition table:

p

Write changes:

w

The new partition should appear:

/dev/sdb1

Verify:

lsblk

docs.title: Lab 4 - Create a Filesystem
docs.text:
Create an ext4 filesystem.

Example:

sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1

Example output:

Creating filesystem with blocks

Filesystem UUID:

abcd-1234

The partition is now ready to store files.

docs.title: Lab 5 - Create a Mount Point
docs.text:
Create a directory for the storage.

Example:

sudo mkdir /data

This directory will become the mount point.

docs.title: Lab 6 - Mount the Filesystem
docs.text:
Mount the new filesystem.

Example:

sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /data

Verify:

df -h

Example:

Filesystem

/dev/sdb1

Mounted on

/data

docs.title: Lab 7 - Test Storage
docs.text:
Create a test file.

sudo touch /data/test-file.txt

Check:

ls -la /data

Expected:

test-file.txt

docs.title: Lab 8 - Find the Filesystem UUID
docs.text:
Display filesystem information.

Run:

blkid

Example:

/dev/sdb1

UUID="abcd-1234"

TYPE="ext4"

Record the UUID.

docs.title: Lab 9 - Configure Persistent Mounting
docs.text:
Edit:

sudo nano /etc/fstab

Add:

UUID=abcd-1234 /data ext4 defaults 0 2

Save the file.

Test:

sudo mount -a

If no errors appear, the configuration is valid.

docs.title: Lab 10 - Check Storage Usage
docs.text:
View filesystem usage.

Run:

df -h

Check:

  • Total size
  • Used space
  • Available space

docs.title: Lab 11 - Monitor Directory Usage
docs.text:
Check directory sizes.

Run:

du -sh /data

Example:

4.0K /data

docs.title: Storage Troubleshooting Exercise
docs.text:
A server administrator receives this alert:

No space left on device

The administrator runs:

df -h

and sees:

Filesystem

/dev/sda2

Use%

95%

docs.title: Troubleshooting Steps
docs.text:
Check filesystem usage:

df -h

Find large directories:

du -sh /*

Find large files:

find / -type f -size +1G

Check logs:

du -sh /var/log/*

Check inodes:

df -i

docs.title: Lab Challenge
docs.text:
A new disk has been added to a Linux server.

The requirements are:

  • Create a partition
  • Format it as ext4
  • Mount it at /data
  • Ensure it survives reboot

Describe the complete process:

  1. Identify the disk
  2. Create the partition
  3. Create the filesystem
  4. Create the mount point
  5. Mount the filesystem
  6. Find the UUID
  7. Configure /etc/fstab
  8. Test the configuration

docs.title: Review Questions
docs.text:
Answer the following:

  1. What command lists block devices?
Answer:
  1. What command creates an ext4 filesystem?
Answer:
  1. Where are persistent mounts configured?
Answer:
  1. Why are UUIDs preferred over device names?
Answer:
  1. What command checks filesystem usage?
Answer:

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lab you practised:

  • Identifying storage devices
  • Managing partitions
  • Creating filesystems
  • Mounting storage
  • Configuring persistent mounts
  • Monitoring disk usage
  • Troubleshooting storage problems

You have now completed the Linux Storage Management module.

Module 08 - Shell Scripting

docs.title: Module 08 - Shell Scripting
docs.text:
Estimated time: 5–8 hours

Prerequisites: - Module 01 – Command Line Fundamentals - Module 04 – Processes and Services - Module 07 – Storage Management

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Shell scripting is an essential skill for Linux administrators, cloud engineers, and DevOps professionals.

Linux administrators often need to automate repetitive tasks such as:

  • System checks
  • Backups
  • Log management
  • Software deployment
  • Service monitoring
  • User management

Shell scripts allow administrators to combine Linux commands into reusable automation tools.

This module introduces Bash scripting fundamentals and builds the skills required to automate Linux administration tasks.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this module you will understand:

  • What shell scripts are
  • How Bash interprets scripts
  • How to create and execute scripts
  • How to use variables
  • How to accept user input
  • How to use conditions and loops
  • How to create reusable functions
  • How to handle errors
  • How to automate Linux administration tasks

docs.title: Lesson 01 - Shell Scripting Fundamentals
docs.text:
Topics covered:

  • What shell scripting is
  • Bash shell overview
  • Creating scripts
  • The shebang line
  • Script permissions
  • Running scripts
  • Basic commands in scripts

docs.title: Lesson 02 - Variables and Input
docs.text:
Topics covered:

  • Creating variables
  • Environment variables
  • Command arguments
  • User input
  • Reading values
  • Exit codes

docs.title: Lesson 03 - Conditions and Loops
docs.text:
Topics covered:

  • Conditional statements
  • if statements
  • case statements
  • for loops
  • while loops
  • File testing

docs.title: Lesson 04 - Functions and Error Handling
docs.text:
Topics covered:

  • Creating functions
  • Passing arguments
  • Returning values
  • Error handling
  • Debugging scripts
  • Logging output

docs.title: Lesson 05 - Automation Lab
docs.text:
Practical exercises:

  • Create system health checks
  • Automate backups
  • Monitor disk usage
  • Check running services
  • Create administration scripts

docs.title: Key Bash Commands
docs.text: Command Purpose bash Run Bash scripts chmod Change script permissions echo Display output read Accept user input export Create environment variables test Perform condition checks grep Search text awk Process text sed Modify text cron Schedule scripts

docs.title: Script Structure
docs.text:
A basic Bash script contains:

Shebang

Variables

Commands

Logic

Output

Example:

#!/bin/bash

echo "Hello Linux"

The first line tells Linux which interpreter should run the script.

docs.title: Automation Concepts
docs.text:
Shell scripting is commonly used for:

  • Server administration
  • Monitoring
  • Backups
  • Deployment tasks
  • Maintenance jobs

Example workflow:

Administrator

      |

Shell Script

      |

Linux Commands

      |

Automated Task

docs.title: Practical Skills Developed
docs.text:
After completing this module you should be able to:

  • Write basic Bash scripts
  • Automate common Linux tasks
  • Create administration utilities
  • Troubleshoot script problems
  • Schedule automated jobs

docs.title: Module Status
docs.text: ⏳ Complete

docs.title: Lesson 01 - Shell Scripting Fundamentals
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 01 – Command Line Fundamentals - Module 04 – Processes and Services

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Shell scripting allows Linux administrators to automate tasks by combining commands into reusable programs.

Instead of manually running the same commands repeatedly, administrators can create scripts that perform tasks automatically.

Common uses of shell scripts include:

  • System administration
  • Backups
  • Monitoring
  • Software installation
  • User management
  • Log processing
  • Server maintenance

This lesson introduces the fundamentals of Bash scripting and how Linux executes shell scripts.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this lesson you will understand:

  • What shell scripting is
  • The purpose of Bash
  • How to create a shell script
  • The shebang line
  • How to execute scripts
  • File permissions
  • Basic script commands
  • How to troubleshoot simple scripts

docs.title: What Is Shell Scripting?
docs.text:
A shell script is a text file containing Linux commands that are executed in sequence.

Example:

Script

   |

Linux Commands

   |

Automated Task

A script allows administrators to turn manual tasks into repeatable automation.

Example tasks:

Manual:

df -h
systemctl status ssh
journalctl -xe

Automated:

./health-check.sh

docs.title: What Is Bash?
docs.text:
Bash stands for:

Bourne Again Shell

Bash is one of the most common Linux shells.

A shell provides an interface between:

User

 |

Shell

 |

Linux Kernel

 |

Hardware

Common Linux shells:

Shell Description bash Default Linux shell sh Bourne shell zsh Extended interactive shell fish User-friendly shell

docs.title: Checking Your Current Shell
docs.text:
The current shell can be checked using:

echo $SHELL

Example:

/bin/bash

The current running shell can be checked with:

echo $0

docs.title: Creating Your First Script
docs.text:
Create a file:

nano hello.sh

Add:

#!/bin/bash

echo "Hello Linux"

Save the file.

docs.title: The Shebang Line
docs.text:
The first line of a script is called the shebang.

Example:

#!/bin/bash

It tells Linux which interpreter should execute the script.

Other examples:

#!/bin/sh

or:

#!/usr/bin/python3

docs.title: Making a Script Executable
docs.text:
A new script is not automatically executable.

Check permissions:

ls -l hello.sh

Example:

-rw-r--r-- hello.sh

Add execute permission:

chmod +x hello.sh

Check again:

ls -l hello.sh

Example:

-rwxr-xr-x hello.sh

The x permission allows execution.

docs.title: Running a Script
docs.text: There are several ways to run a script.

docs.title: Method 1 - Execute Directly
docs.text:
./hello.sh

Output:

Hello Linux

docs.title: Method 2 - Run Using Bash
docs.text:
bash hello.sh

This does not require execute permission.

docs.title: Script Output
docs.text:
The echo command displays text.

Example:

echo "Linux Administration"

Output:

Linux Administration

Scripts often use echo to provide information to users.

Example:

echo "Checking disk usage"

df -h

docs.title: Comments in Scripts
docs.text:
Comments explain what a script does.

Comments start with:

#

Example:

#!/bin/bash

# Display system information

hostname

Comments are ignored by the shell.

docs.title: Running Linux Commands in Scripts
docs.text:
Any normal Linux command can usually be used inside a script.

Example:

#!/bin/bash

hostname

uptime

df -h

When executed:

./system-info.sh

the commands run in order.

docs.title: Script Execution Flow
docs.text:
A script executes from top to bottom.

Example:

#!/bin/bash

echo "Starting"

date

echo "Finished"

Output:

Starting

Sun Aug 02 10:00:00 UTC 2026

Finished

docs.title: Exit Codes
docs.text:
Linux commands return an exit status.

A successful command returns:

0

A failed command returns a non-zero value.

Example:

ls /tmp

Check the exit code:

echo $?

Example:

0

docs.title: Basic Script Example
docs.text:
Example:

#!/bin/bash

echo "System Information"

hostname

uptime

df -h

This script:

  • Displays a heading
  • Shows the hostname
  • Shows system uptime
  • Shows disk usage

docs.title: Troubleshooting Scripts
docs.text: Common problems:

docs.title: Permission Denied
docs.text:
Example:

bash: ./script.sh: Permission denied

Solution:

chmod +x script.sh

docs.title: Wrong Interpreter
docs.text:
Example:

bad interpreter

Check:

head -1 script.sh

Confirm:

#!/bin/bash

docs.title: Syntax Errors
docs.text:
Run:

bash -n script.sh

This checks syntax without running the script.

docs.title: Practical Lab
docs.text:
The objective of this lab is to create and execute basic Bash scripts.

Tasks:

  • Create a script
  • Add commands
  • Make it executable
  • Run the script
  • Troubleshoot errors

docs.title: Lab 1 - Create a Script
docs.text:
Create:

nano system-info.sh

Add:

#!/bin/bash

echo "System Information"

hostname

uptime

df -h

docs.title: Lab 2 - Make Executable
docs.text:
Run:

chmod +x system-info.sh

docs.title: Lab 3 - Execute Script
docs.text:
Run:

./system-info.sh

Verify:

  • Hostname is displayed
  • Uptime is displayed
  • Disk usage is displayed

docs.title: Lab 4 - Check Script Syntax
docs.text:
Run:

bash -n system-info.sh

No output means no syntax errors.

docs.title: Lab Challenge
docs.text:
Create a script called:

server-summary.sh

The script should display:

  • Hostname
  • Current date
  • Current user
  • Disk usage
  • Memory usage

Example commands:

hostname

date

whoami

df -h

free -h

docs.text:
In this lesson you learned:

  • What shell scripting is
  • How Bash works
  • How to create scripts
  • The purpose of the shebang line
  • How to execute scripts
  • How permissions affect execution
  • How to troubleshoot basic script problems

Lesson 02 - Variables and Input

docs.title: Lesson 02 - Variables and Input
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 08 – Shell Scripting - Lesson 01 – Shell Scripting Fundamentals

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Variables allow shell scripts to store and reuse information.

Instead of hard-coding values throughout a script, variables allow administrators to create flexible and reusable automation.

Shell scripts commonly use variables for:

  • File names
  • User input
  • System information
  • Configuration values
  • Command output
  • Script arguments

This lesson introduces Bash variables, user input, environment variables, and command arguments.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this lesson you will understand:

  • What variables are
  • How to create and use variables
  • The difference between local and environment variables
  • How to accept user input
  • How to use command-line arguments
  • How to use special Bash variables
  • How exit codes work

docs.title: What Is a Variable?
docs.text:
A variable stores information that can be used later in a script.

Example:

name="James"

The variable contains:

Variable:

name

Value:

James

Variables allow scripts to reuse information.

docs.title: Creating Variables
docs.text:
Variables are created by assigning a value.

Example:

username="admin"

Important:

There must be no spaces around the equals sign.

Correct:

name="Linux"

Incorrect:

name = "Linux"

docs.title: Using Variables
docs.text:
Variables are accessed using the $ symbol.

Example:

name="Linux"

echo $name

Output:

Linux

docs.title: Script Example
docs.text:
Create:

nano variables.sh

Add:

#!/bin/bash

name="Linux Administrator"

echo "Welcome $name"

Run:

./variables.sh

Output:

Welcome Linux Administrator

docs.title: Variable Naming Rules
docs.text:
Variable names:

  • Can contain letters
  • Can contain numbers
  • Can contain underscores
  • Cannot contain spaces
  • Are case sensitive

Examples:

Valid:

username="james"

server_name="web01"

Invalid:

server name="web01"

docs.title: Quoting Variables
docs.text:
Variables can contain spaces.

Example:

message="Linux Administration Training"

Use quotes when assigning values containing spaces.

Example:

echo "$message"

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Environment variables are available to programs running on the system.

Common environment variables:

Variable Purpose $USER Current user $HOME User home directory $PATH Command search path $SHELL Current shell $HOSTNAME System hostname

Example:

echo $USER

Output:

james

docs.title: Viewing Environment Variables
docs.text:
Display all environment variables:

env

Example:

USER=james

HOME=/home/james

SHELL=/bin/bash

docs.title: Creating Environment Variables
docs.text:
A variable can be exported.

Example:

export APP_NAME="WebServer"

The variable is now available to child processes.

Check:

echo $APP_NAME

docs.title: User Input
docs.text:
Scripts can request information from users.

The read command accepts input.

Example:

read username

echo "Hello $username"

docs.title: Prompting Users
docs.text:
The -p option displays a message.

Example:

read -p "Enter your name: " username

echo "Hello $username"

Example:

Enter your name:

James

Hello James

docs.title: Script Example Using Input
docs.text:
Create:

nano greeting.sh

Add:

#!/bin/bash

read -p "Enter your name: " name

echo "Welcome $name"

Run:

./greeting.sh

docs.title: Command-Line Arguments
docs.text:
Scripts can accept values when they are started.

Example:

./script.sh value

Arguments are stored in special variables.

docs.title: Special Argument Variables
docs.text: Variable Meaning $0 Script name $1 First argument $2 Second argument $3 Third argument $# Number of arguments $@ All arguments

docs.title: Argument Example
docs.text:
Create:

nano arguments.sh

Add:

#!/bin/bash

echo "Script name: $0"

echo "First argument: $1"

echo "Second argument: $2"

Run:

./arguments.sh Linux Admin

Output:

Script name: ./arguments.sh

First argument: Linux

Second argument: Admin

docs.title: Checking Number of Arguments
docs.text:
Scripts can check how many arguments were provided.

Example:

echo "Arguments supplied: $#"

Run:

./script.sh one two three

Output:

Arguments supplied: 3

docs.title: Command Substitution
docs.text:
A variable can store command output.

Example:

hostname=$(hostname)

The command runs and the result is stored.

Example:

#!/bin/bash

server=$(hostname)

echo "Server: $server"

docs.title: Exit Codes
docs.text:
Every Linux command returns an exit code.

Success:

0

Failure:

Non-zero value

Example:

ls /tmp

echo $?

Output:

0

docs.title: Creating Exit Codes
docs.text:
Scripts can return their own exit codes.

Example:

exit 0

Successful completion.

Example:

exit 1

Indicates an error.

docs.title: Practical Lab
docs.text:
The objective of this lab is to create scripts using variables and user input.

Tasks:

  • Create variables
  • Accept user input
  • Use command arguments
  • Check exit codes

docs.title: Lab 1 - Create a Variable Script
docs.text:
Create:

nano system-details.sh

Add:

#!/bin/bash

server=$(hostname)

user=$USER

echo "Server: $server"

echo "User: $user"

Run:

./system-details.sh

docs.title: Lab 2 - User Input
docs.text:
Create:

nano welcome.sh

Add:

#!/bin/bash

read -p "Enter your name: " name

echo "Welcome $name"

docs.title: Lab 3 - Script Arguments
docs.text:
Create:

nano arguments-test.sh

Add:

#!/bin/bash

echo "First value: $1"

echo "Second value: $2"

Run:

./arguments-test.sh Linux Admin

docs.text:
Create a script called:

server-report.sh

The script should:

  • Accept a server name as an argument
  • Display the current user
  • Display the hostname
  • Display disk usage
  • Display memory usage

Example:

./server-report.sh web01

Output:

Server: web01

User: james

Disk:

Memory:

docs.text:
In this lesson you learned:

  • How variables work in Bash
  • How to store and reuse information
  • How to use environment variables
  • How to accept user input
  • How to use command-line arguments
  • How to capture command output
  • How exit codes work

Lesson 03 - Conditions and Loops

docs.title: Lesson 03 - Conditions and Loops
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 08 – Shell Scripting - Lesson 01 – Shell Scripting Fundamentals - Lesson 02 – Variables and Input

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Conditions and loops allow shell scripts to make decisions and repeat tasks.

Without conditions, scripts execute commands in a fixed order.

With conditions and loops, scripts can:

  • Check system states
  • Respond to errors
  • Process multiple files
  • Monitor services
  • Perform repeated tasks

These features are essential for writing useful automation scripts.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this lesson you will understand:

  • How conditional statements work
  • How to use if statements
  • How to compare values
  • How to test files and directories
  • How to use case statements
  • How to create loops
  • How to process multiple items automatically

docs.title: Conditional Logic
docs.text:
Conditional statements allow scripts to make decisions.

Example:

IF something is true

    Do this

ELSE

    Do something else

Example:

if disk space is low

then

send an alert

docs.title: The if Statement
docs.text:
Basic syntax:

if [ condition ]
then
    command
fi

Example:

#!/bin/bash

if [ "$USER" = "root" ]
then
    echo "Running as root"
fi

docs.title: Adding else
docs.text:
The else statement runs when the condition is false.

Example:

#!/bin/bash

if [ "$USER" = "root" ]
then
    echo "Administrator account"
else
    echo "Standard user"
fi

docs.title: Adding elif
docs.text:
Multiple conditions can be checked using elif.

Example:

#!/bin/bash

if [ "$USER" = "root" ]
then
    echo "Root user"

elif [ "$USER" = "admin" ]
then
    echo "Administrator"

else
    echo "Normal user"

fi

docs.title: Comparison Operators
docs.text: Bash provides operators for comparing values.

docs.title: String Comparisons
docs.text:
Operator Meaning = Equal != Not equal -z Empty string -n Not empty

Example:

if [ "$name" = "James" ]
then
    echo "Welcome James"
fi

docs.title: Number Comparisons
docs.text:
Operator Meaning -eq Equal -ne Not equal -gt Greater than -lt Less than -ge Greater or equal -le Less or equal

Example:

if [ $age -ge 18 ]
then
    echo "Adult"
fi

docs.title: File Tests
docs.text:
Scripts often need to check whether files exist.

Common tests:

Test Purpose -f File exists -d Directory exists -r File readable -w File writable -x File executable

Example:

if [ -f "/etc/passwd" ]
then
    echo "File exists"
fi

docs.title: Checking Disk Space Example
docs.text:
Example:

#!/bin/bash

usage=$(df / | tail -1 | awk '{print $5}' | sed 's/%//')

if [ $usage -gt 80 ]
then
    echo "Disk usage is high"
else
    echo "Disk usage is OK"
fi

This checks whether the root filesystem is above 80%.

docs.title: The case Statement
docs.text:
case is useful when checking multiple possible values.

Syntax:

case value in

option1)
    command
    ;;

option2)
    command
    ;;

esac

docs.title: Case Example
docs.text:
Example:

#!/bin/bash

case $1 in

start)
    echo "Starting service"
    ;;

stop)
    echo "Stopping service"
    ;;

restart)
    echo "Restarting service"
    ;;

*)
    echo "Unknown option"
    ;;

esac

Run:

./service.sh start

Output:

Starting service

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
Loops repeat commands automatically.

Common Bash loops:

  • for
  • while
  • until

docs.title: The for Loop
docs.text:
A for loop processes a list of items.

Example:

for item in one two three
do
    echo $item
done

Output:

one

two

three

docs.title: Processing Files With for
docs.text:
Example:

for file in /var/log/*
do
    echo $file
done

This displays every file in /var/log.

docs.title: The while Loop
docs.text:
A while loop continues while a condition is true.

Syntax:

while [ condition ]
do
    command
done

Example:

count=1

while [ $count -le 5 ]
do
    echo $count
    count=$((count+1))
done

Output:

1

2

3

4

5

docs.title: Loop Control
docs.text: Loops can be controlled using:

docs.title: break
docs.text:
Stops a loop.

Example:

break

docs.title: continue
docs.text:
Skips to the next iteration.

Example:

continue

else
    echo "File missing"

for number in 1 2 3 4 5
do
    echo "Number: $number"
done

Lesson 04 - Functions and Error Handling

docs.title: Lesson 04 - Functions and Error Handling
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 08 – Shell Scripting - Lesson 01 – Shell Scripting Fundamentals - Lesson 02 – Variables and Input - Lesson 03 – Conditions and Loops

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Functions and error handling allow shell scripts to become more organised, reliable, and easier to maintain.

As scripts become larger, repeating the same commands makes them harder to manage.

Functions allow administrators to create reusable sections of code.

Error handling allows scripts to detect problems and respond appropriately.

These concepts are important when creating automation used in:

  • System administration
  • Monitoring
  • Backups
  • Deployment tasks
  • Maintenance scripts

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this lesson you will understand:

  • What functions are
  • How to create reusable code
  • How to pass arguments to functions
  • How to return values
  • How to handle command failures
  • How to use exit codes
  • How to debug shell scripts
  • How to create reliable automation

docs.title: What Is a Function?
docs.text:
A function is a reusable block of code.

Instead of writing the same commands multiple times, a function can be called whenever required.

Example:

Function

    |

Reusable Commands

    |

Called Multiple Times

docs.title: Creating a Function
docs.text:
Basic syntax:

function_name()
{
    commands
}

Example:

#!/bin/bash

hello()
{
    echo "Hello Linux"
}

hello

Output:

Hello Linux

docs.title: Function Example
docs.text:
Create:

nano functions.sh

Add:

#!/bin/bash

show_date()
{
    date
}

show_date

Run:

./functions.sh

The function executes the date command.

docs.title: Passing Arguments to Functions
docs.text:
Functions can accept arguments.

Example:

#!/bin/bash

greeting()
{
    echo "Hello $1"
}

greeting James

Output:

Hello James

Function arguments use the same format as script arguments:

Variable Meaning $1 First argument $2 Second argument $# Number of arguments

docs.title: Returning Values
docs.text:
Functions can return exit codes.

Example:

check_file()
{
    if [ -f "/etc/passwd" ]
    then
        return 0
    else
        return 1
    fi
}

A successful result:

0

A failure:

1

docs.title: Using Function Results
docs.text:
Example:

check_file

if [ $? -eq 0 ]
then
    echo "File exists"
else
    echo "File missing"
fi

The $? variable stores the previous command exit code.

docs.title: Why Error Handling Matters
docs.text:
Automation scripts often run without supervision.

A script should be able to:

  • Detect failures
  • Report problems
  • Stop safely
  • Provide useful information

Example:

Bad script:

backup
delete_old_files

If backup fails, files may still be deleted.

Better:

backup

if backup failed

stop script

docs.title: Checking Command Success
docs.text:
Example:

mkdir /backup

if [ $? -ne 0 ]
then
    echo "Failed to create backup directory"
fi

docs.title: Using set -e
docs.text:
The set -e option stops a script when a command fails.

Example:

#!/bin/bash

set -e

command1

command2

command3

If command1 fails:

Script stops

docs.title: Using set -x for Debugging
docs.text:
The set -x option displays commands as they execute.

Example:

#!/bin/bash

set -x

echo "Testing script"

Output:

+ echo Testing script

Testing script

Useful when troubleshooting scripts.

docs.title: Logging Script Output
docs.text:
Scripts can write output to log files.

Example:

echo "Backup started" >> backup.log

The >> operator appends output.

Example:

backup.log

Backup started

docs.title: Redirecting Errors
docs.text:
Standard output:

stdout

Standard errors:

stderr

Redirect errors:

command 2> errors.log

Example:

ls /missing 2> error.log

docs.title: Combining Output and Errors
docs.text:
Save all output:

command > output.log 2>&1

This stores:

  • Normal output
  • Error messages

in the same file.

docs.title: Trap Commands
docs.text:
The trap command allows scripts to respond to events.

Example:

trap cleanup EXIT

The cleanup function runs when the script exits.

Example:

cleanup()
{
    echo "Cleaning up"
}

trap cleanup EXIT

docs.title: Script Debugging Checklist
docs.text: When a script fails:

docs.title: Check Permissions
docs.text: ls -l script.sh

docs.title: Check Syntax
docs.text: bash -n script.sh

docs.title: Run Debug Mode
docs.text: bash -x script.sh

docs.title: Check Exit Codes
docs.text: echo $?

docs.title: Review Logs
docs.text: cat script.log

docs.text:

show_info

docs.text:

#!/bin/bash

mkdir /test-directory

if [ $? -ne 0 ]
then
    echo "Directory creation failed"
    exit 1
fi

echo "Success"

docs.text:

bash -x script.sh

Identify:

  • Commands being executed
  • Where errors occur
  • Exit status

  • How to debug scripts
  • How to create more reliable automation

docs.title: Lesson 05 - Automation Lab
docs.text:
Estimated time: 90–120 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 08 – Shell Scripting - Lesson 01 – Shell Scripting Fundamentals - Lesson 02 – Variables and Input - Lesson 03 – Conditions and Loops - Lesson 04 – Functions and Error Handling

Difficulty: Beginner

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This practical lab combines the scripting skills learned throughout this module.

The objective is to create useful Bash automation scripts that can help Linux administrators perform common operational tasks.

Automation is a key skill in:

  • Linux administration
  • Cloud engineering
  • DevOps
  • Infrastructure support
  • Site reliability engineering

The scripts created in this lab demonstrate real-world administration tasks.

docs.title: Lab Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this lab you will:

  • Create reusable Bash automation scripts
  • Collect system information
  • Monitor system health
  • Check services
  • Monitor disk usage
  • Create backup automation
  • Schedule scripts using cron

docs.title: Lab Environment
docs.text:
Requirements:

  • Linux system
  • Bash shell
  • User with sudo privileges

Check Bash version:

bash --version

docs.title: Lab 1 - System Health Check Script
docs.text:
Create:

nano health-check.sh

Add:

#!/bin/bash

echo "System Health Check"

echo "=================="

echo ""

echo "Hostname:"

hostname

echo ""

echo "Uptime:"

uptime

echo ""

echo "Disk Usage:"

df -h /

echo ""

echo "Memory Usage:"

free -h

Make executable:

chmod +x health-check.sh

Run:

./health-check.sh

docs.title: Lab 2 - Disk Monitoring Script
docs.text:
Create:

nano disk-check.sh

Add:

#!/bin/bash

THRESHOLD=80

USAGE=$(df / | tail -1 | awk '{print $5}' | sed 's/%//')

echo "Disk usage is ${USAGE}%"

if [ $USAGE -gt $THRESHOLD ]
then
    echo "WARNING: Disk usage is high"
else
    echo "Disk usage is normal"
fi

Run:

./disk-check.sh

This script:

  • Checks disk usage
  • Compares against a threshold
  • Reports problems

docs.title: Lab 3 - Service Monitoring Script
docs.text:
Create:

nano service-check.sh

Add:

#!/bin/bash

SERVICE=$1

if systemctl is-active --quiet $SERVICE
then
    echo "$SERVICE is running"
else
    echo "$SERVICE is not running"
fi

Make executable:

chmod +x service-check.sh

Run:

./service-check.sh ssh

Example:

ssh is running

docs.title: Lab 4 - Backup Script
docs.text:
Create:

nano backup.sh

Add:

#!/bin/bash

SOURCE="/etc"

DEST="/backup"

DATE=$(date +%Y%m%d)

mkdir -p $DEST

tar -czf $DEST/etc-backup-$DATE.tar.gz $SOURCE

if [ $? -eq 0 ]
then
    echo "Backup completed successfully"
else
    echo "Backup failed"
    exit 1
fi

Run:

./backup.sh

Check:

ls -lh /backup

docs.title: Lab 5 - Logging Script Output
docs.text:
Scripts often write information to log files.

Example:

./health-check.sh >> health.log

View:

cat health.log

Append timestamps:

date >> health.log

docs.title: Lab 6 - Scheduling Automation
docs.text:
Linux uses cron to schedule automated tasks.

View current cron jobs:

crontab -l

Edit cron jobs:

crontab -e

Example:

Run a health check every day at midnight:

0 0 * * * /home/user/health-check.sh

Cron format:

Minute Hour Day Month Weekday Command

docs.title: Lab 7 - Script Permissions
docs.text:
Check permissions:

ls -l *.sh

Example:

-rwxr-xr-x health-check.sh

Scripts should have execute permission:

chmod +x script.sh

docs.title: Lab 8 - Script Validation
docs.text:
Before running automation scripts:

Check syntax:

bash -n script.sh

Run with debugging:

bash -x script.sh

Check exit status:

echo $?

docs.title: Automation Troubleshooting
docs.text: Common problems:

docs.title: Script Does Not Run
docs.text:
Error:

Permission denied

Solution:

chmod +x script.sh

docs.title: Command Not Found
docs.text:
Check command location:

which command

Example:

which python3

docs.title: Script Works Manually But Not in Cron
docs.text:
Common causes:

  • Different PATH environment
  • Missing absolute paths
  • Permission issues

Use full paths:

Example:

/usr/bin/df

instead of:

df

docs.text:

The script should:

  • Display hostname
  • Display current date
  • Check disk usage
  • Check memory usage
  • Check SSH service status
  • Write output to a log file
  • Return an error if a check fails

server01

Disk:
OK

Memory:
OK

SSH:
Running

docs.text:
Estimated time: 6–10 hours

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Security is a fundamental responsibility for Linux administrators, cloud engineers, and DevOps professionals.

Linux systems are commonly used for servers, cloud platforms, containers, and enterprise infrastructure.

Understanding Linux security allows administrators to:

  • Protect systems from unauthorised access
  • Control user permissions
  • Secure network services
  • Harden server configurations
  • Monitor security events
  • Reduce operational risks

This module introduces the core security concepts required to administer and maintain secure Linux systems.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this module you will understand:

  • Linux security principles
  • The importance of least privilege
  • Users and groups security
  • File permissions and ownership
  • Authentication methods
  • sudo access
  • SSH security
  • Firewall configuration
  • Basic Linux hardening techniques

docs.title: Lesson 01 - Linux Security Fundamentals
docs.text:
Topics covered:

  • Security principles
  • Threats and vulnerabilities
  • Defence in depth
  • Least privilege
  • Linux security model
  • Security best practices

docs.title: Lesson 02 - File Permissions and Ownership
docs.text:
Topics covered:

  • Linux ownership model
  • Users and groups
  • File permissions
  • chmod
  • chown
  • chgrp
  • Special permissions
  • Access Control Lists

docs.title: Lesson 03 - Users, Passwords and Authentication
docs.text:
Topics covered:

  • Creating and managing users
  • Password policies
  • sudo administration
  • Authentication methods
  • SSH keys
  • PAM fundamentals

docs.title: Lesson 04 - Firewalls and Network Security
docs.text:
Topics covered:

  • Firewall concepts
  • Network exposure
  • ufw
  • nftables
  • Service filtering
  • Port security
  • Basic network protection

docs.title: Lesson 05 - Security Hardening Lab
docs.text:
Practical exercises:

  • Review system security
  • Harden user access
  • Secure SSH configuration
  • Configure firewall rules
  • Audit permissions
  • Apply security improvements

docs.title: Key Security Commands
docs.text: Command Purpose id Display user identity whoami Show current user sudo Run commands with elevated privileges chmod Change permissions chown Change ownership passwd Manage passwords ssh Remote secure access ufw Manage firewall rules ss View network connections journalctl View system logs

docs.title: Linux Security Model
docs.text:
Linux security is based on:

Users

    |

Groups

    |

Permissions

    |

Processes

    |

Resources

Access is controlled by:

  • Identity
  • Permissions
  • Authentication
  • Authorisation

docs.title: Security Principles
docs.text: Important security principles include:

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text:
Users and applications should only receive the access required to perform their tasks.

Example:

Web Server

Needs:

Read website files

Does not need:

Administrator access

docs.title: Defence in Depth
docs.text:
Multiple security controls should be used together.

Example:

Firewall

    +

Strong Authentication

    +

Permissions

    +

Monitoring

docs.title: Reduce Attack Surface
docs.text:
Only required services should be running.

Example:

Disable:

Unused services

Unused ports

Unused accounts

docs.title: Lesson 01 - Linux Security Fundamentals
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes
