Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Security is a fundamental part of Linux administration.

Linux systems are widely used for:

  • Servers
  • Cloud platforms
  • Containers
  • Enterprise infrastructure
  • Network services

A Linux administrator must understand how to protect systems from unauthorised access, reduce risks, and maintain secure configurations.

This lesson introduces the core security concepts required before learning permissions, authentication, firewalls, and system hardening.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this lesson you will understand:

  • What Linux security means
  • Common security threats
  • The difference between authentication and authorisation
  • The principle of least privilege
  • Defence in depth
  • The Linux security model
  • Basic security best practices

docs.title: What Is Linux Security?
docs.text:
Linux security is the process of protecting a Linux system from:

  • Unauthorised access
  • Data loss
  • Malware
  • Misconfiguration
  • Service vulnerabilities
  • Network attacks

Security involves protecting:

Users

    |

Applications

    |

Services

    |

Data

    |

Operating System

docs.title: Why Linux Security Matters
docs.text:
Linux is commonly used for critical systems.

Examples:

  • Web servers
  • Database servers
  • Cloud infrastructure
  • Container platforms
  • Network appliances

A compromised Linux system can result in:

  • Data exposure
  • Service disruption
  • Unauthorised access
  • Loss of availability

docs.title: Common Security Threats
docs.text: Linux systems can be affected by many types of threats.

docs.title: Weak Passwords
docs.text:
Weak passwords can allow attackers to gain access.

Examples:

Bad:

password123

Better:

A long unique password

Best:

SSH key authentication

docs.title: Unpatched Software
docs.text:
Software vulnerabilities can be exploited.

Example:

Old package

    |

Known vulnerability

    |

Possible attack

Keeping systems updated reduces risk.

docs.title: Excessive Permissions
docs.text:
Users should not have unnecessary access.

Example:

Incorrect:

Everyone can modify system files

Correct:

Only administrators can modify system files

docs.title: Unnecessary Services
docs.text:
Every running service increases the attack surface.

Example:

Running service

        |

Open port

        |

Potential attack point

Remove or disable services that are not required.

docs.title: Authentication vs Authorisation
docs.text: These two concepts are important in security.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Authentication answers:

Who are you?

Examples:

  • Password
  • SSH key
  • Multi-factor authentication

Example:

User enters password

        |

System verifies identity

docs.title: Authorisation
docs.text:
Authorisation answers:

What are you allowed to do?

Examples:

  • Read files
  • Modify files
  • Run administrative commands

Example:

Authenticated user

        |

Permission check

        |

Access granted or denied

docs.title: Linux Security Model
docs.text:
Linux uses several layers to control access.

User Identity

        |

Groups

        |

File Permissions

        |

Process Permissions

        |

System Resources

Security decisions are based on:

  • User ID
  • Group ID
  • Permissions
  • Privileges

docs.title: Users and Security
docs.text:
Every Linux process runs as a user.

Check your current user:

whoami

Example:

james

Display identity information:

id

Example:

uid=1000(james)

gid=1000(james)

docs.title: The Root User
docs.text:
The root user has full system privileges.

Example:

root

UID:

0

Root can:

  • Modify system files
  • Install software
  • Change permissions
  • Control services

Because of this, root access should be carefully controlled.

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text:
Least privilege means users and applications should only have the access they need.

Example:

A web server needs:

Read website files

It does not need:

Full administrator access

docs.title: Benefits of Least Privilege
docs.text:
Least privilege:

  • Reduces security risks
  • Limits damage from mistakes
  • Limits attacker access
  • Improves accountability

docs.title: Defence in Depth
docs.text:
Defence in depth means using multiple security controls.

Example:

Firewall

    +

Strong Authentication

    +

File Permissions

    +

Updates

    +

Monitoring

If one control fails, other controls still provide protection.

docs.title: Reducing Attack Surface
docs.text:
The attack surface is the number of possible entry points into a system.

Reduce attack surface by:

  • Removing unused software
  • Disabling unused services
  • Closing unnecessary ports
  • Removing unused accounts
  • Applying updates

docs.title: Checking Running Services
docs.text:
View active services:

systemctl list-units --type=service

Check network services:

ss -tulnp

Identify:

  • Listening ports
  • Running applications
  • Exposed services

docs.title: Security Updates
docs.text:
Keeping packages updated is an important security practice.

Debian/Ubuntu example:

sudo apt update

Upgrade packages:

sudo apt upgrade

docs.title: Security Logs
docs.text:
Linux records important system events.

View system logs:

journalctl

View recent events:

journalctl -xe

Logs can help identify:

  • Failed logins
  • Service failures
  • Security events

docs.title: Practical Lab
docs.text:
The objective of this lab is to review basic Linux security information.

Tasks:

  • Identify users
  • Review running services
  • Check network exposure
  • Review system logs

docs.title: Lab 1 - Check Current User
docs.text:
Run:

whoami

Identify:

  • Current username

docs.title: Lab 2 - View User Identity
docs.text:
Run:

id

Identify:

  • User ID
  • Group ID
  • Group memberships

docs.title: Lab 3 - Review Running Services
docs.text:
Run:

systemctl list-units --type=service

Identify:

  • Active services
  • Services that are required

docs.title: Lab 4 - Review Open Ports
docs.text:
Run:

ss -tulnp

Identify:

  • Listening ports
  • Applications using those ports

docs.title: Lab Challenge
docs.text:
A Linux server has the following issues:

- Root login enabled over SSH
- Unused services running
- Weak user passwords
- Open ports that are not required

Describe the security improvements you would make.

Consider:

  • User access
  • Authentication
  • Services
  • Network security
  • Monitoring

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson you learned:

  • What Linux security is
  • Common security threats
  • The difference between authentication and authorisation
  • The principle of least privilege
  • Defence in depth
  • How Linux controls access
  • Basic security checks

The next lesson covers:

Lesson 02 - File Permissions and Ownership

docs.title: Lesson 02 - File Permissions and Ownership
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 03 – Users and Groups - Module 09 – Security Fundamentals

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
File permissions and ownership are a core part of Linux security.

Linux controls access to files and directories by using:

  • Users
  • Groups
  • Permissions
  • Ownership

Understanding permissions allows administrators to control who can:

  • Read files
  • Modify files
  • Execute programs
  • Access directories

Incorrect permissions can create security risks, while correctly configured permissions help protect systems.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this lesson you will understand:

  • How Linux ownership works
  • How file permissions are structured
  • The meaning of read, write, and execute permissions
  • How to use chmod
  • How to use chown
  • How to use chgrp
  • Special permissions
  • Basic Access Control Lists

docs.title: Linux File Ownership Model
docs.text:
Every file and directory has:

  • An owner
  • A group
  • Permissions

Example:

-rwxr-xr-- 1 james developers script.sh

The file contains:

Owner:

james

Group:

developers

Permissions:

-rwxr-xr--

docs.title: Viewing File Permissions
docs.text:
Use:

ls -l

Example:

-rw-r--r-- 1 james james 1024 notes.txt

The first section shows permissions:

-rw-r--r--

docs.title: Understanding Permission Fields
docs.text:
Example:

-rwxr-xr--

Breakdown:

-

rw-

r-x

r--

Meaning:

File type

Owner permissions

Group permissions

Other users permissions

docs.title: File Types
docs.text:
The first character identifies the type.

Examples:

Character Meaning - Regular file d Directory l Symbolic link

Example:

drwxr-xr-x

The d means directory.

docs.title: Permission Types
docs.text:
Linux has three main permissions.

Permission Symbol Meaning Read r View contents Write w Modify contents Execute x Run file

docs.title: File Permissions
docs.text:
Example:

-rwxr-xr--

Owner:

rwx

Can:

  • Read
  • Write
  • Execute

Group:

r-x

Can:

  • Read
  • Execute

Others:

r--

Can:

  • Read

docs.title: Directory Permissions
docs.text: Directory permissions work differently.

docs.title: Read
docs.text:
Allows listing files.

Example:

ls directory

docs.title: Write
docs.text:
Allows creating and deleting files.

Example:

touch file.txt

docs.title: Execute
docs.text:
Allows entering a directory.

Example:

cd directory

docs.title: Numeric Permissions
docs.text:
Permissions can also be represented using numbers.

Values:

Permission Value Read 4 Write 2 Execute 1

docs.title: Calculating Permissions
docs.text:
Example:

rwx

Calculation:

4 + 2 + 1 = 7

Example:

r-x

Calculation:

4 + 1 = 5

Example:

r--

Calculation:

4

docs.title: Common Permission Examples
docs.text:
Full access:

chmod 777 file

Permissions:

rwxrwxrwx

Owner full access:

chmod 700 file

Permissions:

rwx------

Common script permission:

chmod 755 script.sh

Permissions:

rwxr-xr-x

docs.title: Changing Permissions With chmod
docs.text:
The chmod command changes permissions.

Example:

chmod 644 file.txt

Result:

Owner:

rw-

Group:

r--

Others:

r--

docs.title: Symbolic chmod
docs.text:
Permissions can also be changed using letters.

Add execute permission:

chmod +x script.sh

Remove write permission:

chmod -w file.txt

Add group write:

chmod g+w file.txt

docs.title: Changing Ownership With chown
docs.text:
The chown command changes file ownership.

Example:

sudo chown james file.txt

Change owner and group:

sudo chown james:developers file.txt

docs.title: Changing Group Ownership With chgrp
docs.text:
Change group ownership:

sudo chgrp developers file.txt

Verify:

ls -l file.txt

docs.title: Ownership Security Example
docs.text:
Incorrect:

-rwxrwxrwx password.txt

Everyone can modify the file.

Better:

-rw------- password.txt

Only the owner can access it.

docs.title: Special Permissions
docs.text:
Linux has additional permission types:

  • SUID
  • SGID
  • Sticky bit

docs.title: SUID Permission
docs.text:
SUID allows a program to run with the owner's privileges.

Example:

-rwsr-xr-x

The s replaces the execute bit.

Find SUID files:

find / -perm -4000

docs.title: SGID Permission
docs.text:
SGID allows files created in a directory to inherit the group.

Example:

chmod g+s directory

docs.title: Sticky Bit
docs.text:
The sticky bit prevents users deleting other users' files.

Common example:

/tmp

View:

ls -ld /tmp

Example:

drwxrwxrwt

The t represents the sticky bit.

docs.title: Access Control Lists (ACLs)
docs.text:
ACLs provide more detailed permissions.

View ACLs:

getfacl file.txt

Add permission:

setfacl -m u:james:rwx file.txt

Remove ACL:

setfacl -b file.txt

docs.title: Practical Lab
docs.text:
The objective of this lab is to practise Linux permissions and ownership.

Tasks:

  • Create files
  • View permissions
  • Change permissions
  • Change ownership
  • Test access

docs.title: Lab 1 - Create Test Files
docs.text:
Create a directory:

mkdir security-test

Enter:

cd security-test

Create a file:

touch example.txt

View permissions:

ls -l

docs.title: Lab 2 - Change Permissions
docs.text:
Set permissions:

chmod 640 example.txt

Verify:

ls -l

Expected:

-rw-r-----

docs.title: Lab 3 - Change Ownership
docs.text:
View current ownership:

ls -l example.txt

Change ownership:

sudo chown root:root example.txt

Verify:

ls -l example.txt

docs.title: Lab 4 - Test Directory Permissions
docs.text:
Create:

mkdir test-directory

Set permissions:

chmod 700 test-directory

Check:

ls -ld test-directory

docs.title: Lab Challenge
docs.text:
A web server administrator reports:

Users can modify configuration files they should only read.

Investigate:

  • File ownership
  • File permissions
  • Group membership

Suggest a secure permission model.

Consider:

  • Who needs access?
  • Who should only read?
  • Who should not access the files?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson you learned:

  • How Linux permissions work
  • How ownership controls access
  • How to use chmod
  • How to use chown
  • How to use chgrp
  • How special permissions work
  • How ACLs provide additional control

The next lesson covers:

Lesson 03 - Users, Passwords and Authentication

docs.title: Lesson 03 - Users, Passwords and Authentication
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 03 – Users and Groups - Module 09 – Security Fundamentals - Lesson 02 – File Permissions and Ownership

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
User management and authentication are important parts of Linux security.

Linux systems rely on user accounts to control access to:

  • Files
  • Services
  • Applications
  • System resources

Secure authentication ensures that only authorised users can access systems.

This lesson covers Linux users, passwords, sudo access, SSH authentication, and basic authentication security.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this lesson you will understand:

  • How Linux user accounts work
  • How passwords are managed
  • How to create and remove users
  • How sudo provides administrative access
  • How SSH authentication works
  • The role of SSH keys
  • Basic authentication security practices

docs.title: Linux User Accounts
docs.text:
Every user on a Linux system has an identity.

User information includes:

  • Username
  • User ID (UID)
  • Group ID (GID)
  • Home directory
  • Default shell

View your identity:

id

Example:

uid=1000(james)

gid=1000(james)

docs.title: User Database
docs.text:
Linux stores user account information in:

/etc/passwd

View:

cat /etc/passwd

Example:

james:x:1000:1000:James:/home/james:/bin/bash

Fields include:

Username

Password location

UID

GID

Home directory

Login shell

docs.title: Password Storage
docs.text:
Passwords are not stored in plain text.

Encrypted password information is stored in:

/etc/shadow

This file is protected.

View:

sudo cat /etc/shadow

Only administrators should have access.

docs.title: Creating Users
docs.text:
Create a user:

sudo useradd username

A more complete command:

sudo adduser username

Example:

sudo adduser developer

This creates:

  • User account
  • Home directory
  • Password prompt

docs.title: Removing Users
docs.text:
Remove a user:

sudo userdel username

Remove user and home directory:

sudo userdel -r username

Example:

sudo userdel -r developer

docs.title: Changing Passwords
docs.text:
Change your own password:

passwd

Change another user's password:

sudo passwd username

Example:

sudo passwd developer

docs.title: Password Security
docs.text:
Good password practices:

  • Use long passwords
  • Avoid reused passwords
  • Use password managers
  • Enable multi-factor authentication where possible
  • Prefer SSH keys for remote access

Avoid:

password

welcome123

admin123

docs.title: User Groups
docs.text:
Groups allow administrators to manage permissions for multiple users.

View groups:

groups

Example:

james sudo docker

A user can belong to multiple groups.

docs.title: Adding Users to Groups
docs.text:
Add a user to a group:

sudo usermod -aG group username

Example:

sudo usermod -aG sudo developer

Verify:

groups developer

docs.title: The sudo Command
docs.text:
sudo allows users to run commands with elevated privileges.

Example:

sudo systemctl restart ssh

The command runs with administrator privileges.

docs.title: Why Use sudo?
docs.text:
Using sudo is safer than logging in directly as root.

Benefits:

  • Accountability
  • Logging
  • Reduced risk
  • Controlled access

Example:

Incorrect:

Everyone uses root

Better:

Users have limited access

+

sudo when required

docs.title: The sudo Configuration
docs.text:
The sudo configuration is stored in:

/etc/sudoers

Edit safely using:

sudo visudo

This checks for syntax errors before saving.

docs.title: SSH Authentication
docs.text:
SSH provides secure remote access to Linux systems.

Example:

ssh user@server

Authentication can use:

  • Passwords
  • SSH keys

docs.title: Password Authentication
docs.text:
Traditional SSH login:

Username

+

Password

|

Access granted

While convenient, passwords can be attacked using:

  • Brute force
  • Password guessing
  • Credential reuse

docs.title: SSH Key Authentication
docs.text:
SSH keys use cryptographic authentication.

The key pair contains:

Private Key

+

Public Key

The private key stays on the client.

The public key is copied to the server.

docs.title: Generating SSH Keys
docs.text:
Create a key pair:

ssh-keygen

Example:

~/.ssh/id_rsa

~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub

docs.title: Installing SSH Keys
docs.text:
Copy the public key:

ssh-copy-id user@server

After setup:

ssh user@server

The system authenticates using the key.

docs.title: SSH Security Best Practices
docs.text:
Recommended:

  • Use SSH keys
  • Disable root login
  • Disable password authentication where appropriate
  • Use firewall restrictions
  • Monitor login attempts

docs.title: Checking Login History
docs.text:
View successful logins:

last

View failed login attempts:

sudo lastb

docs.title: Authentication Logs
docs.text:
Linux records authentication events.

View logs:

journalctl

Search SSH events:

journalctl | grep ssh

On Debian systems:

sudo tail /var/log/auth.log

docs.title: Account Security Checks
docs.text:
Check logged-in users:

who

Check recent activity:

last

Find users:

cat /etc/passwd

Review unnecessary accounts.

docs.title: Practical Lab
docs.text:
The objective of this lab is to practise user management and authentication.

Tasks:

  • Create users
  • Manage passwords
  • Configure sudo access
  • Review SSH settings
  • Check authentication logs

docs.title: Lab 1 - Create a User
docs.text:
Create:

sudo adduser testuser

Verify:

id testuser

docs.title: Lab 2 - Add User to sudo Group
docs.text:
Run:

sudo usermod -aG sudo testuser

Verify:

groups testuser

docs.title: Lab 3 - Review Authentication Logs
docs.text:
Run:

sudo tail /var/log/auth.log

Identify:

  • Successful logins
  • Failed attempts
  • SSH activity

docs.title: Lab 4 - Generate SSH Keys
docs.text:
Create a key:

ssh-keygen

Review:

ls -la ~/.ssh

docs.title: Lab Challenge
docs.text:
A company has a Linux server with the following issues:

- Multiple users share the root password
- SSH allows root login
- Password authentication is enabled
- Old user accounts remain active

Describe the security improvements required.

Consider:

  • User accounts
  • sudo access
  • SSH configuration
  • Authentication methods
  • Account cleanup

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson you learned:

  • How Linux user accounts work
  • How passwords are managed
  • How sudo provides controlled administration
  • How SSH authentication works
  • How SSH keys improve security
  • How to review authentication activity

The next lesson covers:

Lesson 04 - Firewalls and Network Security

docs.title: Lesson 04 - Firewalls and Network Security
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 06 – Networking Fundamentals - Module 09 – Security Fundamentals - Lesson 03 – Users, Passwords and Authentication

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Network security is an important part of Linux administration.

Linux servers often provide network services such as:

  • Web applications
  • Databases
  • SSH access
  • Monitoring platforms
  • Container services

Every exposed service creates a potential entry point.

Firewalls help administrators control network access by deciding which traffic is allowed or blocked.

This lesson introduces firewall concepts, Linux firewall tools, and basic network security practices.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this lesson you will understand:

  • What a firewall is
  • How network traffic is controlled
  • The difference between inbound and outbound traffic
  • Ports and services
  • Linux firewall tools
  • How to use UFW
  • Basic nftables concepts
  • How to reduce network exposure

docs.title: What Is a Firewall?
docs.text:
A firewall is a security control that filters network traffic.

It decides whether traffic should be:

  • Allowed
  • Blocked
  • Logged

Example:

Internet

    |

 Firewall

    |

 Linux Server

docs.title: Why Firewalls Matter
docs.text:
Without a firewall:

Internet

    |

All Services Exposed

With a firewall:

Internet

    |

Firewall Rules

    |

Only Required Services Accessible

docs.title: Network Traffic Direction
docs.text: Traffic has two main directions.

docs.title: Incoming Traffic
docs.text:
Traffic coming into a system.

Examples:

User connecting to SSH

Web request to server

Database connection

docs.title: Outgoing Traffic
docs.text:
Traffic leaving a system.

Examples:

Server downloading updates

Application connecting to an API

DNS queries

docs.title: Ports and Services
docs.text:
Network services listen on ports.

Example:

192.168.1.50:22

Means:

IP Address:

192.168.1.50

Port:

22

Common ports:

Port Service Purpose 22 SSH Remote administration 53 DNS Name resolution 80 HTTP Web traffic 443 HTTPS Secure web traffic 3306 MySQL Database 5432 PostgreSQL Database

docs.title: Firewall Principle
docs.text:
A good firewall follows:

Allow required traffic

Block everything else

Example:

A web server may allow:

80/tcp

443/tcp

22/tcp

But block:

Unused ports

docs.title: Linux Firewall Options
docs.text:
Common Linux firewall tools:

  • UFW
  • nftables
  • iptables

Modern Linux distributions use:

nftables

as the underlying firewall framework.

docs.title: Checking Firewall Status
docs.text:
On systems using UFW:

sudo ufw status

Example:

Status: active

docs.title: UFW Firewall
docs.text:
UFW stands for:

Uncomplicated Firewall

It provides a simpler interface for managing firewall rules.

docs.title: Enable UFW
docs.text:
Enable firewall:

sudo ufw enable

Check:

sudo ufw status

docs.title: Disable UFW
docs.text:
Disable firewall:

sudo ufw disable

docs.title: Allowing Services
docs.text:
Allow SSH:

sudo ufw allow ssh

Allow a port:

sudo ufw allow 8080/tcp

docs.title: Blocking Services
docs.text:
Block a port:

sudo ufw deny 3306/tcp

docs.title: Removing Rules
docs.text:
View numbered rules:

sudo ufw status numbered

Delete a rule:

sudo ufw delete 1

docs.title: UFW Example Configuration
docs.text:
A basic server firewall:

Allow SSH

Allow HTTP

Allow HTTPS

Deny everything else

Commands:

sudo ufw allow ssh

sudo ufw allow http

sudo ufw allow https

docs.title: nftables
docs.text:
nftables is the modern Linux firewall framework.

It replaces older iptables configurations.

View rules:

sudo nft list ruleset

Example structure:

Table

    |

Chain

    |

Rules

docs.title: nftables Concepts
docs.text: Important components:

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
Contain firewall rules.

Example:

inet filter

docs.title: Chains
docs.text:
Process traffic.

Examples:

input

output

forward

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
Define actions.

Example:

Allow SSH traffic

docs.title: Checking Open Ports
docs.text:
Before securing a server, identify exposed services.

Use:

ss -tulnp

Example:

LISTEN

0.0.0.0:22

0.0.0.0:80

docs.title: Reducing Network Exposure
docs.text:
Security improvements:

  • Remove unused services
  • Close unnecessary ports
  • Restrict access by IP
  • Use encryption
  • Monitor network activity

Example:

Before:

20 open ports

After:

5 required ports

docs.title: Firewall and Containers
docs.text:
Containers can expose services to the network.

Example:

Docker:

docker ps

Shows:

0.0.0.0:8080->80

This means:

Host port 8080

|

Container port 80

Always review exposed container ports.

docs.title: Firewall Logging
docs.text:
Logs help identify blocked traffic.

View system logs:

journalctl

For UFW:

sudo journalctl -k | grep UFW

docs.title: Security Monitoring
docs.text:
Firewall monitoring can identify:

  • Port scans
  • Failed connections
  • Suspicious traffic
  • Attack attempts

Useful tools:

  • journalctl
  • fail2ban
  • CrowdSec
  • SIEM platforms

docs.title: Practical Lab
docs.text:
The objective of this lab is to practise basic firewall management.

Tasks:

  • Check firewall status
  • Allow services
  • Review ports
  • Identify exposed services

docs.title: Lab 1 - Check Open Ports
docs.text:
Run:

ss -tulnp

Identify:

  • Listening ports
  • Running services

docs.title: Lab 2 - Check UFW Status
docs.text:
Run:

sudo ufw status

docs.title: Lab 3 - Allow SSH
docs.text:
Run:

sudo ufw allow ssh

Verify:

sudo ufw status

docs.title: Lab 4 - Review nftables
docs.text:
Run:

sudo nft list ruleset

Identify:

  • Tables
  • Chains
  • Rules

docs.title: Lab Challenge
docs.text:
A Linux server is running:

SSH

Web server

Database

Unused test application

The server is accessible from the internet.

Describe the security improvements required.

Consider:

  • Firewall rules
  • Open ports
  • Service removal
  • Access restrictions
  • Monitoring

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson you learned:

  • What firewalls do
  • How network traffic is controlled
  • How ports relate to services
  • How to manage UFW rules
  • Basic nftables concepts
  • How to reduce network exposure
  • How to review network security

The next lesson covers:

Lesson 05 - Security Hardening Lab

docs.title: Lesson 05 - Security Hardening Lab
docs.text:
Estimated time: 90–120 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 09 – Security - Lesson 01 – Linux Security Fundamentals - Lesson 02 – File Permissions and Ownership - Lesson 03 – Users, Passwords and Authentication - Lesson 04 – Firewalls and Network Security

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This practical lab combines the security skills learned throughout this module.

The objective is to review and improve the security posture of a Linux system.

Security hardening involves:

  • Reducing unnecessary access
  • Securing authentication
  • Protecting files
  • Limiting network exposure
  • Monitoring system activity

These tasks are common responsibilities for Linux administrators and DevOps engineers.

docs.title: Lab Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this lab you will:

  • Review Linux user security
  • Improve file permissions
  • Harden SSH access
  • Configure firewall rules
  • Identify exposed services
  • Review security logs
  • Create a basic security checklist

docs.title: Lab Environment
docs.text:
Requirements:

  • Linux system
  • User with sudo privileges
  • SSH access recommended

Check operating system:

cat /etc/os-release

Check current user:

whoami

docs.title: Lab 1 - Review User Accounts
docs.text:
The first step in securing a system is understanding who has access.

List users:

cat /etc/passwd

Review:

  • Active accounts
  • Unused accounts
  • Service accounts

docs.title: Check Logged In Users
docs.text:
Run:

who

Review:

  • Current sessions
  • Unexpected users

docs.title: Review Groups
docs.text:
Run:

groups

View administrator access:

getent group sudo

Check who has elevated privileges.

docs.title: Lab 2 - Review File Permissions
docs.text:
Incorrect permissions can expose sensitive data.

Check important files:

ls -l /etc/passwd

ls -l /etc/shadow

Expected:

/etc/shadow

Only root access

docs.title: Find World Writable Files
docs.text:
World writable files can be a security risk.

Run:

find / -type f -perm -002 2>/dev/null

Review:

  • Required access
  • Incorrect permissions

docs.title: Correcting Permissions
docs.text:
Example:

chmod 640 file.txt

Change ownership:

sudo chown root:root file.txt

docs.title: Lab 3 - Secure SSH Configuration
docs.text:
SSH is one of the most common attack targets.

Review configuration:

sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config

docs.title: Recommended SSH Settings
docs.text:
Consider:

Disable root login:

PermitRootLogin no

Disable password authentication:

PasswordAuthentication no

Use SSH keys:

PubkeyAuthentication yes

docs.title: Restart SSH
docs.text:
After changes:

sudo systemctl restart ssh

Check status:

systemctl status ssh

docs.title: Lab 4 - Review Open Ports
docs.text:
Identify exposed services.

Run:

ss -tulnp

Review:

  • Listening ports
  • Applications
  • Required services

docs.title: Remove Unnecessary Services
docs.text:
List services:

systemctl list-units --type=service

Stop unused services:

sudo systemctl stop service-name

Disable at boot:

sudo systemctl disable service-name

docs.title: Lab 5 - Configure Firewall Protection
docs.text:
Check firewall:

sudo ufw status

Enable:

sudo ufw enable

docs.title: Allow Required Services
docs.text:
Example:

Allow SSH:

sudo ufw allow ssh

Allow web traffic:

sudo ufw allow http

sudo ufw allow https

docs.title: Review Firewall Rules
docs.text:
Run:

sudo ufw status numbered

Remove unnecessary rules:

sudo ufw delete rule-number

docs.title: Lab 6 - Review Authentication Logs
docs.text:
Security events are recorded in logs.

View authentication activity:

sudo tail /var/log/auth.log

Look for:

  • Failed logins
  • Unknown users
  • SSH attempts

docs.title: Search Failed Login Attempts
docs.text:
Run:

sudo grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log

Example:

Failed password for invalid user

docs.title: Lab 7 - System Updates
docs.text:
Keeping systems updated reduces vulnerabilities.

Update package information:

sudo apt update

Install updates:

sudo apt upgrade

docs.title: Lab 8 - Security Checklist Script
docs.text:
Create:

nano security-check.sh

Add:

#!/bin/bash

echo "Linux Security Check"

echo "==================="

echo ""

echo "Hostname:"
hostname

echo ""

echo "Current User:"
whoami

echo ""

echo "Listening Ports:"
ss -tulnp

echo ""

echo "Disk Usage:"
df -h /

Make executable:

chmod +x security-check.sh

Run:

./security-check.sh

docs.title: Hardening Checklist
docs.text: A secure Linux server should have:

docs.title: User Security
docs.text:
• Remove unused accounts
  • Use strong passwords
  • Limit sudo access

docs.title: File Security
docs.text:
• Correct ownership
  • Correct permissions
  • Protect sensitive files

docs.title: SSH Security
docs.text:
• Disable root login
  • Use SSH keys
  • Limit access

docs.title: Network Security
docs.text:
• Firewall enabled
  • Required ports only
  • Unused services removed

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
• Review logs
  • Monitor authentication
  • Monitor services

docs.title: Final Lab Challenge
docs.text:
You are given a new Linux server.

Current state:

SSH allows root login

Password authentication enabled

Firewall disabled

Unused services running

Multiple unused users exist

Sensitive files have weak permissions

Create a hardening plan.

Your plan should include:

  1. User account changes
  2. SSH improvements
  3. Firewall configuration
  4. Permission corrections
  5. Monitoring improvements

docs.text:
In this module you learned:

Module 09 - Security

Module 10 - Troubleshooting

docs.title: Module 10 - Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Estimated time: 6–10 hours

Prerequisites: - Module 04 – Processes and Services - Module 06 – Networking Fundamentals - Module 07 – Storage Management - Module 08 – Shell Scripting - Module 09 – Security

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Troubleshooting is one of the most important skills for Linux administrators, cloud engineers, and DevOps professionals.

Linux systems can fail in many different ways:

  • Services stop working
  • Applications become unavailable
  • Systems run slowly
  • Storage becomes full
  • Network connections fail
  • Authentication problems occur

Effective troubleshooting requires a structured approach.

This module introduces the tools and techniques used to identify, analyse, and resolve Linux problems.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this module you will understand:

  • A structured troubleshooting methodology
  • How to gather system information
  • How to analyse logs
  • How to troubleshoot services
  • How to diagnose network problems
  • How to investigate performance issues
  • How to document troubleshooting activities

docs.title: Lesson 01 - Linux Troubleshooting Fundamentals
docs.text:
Topics covered:

  • Troubleshooting methodology
  • Problem identification
  • Gathering information
  • Linux diagnostic commands
  • Log analysis
  • Common Linux problems

docs.title: Lesson 02 - Systemd and Service Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Topics covered:

  • systemd architecture
  • Managing services
  • Failed services
  • Service logs
  • Boot troubleshooting
  • Recovery techniques

docs.title: Lesson 03 - Network Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Topics covered:

  • Network diagnostics
  • Connectivity testing
  • DNS troubleshooting
  • Routing problems
  • Ports and services
  • Network tools

docs.title: Lesson 04 - Performance Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Topics covered:

  • CPU investigation
  • Memory troubleshooting
  • Disk performance
  • Process analysis
  • Resource monitoring

docs.title: Lesson 05 - Troubleshooting Lab
docs.text:
Practical exercises:

  • Diagnose failed services
  • Investigate network issues
  • Resolve storage problems
  • Analyse performance problems
  • Document solutions

docs.title: Troubleshooting Methodology
docs.text:
A good troubleshooting process follows:

Identify Problem

        |

Gather Information

        |

Analyse Evidence

        |

Test Possible Causes

        |

Apply Fix

        |

Verify Solution

        |

Document Results

docs.title: Common Troubleshooting Commands
docs.text: Command Purpose top View processes and CPU usage ps Process information systemctl Manage services journalctl View logs df Check disk space du Check directory usage free Memory usage ip Network information ping Connectivity testing ss Network connections dmesg Kernel messages

docs.title: Troubleshooting Principles
docs.text:
Good troubleshooting should:

  • Avoid guessing
  • Use evidence
  • Make one change at a time
  • Record findings
  • Verify fixes

docs.title: Practical Skills Developed
docs.text:
After completing this module you should be able to:

  • Investigate Linux problems systematically
  • Use diagnostic commands
  • Analyse logs
  • Troubleshoot services
  • Diagnose network failures
  • Identify resource problems

docs.title: Lesson 01 - Linux Troubleshooting Fundamentals
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 04 – Processes and Services - Module 06 – Networking Fundamentals - Module 07 – Storage Management - Module 09 – Security

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Troubleshooting is a core skill for Linux administrators.

A Linux system can experience problems involving:

  • Services
  • Applications
  • Hardware
  • Storage
  • Networking
  • Security
  • Performance

Effective troubleshooting requires a structured approach rather than guessing.

A good administrator uses evidence from:

  • Logs
  • System information
  • Monitoring tools
  • Configuration files
  • Command output

to identify the root cause of problems.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this lesson you will understand:

  • A structured troubleshooting process
  • How to identify problems
  • How to collect system information
  • How to analyse logs
  • Common Linux diagnostic commands
  • How to document troubleshooting activities

docs.title: What Is Troubleshooting?
docs.text:
Troubleshooting is the process of:

Identifying a problem

        |

Finding the cause

        |

Applying a solution

        |

Confirming recovery

The goal is not just to fix the issue, but to understand why it happened.

docs.title: Troubleshooting Methodology
docs.text:
A structured approach helps avoid unnecessary changes.

The troubleshooting process:

1. Identify the problem

2. Gather information

3. Analyse evidence

4. Create a theory

5. Test the theory

6. Apply a fix

7. Verify the solution

8. Document the outcome

docs.title: Step 1 - Identify the Problem
docs.text:
Before making changes, understand the issue.

Questions to ask:

  • What is failing?
  • When did it start?
  • Who is affected?
  • Is it always failing?
  • Has anything changed?

Example:

Application is unavailable

Started:

10:30

Affected:

All users

docs.title: Step 2 - Gather Information
docs.text:
Collect facts before making changes.

Useful information:

  • Operating system version
  • Running services
  • Recent changes
  • Error messages
  • Logs
  • Resource usage

docs.title: System Information Commands
docs.text:
View operating system information:

cat /etc/os-release

Example:

Debian GNU/Linux

View kernel information:

uname -a

Example:

Linux server 6.x.x

View hostname:

hostname

docs.title: Checking System Health
docs.text: Basic health checks:

docs.title: Uptime
docs.text:
Shows how long the system has been running.

uptime

Example:

up 15 days

docs.title: Memory Usage
docs.text:
Check RAM usage:

free -h

Example:

total

used

available

docs.title: Disk Usage
docs.text:
Check filesystem space:

df -h

Example:

Filesystem

Size

Used

Available

docs.title: Process Investigation
docs.text:
Processes are a common source of problems.

View running processes:

ps aux

Interactive process view:

top

or:

htop

Look for:

  • High CPU usage
  • High memory usage
  • Stuck processes

docs.title: Checking Services
docs.text:
Many Linux problems involve failed services.

View service status:

systemctl status service-name

Example:

systemctl status ssh

List failed services:

systemctl --failed

docs.title: Logs and Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Logs provide evidence about what happened.

Linux uses:

systemd journal

View logs:

journalctl

View recent errors:

journalctl -p err

View logs for a service:

journalctl -u ssh

docs.title: Kernel Messages
docs.text:
The kernel records hardware and system events.

View kernel messages:

dmesg

Search for errors:

dmesg | grep error

docs.title: Disk Full
docs.text:
Symptoms:

  • Applications fail
  • Logs cannot be written
  • System becomes unstable

Check:

df -h

Find large directories:

du -sh /*

docs.title: High CPU Usage
docs.text:
Symptoms:

  • Slow system
  • Applications respond slowly

Check:

top

Look for:

  • Processes using high CPU
  • Runaway applications

docs.title: High Memory Usage
docs.text:
Symptoms:

  • Applications crash
  • System becomes slow

Check:

free -h

Find memory users:

ps aux --sort=-%mem

docs.title: Service Failure
docs.text:
Symptoms:

  • Application unavailable
  • Connection failures

Check:

systemctl status service-name

Review logs:

journalctl -u service-name

docs.title: Network Problems
docs.text:
Symptoms:

  • Cannot reach systems
  • Applications cannot connect

Check IP configuration:

ip address

Test connectivity:

ping 8.8.8.8

Check routes:

ip route

docs.title: Documentation During Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Good documentation should record:

Problem:

Evidence:

Investigation:

Root Cause:

Fix:

Verification:

Example:

Problem:

Web service unavailable

Evidence:

Apache service stopped

Root Cause:

Configuration error

Fix:

Corrected configuration

Verification:

Website accessible

docs.text:

Lesson 02 - Systemd and Service Troubleshooting

docs.title: Lesson 02 - Systemd and Service Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 04 – Processes and Services - Module 10 – Troubleshooting Fundamentals

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Linux systems rely on services to provide essential functionality.

Examples:

  • SSH access
  • Web servers
  • Databases
  • Monitoring agents
  • Container platforms

When a service fails, administrators need to identify:

  • What failed
  • Why it failed
  • How to restore operation

Modern Linux distributions use systemd to manage services and system startup.

This lesson covers service troubleshooting, system logs, and recovery techniques.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this lesson you will understand:

  • How systemd manages services
  • How to check service status
  • How to start and stop services
  • How to investigate failed services
  • How to use journalctl for troubleshooting
  • How to troubleshoot boot problems
  • How to recover failed services

docs.title: What Is systemd?
docs.text:
systemd is the service manager used by many modern Linux distributions.

It manages:

  • System startup
  • Services
  • Background processes
  • Logging
  • Dependencies

Example:

System Boot

    |

systemd

    |

Services Start

    |

System Ready

docs.title: Checking systemd Version
docs.text:
View systemd information:

systemctl --version

Example:

systemd 255

docs.title: Understanding Services
docs.text:
A service is a background process that provides functionality.

Examples:

Service Purpose ssh Remote access nginx Web server docker Container management cron Scheduled tasks

docs.title: Viewing Service Status
docs.text:
Check a service:

systemctl status service-name

Example:

systemctl status ssh

Output includes:

Active:

running

or:

failed

docs.title: Service States
docs.text:
Common states:

State Meaning active Running inactive Stopped failed Error occurred activating Starting deactivating Stopping

docs.title: Starting Services
docs.text:
Start a service:

sudo systemctl start service-name

Example:

sudo systemctl start ssh

docs.title: Stopping Services
docs.text:
Stop a service:

sudo systemctl stop service-name

Example:

sudo systemctl stop ssh

docs.title: Restarting Services
docs.text:
Restart a service:

sudo systemctl restart service-name

Common after:

  • Configuration changes
  • Updates
  • Troubleshooting fixes

docs.title: Reloading Services
docs.text:
Some services can reload configuration without restarting.

Example:

sudo systemctl reload nginx

docs.title: Enable Services at Boot
docs.text:
Enable automatic startup:

sudo systemctl enable service-name

Example:

sudo systemctl enable docker

docs.title: Disable Services at Boot
docs.text:
Disable startup:

sudo systemctl disable service-name

docs.title: Listing Services
docs.text:
List running services:

systemctl list-units --type=service

List failed services:

systemctl --failed

docs.title: Investigating Failed Services
docs.text:
When a service fails:

Start with:

systemctl status service-name

Look for:

  • Error messages
  • Exit codes
  • Configuration problems
  • Missing files

docs.title: Viewing Service Logs
docs.text:
systemd stores service logs using journald.

View service logs:

journalctl -u service-name

Example:

journalctl -u ssh

docs.title: Viewing Recent Logs
docs.text:
Show recent entries:

journalctl -u service-name -n 50

Example:

journalctl -u docker -n 100

docs.title: Following Live Logs
docs.text:
Watch logs as they appear:

journalctl -u service-name -f

Useful when:

  • Restarting services
  • Testing changes
  • Watching errors

docs.title: Configuration Errors
docs.text:
Symptoms:

Service fails immediately

Check:

  • Configuration syntax
  • Recent changes
  • Log messages

Example:

nginx -t

docs.title: Port Already in Use
docs.text:
Symptoms:

Cannot start service

Check ports:

ss -tulnp

Example:

Port 8080 already used

docs.title: Missing Files
docs.text:
Symptoms:

Service starts then stops

Check:

journalctl -u service-name

docs.title: Permission Problems
docs.text:
Symptoms:

Access denied

Check:

  • File ownership
  • Permissions
  • Service user

Example:

ls -l /path/to/file

docs.title: Dependency Problems
docs.text:
Some services require other services.

View dependencies:

systemctl list-dependencies service-name

Example:

systemctl list-dependencies docker

docs.title: Boot Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If Linux fails during startup:

Check previous boot logs:

journalctl -b -1

View current boot:

journalctl -b

docs.title: Checking Boot Performance
docs.text:
View startup time:

systemd-analyze

Example:

Startup finished in 8s

View slow services:

systemd-analyze blame

docs.title: Recovery Mode
docs.text:
Linux provides recovery options.

Examples:

  • Single user mode
  • Emergency mode
  • Rescue mode

Useful for:

  • Password recovery
  • Repairing systems
  • Fixing failed services

docs.title: Practical Lab
docs.text:
The objective of this lab is to troubleshoot Linux services.

Tasks:

  • Check service status
  • Review logs
  • Restart services
  • Investigate failures

docs.text:

Identify:

  • Current state
  • Process ID
  • Recent messages

docs.title: Lab 2 - Review Service Logs
docs.text:

Identify:

  • Service events
  • Errors

docs.title: Lab 3 - Find Failed Services
docs.text:
Run:

systemctl --failed

Investigate any failures.

docs.title: Lab 4 - Analyse Boot Performance
docs.text:
Run:

systemd-analyze

Then:

systemd-analyze blame

Identify:

  • Slow services
  • Startup delays

docs.text:

Troubleshoot:

  1. Check service status
systemctl status nginx
  1. Review logs
journalctl -u nginx
  1. Check configuration
nginx -t

  1. Identify the cause

  2. Apply the fix

  3. Verify the service is running

docs.text:
In this lesson you learned:

  • How systemd manages services
  • How to check service status
  • How to start and stop services
  • How to analyse service failures
  • How to use journalctl
  • How to troubleshoot boot issues

Lesson 03 - Network Troubleshooting

docs.title: Lesson 03 - Network Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 06 – Networking Fundamentals - Module 10 – Linux Troubleshooting Fundamentals

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Network problems are one of the most common issues Linux administrators troubleshoot.

Applications, services, and users depend on reliable network connectivity.

Network failures can be caused by:

  • Incorrect IP configuration
  • DNS problems
  • Routing issues
  • Firewall rules
  • Service failures
  • Hardware problems

A structured approach helps identify where the problem exists.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this lesson you will understand:

  • A network troubleshooting process
  • How to check network configuration
  • How to test connectivity
  • How to troubleshoot DNS problems
  • How to investigate ports and services
  • How to analyse network routes
  • Common network troubleshooting tools

docs.title: Network Troubleshooting Methodology
docs.text:
A good troubleshooting process follows the network path.

Physical Connection

        |

Network Interface

        |

IP Configuration

        |

Routing

        |

DNS

        |

Application Service

docs.title: Step 1 - Check the Network Interface
docs.text:
The first step is confirming the network interface exists.

View interfaces:

ip link

Example:

eth0

state UP

A working interface should show:

UP

docs.title: Step 2 - Check IP Configuration
docs.text:
View IP addresses:

ip address

Example:

inet 192.168.1.50/24

Check:

  • Correct IP address
  • Correct subnet
  • Active interface

docs.title: Common IP Problems
docs.text:
Symptoms:

Cannot communicate with network

Possible causes:

  • No IP address
  • Incorrect subnet
  • Disabled interface

docs.title: Step 3 - Check Routing
docs.text:
The routing table determines where traffic is sent.

View routes:

ip route

Example:

default via 192.168.1.1

The default route should normally point to the gateway.

docs.title: Common Routing Problems
docs.text:
Symptoms:

Local network works

Internet does not work

Check:

ip route

Possible causes:

  • Missing gateway
  • Incorrect route
  • Wrong interface

docs.title: Step 4 - Test Local Connectivity
docs.text:
Test the local network.

Ping the gateway:

ping 192.168.1.1

Successful response:

64 bytes from 192.168.1.1

Failure may indicate:

  • Network cable issue
  • Wi-Fi issue
  • Interface problem
  • Firewall blocking traffic

docs.title: Step 5 - Test Internet Connectivity
docs.text:
Test an external IP address:

ping 8.8.8.8

If this works:

Network connectivity exists

If it fails:

Investigate routing and firewall

docs.title: Step 6 - Troubleshoot DNS
docs.text:
DNS converts names into IP addresses.

Example:

google.com

        |

142.250.x.x

docs.title: Test DNS Resolution
docs.text:
Use:

nslookup google.com

Example:

Name:

google.com

Address:

142.250.x.x

docs.title: Check DNS Configuration
docs.text:
View DNS settings:

cat /etc/resolv.conf

Example:

nameserver 1.1.1.1

docs.title: DNS Troubleshooting Process
docs.text:
If:

ping 8.8.8.8

works

but:

ping google.com

fails

The problem is likely DNS.

docs.title: Step 7 - Check Listening Services
docs.text:
A service may be running but unavailable.

View listening ports:

ss -tulnp

Example:

LISTEN

0.0.0.0:443

Check:

  • Service running
  • Correct port
  • Correct address binding

docs.title: Testing Ports
docs.text:
Test if a port is reachable:

nc -zv hostname port

Example:

nc -zv server 443

docs.title: Firewall Troubleshooting
docs.text:
A firewall can block valid traffic.

Check UFW:

sudo ufw status

Check nftables:

sudo nft list ruleset

docs.title: Network Tools Reference
docs.text: Command Purpose ip address View IP configuration ip route View routes ping Test connectivity traceroute View network path nslookup DNS testing dig DNS troubleshooting ss View ports curl Test applications

docs.title: Traceroute
docs.text:
Traceroute shows the path traffic takes.

Install if required:

sudo apt install traceroute

Run:

traceroute google.com

Example:

Computer

 |

Router

 |

ISP

 |

Destination

docs.title: Curl Testing
docs.text:
curl can test application connectivity.

Example:

curl https://example.com

Useful for:

  • Web services
  • APIs
  • HTTP troubleshooting

docs.title: Cannot Reach Internet
docs.text:
Check:

ip address

ip route

ping 8.8.8.8

docs.title: DNS Failure
docs.text:
Check:

cat /etc/resolv.conf

nslookup google.com

docs.title: Service Not Accessible
docs.text:
Check:

ss -tulnp

systemctl status service-name

docs.title: Firewall Blocking Traffic
docs.text:
Check:

sudo ufw status

sudo nft list ruleset

docs.title: Practical Lab
docs.text:

  • Test connectivity
  • Diagnose DNS
  • Check services

docs.text:

ip address

Record:

  • IP address
  • Interface
  • Gateway

docs.title: Lab 2 - Test Connectivity
docs.text:
Run:

ping 8.8.8.8

Then:

Compare results.

docs.title: Lab 3 - Test DNS
docs.text:
Run:

Identify:

  • DNS server
  • Returned IP address

docs.title: Lab 4 - Check Services
docs.text:

Identify:

  • Listening services
  • Open ports

docs.text:

Check:

  1. Network interface
  2. IP address
  3. Gateway
  4. DNS

  6. Web service
  7. Application logs

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson you learned:

  • A structured network troubleshooting approach
  • How to check interfaces and IP addresses
  • How to test connectivity
  • How to troubleshoot DNS
  • How to investigate ports and services
  • How firewalls affect networking

Lesson 04 - Performance Troubleshooting

docs.title: Lesson 04 - Performance Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 04 – Processes and Services - Module 07 – Storage Management - Module 10 – Linux Troubleshooting Fundamentals

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Performance problems are common in Linux environments.

A system may become slow because of:

  • High CPU usage
  • Memory pressure
  • Disk problems
  • Excessive processes
  • Resource-hungry applications
  • Poor configuration

Performance troubleshooting requires identifying which resource is causing the problem.

The main areas to investigate are:

CPU

Memory

Disk

Network

Processes

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this lesson you will understand:

  • How to investigate system performance
  • How to analyse CPU usage
  • How to troubleshoot memory problems
  • How to identify disk issues
  • How to investigate processes
  • How to use Linux monitoring tools

docs.title: Performance Troubleshooting Methodology
docs.text:
A structured approach:

Identify Slow System

        |

Check Resources

        |

Find Bottleneck

        |

Investigate Cause

        |

Apply Fix

        |

Verify Improvement

docs.title: System Load
docs.text:
Linux tracks system load.

View load:

uptime

Example:

load average:

0.25 0.40 0.35

The three values represent:

1 minute

5 minutes

15 minutes

docs.title: Understanding Load Average
docs.text:
A high load does not always mean high CPU usage.

Load can be caused by:

  • CPU processes
  • Disk waits
  • Resource contention

Example:

CPU:

20%

Load:

10

This may indicate processes waiting on another resource.

docs.title: CPU Troubleshooting
docs.text:
High CPU usage can cause:

  • Slow applications
  • Delayed responses
  • Increased latency

docs.title: Viewing CPU Usage
docs.text:
Use:

top

or:

htop

Look for:

  • Processes using CPU
  • Number of running tasks
  • Load average

docs.title: Finding CPU Intensive Processes
docs.text:
Sort processes:

ps aux --sort=-%cpu

Example:

USER

PID

CPU%

COMMAND

docs.title: CPU Troubleshooting Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

  • Is one process consuming CPU?
  • Is CPU usage consistently high?
  • Did a recent change cause the issue?
  • Is the application expected to use CPU?

docs.title: Memory Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Insufficient memory can cause:

  • Slow applications
  • System freezes
  • Processes being terminated

docs.title: Checking Memory Usage
docs.text:
Run:

free -h

Example:

total

used

free

available

docs.title: Understanding Linux Memory
docs.text:
Linux uses available memory efficiently.

Memory may be used for:

  • Applications
  • Cache
  • Buffers

High cache usage is not necessarily a problem.

docs.title: Finding Memory Heavy Processes
docs.text:
Run:

ps aux --sort=-%mem

Look for:

  • Large applications
  • Memory leaks
  • Unexpected processes

docs.title: Swap Usage
docs.text:
Check swap:

swapon --show

or:

free -h

High swap usage can indicate:

  • Memory pressure
  • Insufficient RAM
  • Poor application behaviour

docs.title: Disk Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Disk problems can affect:

  • Application performance
  • Boot times
  • Logging
  • Databases

docs.title: Checking Disk Space
docs.text:
View filesystem usage:

df -h

Example:

Filesystem

Size

Used

Available

docs.title: Finding Large Files
docs.text:
Find large directories:

du -sh /*

Example:

/var

20G

docs.title: Checking Disk Performance
docs.text:
Install tools:

sudo apt install sysstat

Use:

iostat

Look for:

  • High utilisation
  • High wait times
  • Slow storage

docs.title: Inode Problems
docs.text:
A filesystem can run out of inodes even with free space available.

Check:

df -i

Symptoms:

  • Cannot create files
  • Applications fail to write data

docs.title: Process Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Processes can cause many performance issues.

View processes:

ps aux

docs.title: Process States
docs.text:
Common states:

State Meaning R Running S Sleeping D Waiting for I/O Z Zombie process

docs.title: Finding Stuck Processes
docs.text:
View process tree:

pstree

Find process details:

ps -fp PID

docs.title: Stopping Processes
docs.text:
Terminate a process:

kill PID

Force stop:

kill -9 PID

Use carefully.

docs.title: Monitoring Tools
docs.text:
Common Linux monitoring tools:

Tool Purpose top Process monitoring htop Interactive monitoring vmstat System statistics iostat Disk performance free Memory usage df Disk space sar Historical performance

docs.title: Application Performance
docs.text:
Applications can become slow because of:

  • Database problems
  • Configuration issues
  • Resource limits
  • Network delays

Always check:

  • Application logs
  • Service status
  • System resources

docs.title: Containers and Performance
docs.text:
Containers can also consume excessive resources.

View containers:

docker ps

View resource usage:

docker stats

Look for:

  • High CPU containers
  • Memory limits
  • Restarting containers

docs.title: Practical Lab
docs.text:
The objective of this lab is to investigate system performance.

Tasks:

  • Check CPU usage
  • Check memory usage
  • Check disk space
  • Investigate processes

docs.title: Lab 1 - Check System Load
docs.text:
Run:

uptime

Record:

  • Load average
  • System uptime

docs.title: Lab 2 - Investigate CPU Usage
docs.text:
Run:

top

Identify:

  • Highest CPU process
  • CPU utilisation

docs.title: Lab 3 - Check Memory
docs.text:
Run:

free -h

Identify:

  • Available memory
  • Swap usage

docs.title: Lab 4 - Check Disk Space
docs.text:
Run:

df -h

Identify:

  • Full filesystems
  • Available space

docs.title: Lab 5 - Check Docker Resources
docs.text:
If Docker is installed:

docker stats

Identify:

  • High resource containers

docs.title: Lab Challenge
docs.text:
A Linux server has become very slow.

Initial checks show:

CPU: 20%

Memory: 95%

Disk: 60%

Determine:

  1. Which resource is most likely the issue?
  2. What commands would you run next?
  3. How would you identify the cause?
  4. What actions could resolve the problem?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson you learned:

  • How to investigate performance problems
  • How to analyse CPU usage
  • How to troubleshoot memory issues
  • How to investigate disk problems
  • How to analyse processes
  • How to monitor Linux systems

Lesson 05 - Troubleshooting Lab

docs.title: Lesson 05 - Troubleshooting Lab
docs.text:
Estimated time: 90–120 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 10 – Troubleshooting - Lesson 01 – Linux Troubleshooting Fundamentals - Lesson 02 – Systemd and Service Troubleshooting - Lesson 03 – Network Troubleshooting - Lesson 04 – Performance Troubleshooting

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This practical lab brings together the troubleshooting skills learned throughout this module.

Real-world Linux administration involves investigating problems where the cause is not immediately obvious.

This lab focuses on:

  • Gathering evidence
  • Identifying root causes
  • Applying fixes
  • Verifying recovery
  • Documenting solutions

docs.title: Troubleshooting Process
docs.text:
Use this approach for every scenario:

Identify Problem

        |

Gather Evidence

        |

Analyse Information

        |

Find Root Cause

        |

Apply Fix

        |

Verify Recovery

        |

Document Result

docs.title: Lab Environment
docs.text:
You will need:

  • Linux system
  • sudo access
  • Terminal access

Check your system:

hostname

uname -a

cat /etc/os-release

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
A user reports:

The SSH service is unavailable.

docs.title: Investigation
docs.text:
Check service status:

systemctl status ssh

Check logs:

journalctl -u ssh

Check if the service is running:

systemctl is-active ssh

docs.title: Possible Causes
docs.text:
Investigate:

  • Service stopped
  • Configuration error
  • Port conflict
  • Permission issue

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
Start the service:

sudo systemctl start ssh

Verify:

systemctl status ssh

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
A server reports:

Applications are failing.

Logs cannot be written.

docs.title: Investigation
docs.text:
Check disk usage:

df -h

Find large directories:

du -sh /*

Check log usage:

du -sh /var/log/*

docs.title: Possible Causes
docs.text:
Examples:

  • Large log files
  • Application data growth
  • Temporary files

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
Possible actions:

  • Remove unnecessary files
  • Rotate logs
  • Increase storage capacity

Verify:

df -h

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A server cannot access the internet.

docs.title: Investigation
docs.text:
Check interfaces:

ip address

Check routes:

ip route

Test gateway:

ping gateway-address

Test external connectivity:

ping 8.8.8.8

docs.title: DNS Test
docs.text:
Test name resolution:

nslookup google.com

docs.title: Possible Causes
docs.text:
Examples:

  • Missing IP address
  • Incorrect gateway
  • DNS failure
  • Firewall restriction

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
Correct:

  • Network configuration
  • DNS settings
  • Firewall rules

Verify:

ping google.com

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A server is running slowly.

docs.title: Investigation
docs.text:
Check load:

uptime

View processes:

top

Find CPU intensive processes:

ps aux --sort=-%cpu

docs.title: Possible Causes
docs.text:
Examples:

  • Runaway process
  • Application bug
  • Excessive workload

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
Possible actions:

Stop process:

kill PID

Restart service:

sudo systemctl restart service-name

Verify:

top

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Applications are crashing.

docs.title: Investigation
docs.text:
Check memory:

free -h

Find memory users:

ps aux --sort=-%mem

Check swap:

swapon --show

docs.title: Possible Causes
docs.text:
Examples:

  • Memory leak
  • Too many applications
  • Insufficient RAM

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
Possible actions:

  • Restart application
  • Adjust memory limits
  • Increase available memory

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A Docker application is unavailable.

docs.title: Investigation
docs.text:
List containers:

docker ps

Check stopped containers:

docker ps -a

View logs:

docker logs container-name

Check resources:

docker stats

docs.title: Possible Causes
docs.text:
Examples:

  • Container stopped
  • Application crash
  • Resource exhaustion
  • Port conflict

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
Restart container:

docker restart container-name

Review configuration:

docker inspect container-name

docs.title: Troubleshooting Documentation Exercise
docs.text:
Document one problem using:

Problem:

Impact:

Evidence Collected:

Investigation Performed:

Root Cause:

Resolution:

Verification:

Example:

Problem:

Web service unavailable

Impact:

Users cannot access website

Evidence:

Service stopped

Root Cause:

Configuration error

Resolution:

Fixed configuration

Verification:

Website accessible

docs.title: Final Challenge
docs.text:
A Linux server has multiple issues:

Users cannot access the website

CPU usage is high

Disk usage is 95%

A Docker container keeps restarting

Create a troubleshooting plan.

Investigate:

  1. System resources
CPU

Memory

Disk
  1. Services
systemctl

journalctl
  1. Network
ip

ss

ping
  1. Containers
docker ps

docker logs

docker stats

Explain:

  • What information you collected
  • How you identified the causes
  • What fixes you applied

docs.text:
In this module you learned:

  • How to troubleshoot Linux systematically
  • How to investigate services
  • How to diagnose network problems
  • How to analyse performance issues
  • How to troubleshoot containers
  • How to document solutions

docs.title: Practical Exercise
docs.text:
1. Prepare a control node and one or more managed Linux hosts.

  5. Apply the configuration.
  6. Run the automation again to confirm idempotency.
  7. Capture evidence and commit it to Git.

docs.title: Validation Checklist
docs.text:

  • Authentication succeeds

  • Secrets are not stored in plaintext
  • Results are documented

  • Variable precedence
  • Privilege escalation
  • Module arguments
  • File paths
  • Handler notifications
  • Host facts

docs.text: You have reviewed, implemented, validated, and documented What Is Ansible.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are responsible for a small engineering repository that will be handed to another engineer. The repository must show a professional change workflow from requirement through branch, review, release and recovery planning.

The project can contain documentation, a small script, Terraform, Ansible, Docker Compose or Kubernetes configuration. The technology is less important than the Git workflow.

docs.title: Required Repository Content
docs.text:

git-final-project/
├── README.md
├── docs/
│   └── design.md
├── src-or-infrastructure/
├── .gitignore
└── .github/

Your README must explain the purpose, prerequisites, validation steps and how changes are reviewed.

docs.title: Delivery Tasks
docs.text:
1. Initialise or clone the repository.
  2. Create an issue describing a small improvement with acceptance criteria.
  3. Create a feature branch from main.
  4. Make at least two coherent commits.
  5. Use git diff, git status and git log to review your own work.
  6. Push the branch and open a pull request.
  7. In the PR description include:
  8. objective
  9. implementation
  10. validation
  11. risk
  12. rollback
  13. Resolve any review comments through additional commits.
  14. Merge using the repository's chosen merge method.
  15. Tag the merged result v0.1.0.
  16. Create release notes.
  17. Delete the merged feature branch.
  18. Create a second small change and demonstrate a safe revert in a disposable context.
  19. Use git reflog to identify recent local HEAD movement.

docs.title: Required Evidence
docs.text:
Capture the output of:

git status
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
git tag --list
git remote -v
git branch -vv

Also provide the pull request link and explain which checks or reviews protected main.

docs.title: Review Questions
docs.text:
• Can another engineer understand why each commit exists?
  • Is there any sensitive or generated content that should not be tracked?
  • Does the pull request explain how the change was validated?
  • Is the repository recoverable if the release is faulty?
  • Are GitHub controls appropriate to the risk of the repository?

docs.title: Definition of Done
docs.text: The project is complete when the history is understandable, the change has passed through review, a version is tagged, and you can explain both rollback and local recovery options without rewriting shared history.

  5. Pull request and review
  6. Tag and release
  7. Recovery with revert and reflog

The final review demonstrates a complete change from branch creation through a review-ready history.

docs.title: What is Version Control?
docs.text:
Version control is a system that records changes to files over time.

It allows you to:

  • See what changed
  • Understand who changed it
  • Restore previous versions
  • Work safely with others

Without version control, teams often rely on:

project-final.zip
project-final-v2.zip
project-final-v2-really-final.zip

This quickly becomes difficult to manage.

docs.title: What is Git?
docs.text:
Git is a distributed version control system.

Distributed means every developer has a complete copy of the repository, including its history.

Example:

             Git Repository

        +----------------+
        |   History      |
        |   Commits      |
        |   Branches     |
        +----------------+

              /   |   \

          Developer A

          Developer B

          Developer C

Each person can work independently and synchronise changes later.

docs.title: Why Was Git Created?
docs.text:
Git was created in 2005 by Linus Torvalds.

It was developed to manage the source code for the Linux kernel.

The Linux kernel project required:

  • Very large numbers of contributors
  • Fast performance
  • Reliable history tracking
  • Distributed development

Git was designed to handle these requirements.

docs.title: Tracking Changes
docs.text:
Git records every change.

Example:

Commit 1
|
+ Add website files

Commit 2
|
+ Update documentation

Commit 3
|
+ Fix configuration

You can review the complete history.

docs.title: Recovering From Mistakes
docs.text:
If a change causes a problem, Git allows you to:

  • Review previous versions
  • Restore files
  • Undo changes

Example:

Working version

        |
        v

Problem introduced

        |
        v

Restore previous commit

Git and GitHub are closely related, but they are not the same thing.

A common beginner mistake is thinking:

GitHub is Git.

GitHub is a platform that hosts Git repositories and provides collaboration tools.

docs.title: What is Git?
docs.text:
Git is software that runs on your computer.

It allows you to:

  • Create repositories
  • Track file changes
  • Create commits
  • Create branches
  • Merge changes
  • View project history

Git works locally without needing an internet connection.

Example:

git init

git add README.md

git commit -m "Initial commit"

These commands operate on your local machine.

docs.title: What is GitHub?
docs.text:
GitHub is a cloud-based platform for hosting Git repositories.

GitHub adds collaboration features on top of Git.

It provides:

  • Remote repositories
  • Pull requests
  • Code reviews
  • Issue tracking
  • Project management
  • Automation

Example:

Your Computer

      |
      |
      v

     Git

      |
      |
      v

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This lesson introduces the core concepts that make Git work.

Understanding these concepts is essential before learning commands like:

  • git add
  • git commit
  • git branch
  • git merge
  • git push

Git is built around tracking changes as they move through different stages.

docs.title: Git Repository
docs.text:
A Git repository is a directory that Git manages.

When Git is initialised, it creates a hidden .git directory.

Example:

my-project/

├── README.md
├── application.py
└── .git/

The .git directory stores:

  • Commit history
  • Branch information
  • Configuration
  • Repository metadata

docs.title: Creating a Repository
docs.text:
A new repository is created using:

git init

Example:

mkdir my-project

cd my-project

git init

Git now tracks this directory.

docs.title: The Git Workflow
docs.text:
Git uses a three-stage workflow:

Working Directory

        |
        | git add

        v

Staging Area

        |
        | git commit

        v

Repository

Understanding this workflow is one of the most important Git concepts.

docs.title: Working Directory
docs.text:
The working directory is where you create and edit files.

Example:

my-project/

├── README.md
├── app.py
└── config.yml

Changes exist here before Git records them.

Example:

You edit:

README.md

Git knows the file has changed, but the change is not yet saved.

Check:

git status

Example output:

modified: README.md

docs.title: Staging Area
docs.text:
The staging area is where you prepare changes before committing.

You move files into staging with:

git add

Example:

git add README.md

Now Git knows:

Include this change in the next commit.

The workflow becomes:

Edit File

    |

    v

Working Directory

    |

git add

    |

    v

Staging Area

docs.title: Commits
docs.text:
A commit is a saved snapshot of your changes.

Example:

git commit -m "Update documentation"

A commit contains:

  • Changed files
  • Author information
  • Date and time
  • Commit message
  • Unique identifier

Example history:

Commit 3
|
+ Add networking documentation

Commit 2
|
+ Add installation guide

Commit 1
|
+ Initial project setup

docs.title: Viewing Commits
docs.text:

git log

commit a82f92d

Author: James

Message:
Add documentation

docs.title: Branches
docs.text:
A branch is an independent line of development.

Branches allow engineers to work on changes safely.

Example:

                 main

                  |

        -------------------

        |                 |

 feature-login     feature-api

The default branch is usually:

main

Branches are commonly used for:

  • New features
  • Bug fixes
  • Experiments

docs.text:
A remote repository is a copy of your repository stored somewhere else.

Examples:

  • GitHub

  • Collaboration

  • Automation

Examples of CI/CD platforms:

  • GitHub Actions
  • Jenkins
  • GitLab CI
  • Azure DevOps Pipelines

Professional teams usually review changes before deployment.

docs.text:
GitOps extends the idea of using Git as the source of truth.

The desired state of a system is stored in Git.

Example:

passwords
API keys

docs.text:
Topics:

  • Working with repositories
  • Understanding commits
  • Viewing changes

docs.title: Module 02 - Git Basics
docs.text: This module moves from Git terminology into the everyday workflow you will use constantly: edit files, inspect changes, stage exactly what belongs in the next commit, create the commit, and read the history afterwards. The most important skill here is not remembering commands; it is understanding which state Git is showing you.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Understand the core concepts in this module.
  • Use the relevant Git/GitHub commands deliberately.
  • Validate repository state before and after a change.
  • Recognise common failure modes and choose a safe recovery path.

docs.title: Working tree, staging area and repository
docs.text:
Git separates your work into three useful states. The working tree is the files you are editing. The staging area (also called the index) is the exact content prepared for the next commit. The repository contains committed history.

That separation is what lets you build a clean commit from only part of your current work. You may have edited three files but decide that only two belong to the next change. git add does not mean "save everything"; it means "put this version of these changes into the next commit".

docs.title: Reading status before acting
docs.text:
git status is the command to build a habit around. It tells you the current branch, which files are untracked, which changes are unstaged, and which changes are staged. Run it before and after important commands.

Use the short form when you become comfortable:

git status --short

Typical prefixes include ?? for untracked files and M for modified files. The two status columns represent staged and unstaged state, which is useful when a file contains both.

docs.title: Inspecting changes with diff
docs.text:
git diff shows changes in the working tree that have not been staged. git diff --staged shows what will be included in the next commit.

Before committing, compare both:

git diff
git diff --staged

For focused commits, git add -p lets you stage individual change hunks instead of an entire file. This is especially useful when you fixed a typo while also working on a larger feature.

docs.title: Creating useful commits
docs.text:
A commit should represent one understandable change. A message such as Fix DNS validation in deployment script is more useful than updates because the history becomes operational documentation.

Useful inspection commands:

git log --oneline --decorate -10
git show HEAD
git show --stat HEAD

Every commit has an identifier derived from its contents and parent history. Git usually displays an abbreviated form because the full hash is long.

docs.title: .gitignore and tracked files
docs.text:
.gitignore prevents new matching files from being added accidentally. It is commonly used for editor files, build output, local state and generated artefacts.

Example:

.venv/
*.log
.env
site/

A critical detail: adding a pattern to .gitignore does not stop Git tracking a file that is already committed. You must remove it from the index separately, for example git rm --cached .env, and if that file contained a real secret you must rotate the secret rather than assuming the ignore rule fixes the exposure.

docs.title: Undoing uncommitted work safely
docs.text:
Modern Git provides explicit restore commands:

git restore README.md
git restore --staged README.md

The first replaces working-tree changes with the version from the index. The second removes a file from staging but keeps your working-tree edits. Always inspect the file first; restoring work can discard changes that are not committed anywhere.

docs.title: Command Walkthrough
docs.text:
mkdir git-basics-lab
cd git-basics-lab
git init
printf "# Git basics lab\n" > README.md
git status
git add README.md
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Create lab README"
printf "\nFirst exercise\n" >> README.md
printf "temporary.log\n" > temporary.log
git status --short
git diff
printf "*.log\n" > .gitignore
git add README.md .gitignore
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Add first exercise and ignore log files"
git log --oneline --decorate

Run these commands in a disposable repository and read the output after each step. The output is part of the lesson; do not treat commands as a script to paste without understanding.

docs.title: Practical Lab
docs.text:
1. Create the repository shown above.
  2. Make two unrelated changes in the same file.
  3. Use git add -p to stage only one hunk.
  4. Confirm the difference between git diff and git diff --staged.
  5. Commit the staged hunk.
  6. Use git restore on the remaining disposable change.
  7. Add a test file matched by .gitignore and prove Git ignores it with git status.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Using git add . without reviewing what it stages.
  • Committing generated files, local state or credentials.
  • Using git restore before checking whether the discarded work exists anywhere else.
  • Treating a commit message as an afterthought rather than part of the project history.

docs.title: Knowledge Check
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between the working tree and the staging area?
  2. What does git diff --staged show?
  3. Why might git add -p produce a better commit?
  4. Why can adding .env to .gitignore be insufficient after a secret was already committed?
