docs.title: Module 03 - Branching
docs.text: Branches let you develop a change without moving the main line of work until the change is ready. Git branches are lightweight references to commits, not full copies of the repository. Understanding that pointer model makes branching much less mysterious.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Understand the core concepts in this module.
  • Use the relevant Git/GitHub commands deliberately.
  • Validate repository state before and after a change.
  • Recognise common failure modes and choose a safe recovery path.

docs.title: Branches are pointers
docs.text:
A branch name such as main or feature/add-dashboard points at a commit. When you create a new commit while that branch is checked out, the branch pointer advances to the new commit.

HEAD tells Git which branch or commit you currently have checked out. You can see the current branch with:

git branch --show-current

docs.title: Creating and switching branches
docs.text:
Create and switch in one command:

git switch -c feature/add-readme

Switch back:

git switch main

List branches:

git branch

Older material often uses git checkout for several different jobs. git switch is clearer for branch switching and git restore is clearer for restoring files.

docs.title: Why feature branches help
docs.text:
A feature branch gives a change its own line of history. That supports review, CI testing and easy abandonment if an idea turns out to be wrong.

For infrastructure work, a branch might contain a Terraform network change, an Ansible role update or a documentation fix. The important property is that the branch groups a coherent change that can be reviewed before it affects main.

docs.title: Branch naming
docs.text:
Names should communicate intent. Common patterns include:

feature/add-monitoring
fix/dns-timeout
docs/update-runbook
chore/upgrade-dependency

A team does not need a complicated naming policy, but consistent names make pull requests and automation easier to understand.

docs.title: Divergence
docs.text:
If both main and a feature branch receive commits, they have diverged:

A---B---C  main
     \
      D---E  feature

Later you can merge or rebase the feature work depending on the team workflow. You will explore merging in the next module and rebasing later in the course.

docs.title: Deleting completed branches
docs.text:
After a branch has been merged and is no longer needed:

git branch -d feature/add-readme

The safe -d form refuses to delete an unmerged branch. -D forces deletion, so use it only when you have deliberately decided that the unmerged commits are disposable.

docs.title: Command Walkthrough
docs.text:
git switch -c feature/add-training-note
printf "\nTraining branch change\n" >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "Add training branch note"
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
git switch main
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all

Run these commands in a disposable repository and read the output after each step. The output is part of the lesson; do not treat commands as a script to paste without understanding.

docs.title: Practical Lab
docs.text:
1. Start from a clean repository on main.
  2. Create feature/add-networking-notes.
  3. Add a file called networking.md and commit it.
  4. Switch back to main and confirm the file is absent there.
  5. Compare main and the feature branch with git log --graph --all and git diff main...feature/add-networking-notes.
  6. Do not merge yet; keep the branch for the merge lab.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Making changes on main before creating the feature branch.
  • Leaving dozens of old branches and losing track of active work.
  • Using -D to delete a branch without checking whether the commits are needed.
  • Putting several unrelated features into one branch.

docs.title: Knowledge Check
docs.text:
1. What does a branch name point to?
  2. What does HEAD represent?
  3. Why is git branch -d safer than git branch -D?
  4. How does a feature branch support code review?

docs.title: Module 04 - Merging and Conflict Resolution
docs.text: Merging combines lines of development. Most merges are routine. Conflicts appear only when Git cannot determine how to combine competing changes safely, and the correct response is to understand the intended final content rather than simply deleting conflict markers.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Understand the core concepts in this module.
  • Use the relevant Git/GitHub commands deliberately.
  • Validate repository state before and after a change.
  • Recognise common failure modes and choose a safe recovery path.

docs.title: Fast-forward merges
docs.text:
If main has not changed since a feature branch was created, Git may only need to move the main pointer forward:

A---B  main
     \
      C---D feature

After a fast-forward merge, main points to D. No merge commit is required because the history is already linear.

docs.title: Three-way merges
docs.text:
When both sides have new commits, Git finds their common ancestor and combines the changes. A merge commit may record the two parent histories:

A---B---C------M
     \        /
      D---E---

The exact history depends on repository settings and whether the team uses merge commits, squash merges or rebasing.

docs.title: Creating a merge
docs.text:
A local merge normally looks like:

git switch main
git merge feature/add-networking-notes

Immediately inspect:

git status
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all

A successful merge is not the end of validation; run the relevant tests or configuration validation as well.

docs.title: Understanding conflict markers
docs.text:
If two branches modify the same lines differently, Git may produce:

<<<<<<< HEAD
current main content
=======
feature branch content
>>>>>>> feature/add-networking-notes

These markers show the competing versions. The final file should contain the correct intended result, which may be one side, the other side, or a new combination of both.

docs.title: Resolving a conflict
docs.text:
The basic sequence is:

git status
# edit the conflicted files
git diff
git add <resolved-file>
git status
git commit

For a merge already in progress you can abandon it before committing with:

git merge --abort

That is valuable when you realise you do not understand the conflict well enough to resolve it safely.

docs.title: Conflict prevention
docs.text: Small branches, frequent synchronisation and focused commits reduce conflict size. They do not eliminate conflicts, but they make conflicts understandable. Generated files and large reformats can create unnecessary conflict noise, so separate them from functional changes where practical.

docs.title: Command Walkthrough
docs.text:
git switch main
git merge feature/add-networking-notes
git status
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all

Run these commands in a disposable repository and read the output after each step. The output is part of the lesson; do not treat commands as a script to paste without understanding.

docs.title: Practical Lab
docs.text: Create a controlled conflict: 1. Create conflict-demo.txt on main with one line and commit it. 2. Create branch feature/conflict-demo. 3. Change the same line on the feature branch and commit. 4. Switch to main, change the same line differently, and commit. 5. Run git merge feature/conflict-demo. 6. Inspect the markers. 7. Edit the file to the final intended value. 8. Stage and commit the resolution. 9. Use git log --graph --all to explain the history.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Choosing 'ours' or 'theirs' without understanding the intended final behaviour.
  • Resolving the text conflict but forgetting to run tests afterwards.
  • Editing unrelated files while a conflict resolution is in progress.
  • Force-resetting a branch because a normal conflict feels alarming.

docs.title: Knowledge Check
docs.text:
1. When can Git fast-forward a branch?
  2. What information do conflict markers represent?
  3. What does git merge --abort do?
  4. Why should you test after resolving a conflict?

docs.title: Module 05 - Remote Repositories
docs.text: A remote connects your local Git repository to another repository, commonly on GitHub. The remote is not magical cloud state: Git tracks remote URLs and remote-tracking references so you can deliberately fetch, compare and publish commits.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Understand the core concepts in this module.
  • Use the relevant Git/GitHub commands deliberately.
  • Validate repository state before and after a change.
  • Recognise common failure modes and choose a safe recovery path.

docs.title: The origin remote
docs.text:
When you clone a repository, Git normally creates a remote named origin. Inspect it with:

git remote -v

The name is only a convention. A repository can have multiple remotes, for example origin for your fork and upstream for the original project.

docs.title: Clone
docs.text:
git clone copies the repository history and checks out a working tree:

git clone git@github.com:owner/project.git
cd project

After cloning, inspect the branch and remotes rather than immediately making changes.

docs.title: Fetch
docs.text:
git fetch downloads remote objects and updates remote-tracking references such as origin/main. It does not automatically modify your working branch.

git fetch --prune origin
git log --oneline main..origin/main

This makes fetch a good low-risk first step when checking what changed remotely.

docs.title: Pull
docs.text:
git pull combines a fetch with an integration step. The integration may merge or rebase depending on configuration. For a simple branch where you only want a fast-forward update:

git pull --ff-only

The command fails instead of silently creating a merge if local and remote history diverged.

docs.title: Push and upstream tracking
docs.text:
To publish a new branch:

git push -u origin feature/example

The -u option records the upstream branch, allowing later git push and git pull commands without repeating the remote and branch names.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
GitHub commonly uses SSH keys or HTTPS-based credentials/tokens. Private keys and access tokens must not be committed to repositories.

With SSH, validate the configured remote:

git remote get-url origin

Credential problems are separate from Git history problems. Distinguish authentication failures from rejected pushes caused by branch protection or non-fast-forward history.

docs.title: Force pushes
docs.text:
A normal push is rejected if it would discard remote history. That protection is useful. If history rewriting is genuinely required on a personal feature branch, --force-with-lease is safer than --force because it checks that the remote branch still points where you expect.

Never treat force pushing a shared branch as routine.

docs.title: Command Walkthrough
docs.text:
git remote -v
git fetch --prune origin
git branch -vv
git log --oneline --decorate --all -12
git status

Run these commands in a disposable repository and read the output after each step. The output is part of the lesson; do not treat commands as a script to paste without understanding.

docs.title: Practical Lab
docs.text:
1. Create a disposable GitHub repository.
  2. Clone it into a new directory.
  3. Create a feature branch locally.
  4. Add and commit a small change.
  5. Push with git push -u origin <branch>.
  6. View the branch on GitHub.
  7. Make another small commit locally and push it.
  8. Run git fetch --prune and explain the local branch versus origin/<branch>.
  9. Delete the remote feature branch after the lab and fetch with prune again.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Using git pull without understanding whether it will merge or rebase.
  • Confusing origin/main with the local main branch.
  • Saving tokens or private keys inside the repository.
  • Using force push to work around a rejected push instead of understanding the divergence.

docs.title: Knowledge Check
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?
  2. What is a remote-tracking branch?
  3. What does -u do on the first push?
  4. Why is --force-with-lease safer than --force?

docs.title: Module 06 - GitHub Collaboration
docs.text: Git manages commits and branches; GitHub adds the collaborative controls around them. Pull requests, reviews, issues and branch protection turn a collection of commits into a team change process.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Understand the core concepts in this module.
  • Use the relevant Git/GitHub commands deliberately.
  • Validate repository state before and after a change.
  • Recognise common failure modes and choose a safe recovery path.

docs.title: Pull request lifecycle
docs.text:
A common change path is:

Issue / requirement
      |
feature branch
      |
commits + tests
      |
pull request
      |
review + CI
      |
merge
      |
delete feature branch

A pull request is not just a request to press Merge. It is the discussion and evidence around a proposed change.

docs.title: Writing a useful pull request
docs.text:
A reviewer should be able to understand what changed, why it changed, how it was tested, and what risk remains.

A useful description might include: - problem or objective - implementation summary - validation performed - screenshots/logs only when they add evidence - rollback or operational consideration for infrastructure changes - linked issue/change record where relevant

docs.title: Code review
docs.text:
Review the change, not the person. Good review comments are specific and explain the risk or reasoning.

Look for: - correctness - security - maintainability - unexpected scope - missing tests or validation - secrets or sensitive data - operational impact

For Infrastructure as Code, the plan/diff is important evidence, but it does not replace understanding the code itself.

docs.title: Issues
docs.text:
Issues are useful for work that needs to be discussed or tracked before code exists. A small issue should state the problem, expected outcome and acceptance criteria.

Linking a pull request to an issue creates traceability from requirement to implementation and history.

docs.title: Draft pull requests
docs.text: A draft pull request is useful when you want early feedback but the change is not ready to merge. It keeps work visible without pretending it has met its final quality gate.

docs.title: Branch protection
docs.text:
Protected branches can require pull requests, reviews, passing checks or other policies before updates are accepted. These controls protect the change process, particularly for deployment or infrastructure repositories.

Do not design a workflow that depends on administrators routinely bypassing its protections.

docs.title: GitHub CLI
docs.text:
The GitHub CLI can make collaboration repeatable:

gh issue list
gh pr create --fill
gh pr status
gh pr view

The web interface is equally valid. The learning goal is the workflow, not a preference for one client.

docs.title: Command Walkthrough
docs.text:
git switch -c docs/collaboration-lab
printf "\nCollaboration lab\n" >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "Document collaboration lab"
git push -u origin docs/collaboration-lab
gh pr create --fill
gh pr status

Run these commands in a disposable repository and read the output after each step. The output is part of the lesson; do not treat commands as a script to paste without understanding.

docs.title: Practical Lab
docs.text:
1. Create an issue describing a small documentation improvement.
  2. Create a branch named from the work.
  3. Make a focused commit.
  4. Push the branch.
  5. Open a draft pull request and link the issue.
  6. Add a clear validation section.
  7. Mark it ready for review.
  8. Review the diff as if it were somebody else's work.
  9. Merge only when the stated acceptance criteria are met.
  10. Confirm the issue and branch state afterwards.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Opening enormous pull requests that are difficult to reason about.
  • Writing a PR description that only repeats the title.
  • Approving a change without reading the actual diff.
  • Bypassing protection because a check is inconvenient instead of understanding why it failed.

docs.title: Knowledge Check
docs.text:
1. What information should a useful pull request provide?
  2. When is a draft pull request appropriate?
  3. How do branch protections improve a team workflow?
  4. What should you focus on during code review?

docs.title: Module 07 - GitHub Features
docs.text: GitHub can act as more than remote Git storage. Issues, labels, milestones, Projects, Discussions and repository settings provide lightweight engineering workflow around the code. The goal is to use only the features that improve visibility and control, not to add administration for its own sake.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Understand the core concepts in this module.
  • Use the relevant Git/GitHub commands deliberately.
  • Validate repository state before and after a change.
  • Recognise common failure modes and choose a safe recovery path.

docs.title: Issues and labels
docs.text:
Issues track work, defects, questions or improvements. Labels add categorisation such as bug, documentation, security, priority-high or team ownership.

A label scheme should be small enough that people actually use it. Too many overlapping labels create noise rather than useful filtering.

docs.title: Milestones
docs.text: Milestones group issues and pull requests around a delivery goal such as v1.0 or Q4 platform baseline. They are most useful when the group has a clear outcome and end point.

docs.title: GitHub Projects
docs.text:
Projects can provide a board or table view of issues and pull requests. A simple Agile-style project might use:

Backlog -> Ready -> In Progress -> Review -> Done

The board should reflect work state rather than becoming a second source of truth that must be manually reconciled with issues.

docs.title: Discussions
docs.text: Discussions suit open-ended conversation, design questions and community knowledge that do not yet represent actionable work. Once a decision creates a concrete task, capture that task as an issue or pull request.

docs.title: Repository documentation
docs.text: A repository should explain what it is, how to use it and how to contribute. Typical files include: - README.md - CONTRIBUTING.md - SECURITY.md - architecture/runbook documents - issue and pull request templates where they genuinely reduce ambiguity

docs.title: Repository settings
docs.text: Important settings include default branch, merge methods, branch/ruleset protection, Actions permissions and access management. Repository settings are part of the engineering system and should be reviewed deliberately rather than left as unknown defaults.

docs.title: Automation awareness
docs.text: GitHub Actions can run on events such as pushes and pull requests. Even before writing workflows, understand that repository changes can trigger automation. A commit may therefore cause tests, builds or deployments outside Git itself.

docs.title: Command Walkthrough
docs.text:
gh repo view
gh issue list
gh issue create --title "Document recovery procedure" --body "Add a short recovery section and validation steps."
gh pr list
gh run list

Run these commands in a disposable repository and read the output after each step. The output is part of the lesson; do not treat commands as a script to paste without understanding.

docs.title: Practical Lab
docs.text:
1. Create three small issues in a disposable repository.
  2. Add a minimal label set.
  3. Create a Project with Backlog, In Progress, Review and Done states.
  4. Move one issue through the workflow by creating a branch and pull request.
  5. Add or improve the README so a new engineer can identify the repository purpose and basic workflow.
  6. Review repository settings and write down which protections you would apply to main.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Creating project-management structure that nobody maintains.
  • Using Discussions for work that needs an owner and completion criteria.
  • Leaving repository purpose or setup undocumented.
  • Changing repository settings without understanding their effect on CI or merge behaviour.

docs.title: Knowledge Check
docs.text:
1. When should work be an issue rather than a Discussion?
  2. What makes a useful label scheme?
  3. Why can a Project become harmful if it duplicates other tracking?
  4. Which repository settings directly affect change safety?

docs.title: Module 08 - Tags and Releases
docs.text: Commits identify every change, but releases need human-friendly version markers. Git tags identify important commits; GitHub Releases can then attach release notes and artefacts to those versions.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Understand the core concepts in this module.
  • Use the relevant Git/GitHub commands deliberately.
  • Validate repository state before and after a change.
  • Recognise common failure modes and choose a safe recovery path.

docs.title: Lightweight and annotated tags
docs.text:
A lightweight tag is simply a name pointing to a commit. An annotated tag stores extra metadata such as tagger, date and message.

Create an annotated tag:

git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Release v1.0.0"

Inspect it:

git show v1.0.0

docs.title: Tags are not pushed automatically
docs.text:
Creating a tag locally does not automatically publish it:

git push origin v1.0.0

You can push multiple intended tags with git push --tags, but explicit tag pushes are often clearer in controlled release workflows.

docs.title: Semantic Versioning
docs.text:
Semantic Versioning uses a MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH pattern: - MAJOR for incompatible changes - MINOR for backward-compatible functionality - PATCH for backward-compatible fixes

Not every project needs SemVer, but a predictable version scheme makes release communication easier.

docs.title: GitHub Releases
docs.text: A GitHub Release usually corresponds to a tag and can include release notes, links and downloadable artefacts. The release notes should explain user-visible or operational changes rather than dump raw commit messages.

docs.title: Release traceability
docs.text:
A useful release answers: - which commit was released? - what changed? - what validation passed? - are there migrations or operational steps? - how can we return to the previous version?

For infrastructure, a tag can identify the exact configuration used for a controlled deployment, but the runtime state still needs independent validation.

docs.title: Moving tags is dangerous
docs.text: Published tags are expected to be stable references. Re-pointing an existing release tag creates ambiguity because different users may have cached different objects. If a release is wrong, normally create a new corrected version instead of silently moving the existing tag.

docs.title: Command Walkthrough
docs.text:
git log --oneline -5
git tag -a v0.1.0 -m "Training release v0.1.0"
git show v0.1.0
git push origin v0.1.0
git tag --list

Run these commands in a disposable repository and read the output after each step. The output is part of the lesson; do not treat commands as a script to paste without understanding.

docs.title: Practical Lab
docs.text:
1. Choose a clean commit from your training repository.
  2. Create annotated tag v0.1.0.
  3. Inspect the tag and commit.
  4. Push the tag.
  5. Create a GitHub Release from it.
  6. Write release notes with Summary, Changes, Validation and Rollback sections.
  7. Make another small change and release v0.1.1 rather than moving v0.1.0.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming a local tag is already on the remote.
  • Moving a published release tag instead of creating a corrective release.
  • Using version numbers without defining what they mean for the project.
  • Creating release notes that provide no operational context.

docs.title: Knowledge Check
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between a branch and a tag?
  2. Why are annotated tags useful for releases?
  3. What does Semantic Versioning communicate?
  4. Why should published release tags normally be immutable?

docs.title: Module 09 - Git Workflows
docs.text: A Git workflow is an agreement about how branches, reviews and releases are used. There is no universal best workflow. The right choice minimises risk and coordination overhead for the team and delivery model.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Understand the core concepts in this module.
  • Use the relevant Git/GitHub commands deliberately.
  • Validate repository state before and after a change.
  • Recognise common failure modes and choose a safe recovery path.

docs.title: GitHub Flow
docs.text:
GitHub Flow is straightforward: 1. create a branch from main 2. make and push commits 3. open a pull request 4. review and run checks 5. merge to main 6. deploy or release from the main line

It works well when main is kept in a releasable state and changes are small.

docs.title: Trunk-based development
docs.text:
Trunk-based development keeps integration close to one main branch. Engineers use very short-lived branches or commit directly under strong controls. Feature flags may separate deployment from feature exposure.

The benefit is reducing long-lived divergence. The cost is that automated testing and disciplined small changes become essential.

docs.title: Git Flow
docs.text:
Git Flow uses more persistent branch roles such as develop, feature branches, release branches and hotfix branches. It can fit products with formal release trains, but it introduces more branch management and merge paths.

Do not adopt it because it sounds more 'enterprise'. Use it only when the release model justifies the extra structure.

docs.title: Infrastructure repositories
docs.text:
Infrastructure often benefits from short-lived feature branches and pull-request validation. Avoid using long-lived environment branches unless you have a clear reason; they can drift and make it difficult to understand which version is authoritative.

A common approach is one main code line with environment-specific variables/configuration and controlled deployment stages.

docs.title: Choosing a workflow
docs.text:
Ask: - how often do we integrate? - must main always be deployable? - how are releases approved? - how long do branches live? - what automated validation exists? - do we need emergency fixes? - what audit/change controls apply?

The workflow is successful when engineers can predict how a change gets from idea to reviewed, tested, deployed state.

docs.title: Command Walkthrough
docs.text:
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
git branch -vv
git status

Run these commands in a disposable repository and read the output after each step. The output is part of the lesson; do not treat commands as a script to paste without understanding.

docs.title: Practical Lab
docs.text: Simulate two workflows in a disposable repository: 1. Complete one change using a short-lived GitHub Flow branch. 2. Record how many branch and merge steps were required. 3. Sketch how the same change would move through Git Flow with develop/release branches. 4. Compare the workflows for a small infrastructure team that deploys frequently. 5. Write a short decision explaining which you would choose and why.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Choosing a complex workflow because it appears more professional.
  • Keeping feature branches open for weeks and accumulating large divergence.
  • Using separate environment branches with no strategy for preventing drift.
  • Defining a workflow that depends on manual memory rather than repository controls and CI.

docs.title: Knowledge Check
docs.text:
1. What assumption does GitHub Flow make about main?
  2. What problem does trunk-based development try to reduce?
  3. When might Git Flow be justified?
  4. Which workflow would you choose for an IaC repository and why?

docs.title: Module 10 - Advanced Git
docs.text: Advanced Git commands are powerful because they manipulate history and work in progress. The aim is not to use them frequently; it is to understand exactly which commands are safe before publication, which create new corrective history, and which can destroy unreferenced work.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Understand the core concepts in this module.
  • Use the relevant Git/GitHub commands deliberately.
  • Validate repository state before and after a change.
  • Recognise common failure modes and choose a safe recovery path.

docs.title: Stash
docs.text:
git stash temporarily records tracked working changes so you can switch context:

git stash push -m "WIP monitoring change"
git stash list
git stash show -p stash@{0}
git stash pop

A stash is convenient temporary storage, not a substitute for meaningful commits or long-term backup.

docs.title: Rebase
docs.text:
Rebase replays commits onto a new base. A common feature-branch use is:

git switch feature/example
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main

This rewrites the feature commits, giving them new hashes. That is normally acceptable on your own unpublished or explicitly coordinated branch, but dangerous on shared history because collaborators may still have the old commits.

docs.title: Interactive rebase
docs.text:
git rebase -i can reorder, squash, reword or drop commits before review. It is useful for cleaning your own local feature history.

Do not use history rewriting to hide mistakes that should remain visible for audit, and do not rewrite shared protected branches.

docs.title: Cherry-pick
docs.text: git cherry-pick <commit> applies the change represented by a specific commit onto the current branch. It is useful for deliberately copying a fix between lines of development, but routine cherry-picking can create duplicated history and complicate future merges.

docs.title: Revert
docs.text:
git revert <commit> creates a new commit that applies the inverse of an earlier commit. This is usually the safest way to undo a bad change that has already been shared:

git revert <commit>

Because history is preserved, collaborators do not need to reconcile rewritten branch state.

docs.title: Reset
docs.text:
git reset moves a branch reference and can also change the index and working tree. Its modes matter: - --soft: move HEAD, keep changes staged - mixed/default: move HEAD, keep changes in working tree - --hard: move HEAD and overwrite tracked working-tree changes

--hard can discard uncommitted work. Use reset mainly for local history you control.

docs.title: Reflog
docs.text:
The reflog records where local references such as HEAD have pointed:

git reflog

If you reset or move a branch incorrectly, the previous commit often remains recoverable through the reflog until Git eventually prunes unreachable objects. Reflog is local; it is not a remote audit history.

docs.title: Command Walkthrough
docs.text:
git status
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
git stash list
git reflog

Run these commands in a disposable repository and read the output after each step. The output is part of the lesson; do not treat commands as a script to paste without understanding.

docs.title: Practical Lab
docs.text: Use a disposable repository: 1. Create three commits. 2. Make an uncommitted change and stash it. 3. Create a feature branch with two commits. 4. Rebase that branch onto a new commit on main. 5. Cherry-pick one harmless commit onto another test branch. 6. Revert a published-style test commit. 7. Create a disposable commit, reset it locally, then recover its hash using git reflog. 8. Do not use these exercises on important shared history.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Rebasing commits that other people already use without coordination.
  • Using reset --hard as a generic undo command.
  • Cherry-picking repeatedly instead of fixing the underlying branch strategy.
  • Assuming reflog exists on GitHub or on another engineer's clone.

docs.title: Knowledge Check
docs.text:
1. Why does rebase change commit hashes?
  2. Why is revert usually safer for shared history?
  3. What can reset --hard destroy?
  4. What problem can reflog help recover from?

docs.title: Module 11 - Git for DevOps
docs.text: In DevOps and infrastructure engineering, Git is often the review and audit boundary for changes that eventually affect real systems. This increases the importance of small commits, automated validation, secrets handling and clear deployment evidence.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Understand the core concepts in this module.
  • Use the relevant Git/GitHub commands deliberately.
  • Validate repository state before and after a change.
  • Recognise common failure modes and choose a safe recovery path.

docs.title: Infrastructure as Code as source
docs.text:
Terraform, Ansible, Kubernetes manifests and CI/CD definitions are text-based desired state, which makes them natural Git content.

A repository might contain:

platform/
├── README.md
├── docs/
├── terraform/
├── ansible/
├── kubernetes/
├── scripts/
└── .github/workflows/

The repository should explain how those pieces relate and which automation can make changes to infrastructure.

docs.title: Plan before apply
docs.text:
For Terraform-style workflows, the pull request should normally produce validation and a plan before any apply step. The plan helps reviewers understand expected infrastructure changes.

A safe conceptual flow:

branch -> pull request -> fmt/validate -> plan -> review -> merge -> controlled apply -> verify

The exact deployment trigger depends on risk and organisational controls.

docs.title: Configuration management
docs.text: Ansible changes also benefit from source control and review. Linting, syntax checks and check mode can provide evidence before execution, but check mode is not perfect for every module. Actual post-change validation still matters.

docs.title: Kubernetes and GitOps
docs.text:
A GitOps controller such as Argo CD or Flux can continuously reconcile cluster state from Git. In that model, merging a repository change may be equivalent to authorising a deployment.

That makes branch protection, review and repository security part of the production control plane.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
Never commit: - cloud credentials - private keys - access tokens - unencrypted password files - Terraform state containing sensitive values

Use an approved secret store or encrypted secret workflow. If a secret is committed, deleting the file in a later commit does not erase it from earlier history. Rotate the credential first.

docs.title: CI/CD evidence
docs.text:
A pipeline should answer what was validated: - syntax/lint - unit or integration tests - security scans where useful - rendered configuration or plan - artefact/image identity - deployment result - health checks after change

Passing CI does not prove an infrastructure change is risk-free, but it reduces avoidable mistakes and creates repeatable evidence.

docs.title: Environment design
docs.text:
Prefer one source of truth with explicit environment inputs rather than manually divergent copies. Examples include directories such as environments/dev and environments/prod, parameter files, or pipeline environment selection.

The design must make it obvious which code version is intended for each environment.

docs.title: Command Walkthrough
docs.text:
git status
git diff main...HEAD
git log --oneline --decorate main..HEAD
git grep -n -E '(password|token|secret|private_key)' -- ':!*.md' || true

Run these commands in a disposable repository and read the output after each step. The output is part of the lesson; do not treat commands as a script to paste without understanding.

docs.title: Practical Lab
docs.text: Create a small Infrastructure as Code change in a disposable repository: 1. Add a simple Terraform, Ansible or Kubernetes configuration. 2. Create a feature branch for one change. 3. Add validation commands to the README. 4. Add a CI workflow or documented CI design that runs validation on pull requests. 5. Generate the plan/rendered output locally. 6. Review the Git diff and generated evidence separately. 7. Open a pull request with Risk, Validation and Rollback sections. 8. Confirm no credentials or generated state files are tracked.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating a green pipeline as permission to ignore the actual diff.
  • Committing Terraform state or credentials.
  • Mixing unrelated infrastructure changes in one PR.
  • Allowing automation to deploy from an unprotected branch with no review boundary.

docs.title: Knowledge Check
docs.text:
1. Why is Git especially important when repositories can trigger deployments?
  2. What evidence should an IaC pull request provide?
  3. Why is deleting a leaked secret in a later commit insufficient?
  4. What changes about Git controls in a GitOps model?

docs.title: Module Completion Criteria
docs.text:
• [ ] I can explain the module without reading the command list.
  • [ ] I completed the practical lab in a disposable repository.
  • [ ] I inspected the resulting history/state.
  • [ ] I can explain one safe recovery action.

docs.title: Module 12 - Git Best Practices
docs.text: Best practices are habits that make a repository easier to review, recover and hand over. The goal is not a long rulebook. A professional repository should make the safe path obvious and the history understandable.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Understand the core concepts in this module.
  • Use the relevant Git/GitHub commands deliberately.
  • Validate repository state before and after a change.
  • Recognise common failure modes and choose a safe recovery path.

docs.title: Small coherent commits
docs.text:
Each commit should have one purpose. This improves review, rollback, bisecting and history.

Before committing: 

git status
git diff
git diff --staged

If the staged diff contains two unrelated reasons for change, consider splitting it.

docs.title: Commit messages
docs.text:
A useful subject is short and specific:

Add health check to Grafana container
Fix DNS resolver validation
Document Proxmox backup recovery

For larger changes, the commit body can explain why the change was needed and any non-obvious trade-off.

docs.title: README and operational documentation
docs.text:
A new engineer should be able to discover: - repository purpose - prerequisites - how to validate/test - how changes reach an environment - where secrets come from - recovery or rollback expectations - ownership/contact information where appropriate

Documentation that cannot survive repository handover is a support risk.

docs.title: Protected default branch
docs.text: For important repositories, protect the default branch with pull requests and relevant required checks. Avoid routine direct pushes by administrators because bypass culture undermines the value of controls.

docs.title: Repository security
docs.text:
Use least-privilege access and remove stale collaborators. Enable secret scanning/dependency/security features where available and appropriate. Do not expose secrets in examples, screenshots, logs or Actions output.

Consider CODEOWNERS when specific paths require specialist review, such as networking, security or production deployment files.

docs.title: Signed commits and tags
docs.text: Cryptographic signing can provide stronger evidence about who created a commit or tag. Whether to require signing depends on the organisation's threat model and operational overhead. It is a useful control, not a replacement for code review.

docs.title: Repository hygiene
docs.text: Keep generated output, caches and temporary files out of source control unless they are deliberately required artefacts. Remove merged branches, prune stale remote references and periodically review repository settings and workflows.

docs.title: Recovery mindset
docs.text:
Before a risky history operation, identify: - what commit/reference you are on - whether the history is shared - whether uncommitted changes exist - how you can recover

Commands such as git status, git log --graph --all and git reflog should come before destructive guesses.

docs.title: Command Walkthrough
docs.text:
git status
git diff --staged
git log --oneline --graph --decorate -15
git branch -vv
git remote -v
git ls-files

Run these commands in a disposable repository and read the output after each step. The output is part of the lesson; do not treat commands as a script to paste without understanding.

docs.title: Practical Lab
docs.text: Audit one of your own repositories: 1. Read the README as if you had never seen the project. 2. Review the last ten commit messages. 3. Check the default branch protections/rules. 4. Review tracked files for generated output or secrets risk. 5. Check stale branches. 6. Confirm how validation runs before merge. 7. Add a short REPOSITORY-STANDARDS.md or improve existing documentation with the standards you actually want to follow. 8. Open the change through the normal branch and PR workflow.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Creating a huge standards document nobody follows.
  • Protecting branches without ensuring required checks are reliable.
  • Putting sensitive values into examples because they are 'only documentation'.
  • Cleaning history with destructive commands when a normal revert would be safer.

docs.title: Knowledge Check
docs.text:
1. What makes a commit useful to a future reviewer?
  2. Which controls would you apply to an important default branch?
  3. When might CODEOWNERS help?
  4. What should you check before rewriting history?

docs.text:

  • [ ] I inspected the resulting history/state.
  • [ ] I can explain one safe recovery action.

docs.title: GitHub Enterprise Server Installation & Administration Training
docs.text:
Draft course refresh: installation-first learning path for review. Do not publish this branch until approved.

This course is centred on installing GitHub Enterprise Server (GHES) and bringing the appliance into service. Administration, security, identity, repositories, Actions and operations are taught as supporting skills around a successful installation.

docs.title: What You Will Build
docs.text:
By the end of the course you should be able to take GHES from an approved design to a working, supportable platform:

  • choose a supported deployment platform
  • size CPU, memory and storage using current GitHub guidance
  • design DNS, TLS and firewall requirements
  • build a lab or staging appliance
  • deploy the GHES appliance
  • use the Management Console for initial setup
  • apply the licence, hostname and TLS configuration
  • validate administrator access
  • configure identity
  • create the first organisation, team and repository
  • prove Git clone, branch, push and pull-request workflows
  • configure backup and monitoring
  • plan upgrade and recovery
  • hand over the platform with installation evidence and runbooks

docs.text:
1. Installation orientation
  2. Plan the deployment
  3. Build the lab or staging environment
  4. Install GitHub Enterprise Server
  5. Complete initial configuration
  6. Configure identity and access
  7. Prove repository services
  8. Apply the security baseline
  9. Add GitHub Actions if required
  10. Operate, back up, upgrade and recover
  11. Complete the installation project

docs.title: GitHub Enterprise Overview
docs.text: GitHub Enterprise Server is a self-hosted appliance that provides repositories, pull requests, issues, projects, packages, automation and security controls.

docs.title: Enterprise Use Cases
docs.text: Typical uses include private source-code hosting, internal developer collaboration, regulated workloads, secure software delivery and platform engineering.

docs.title: Core Platform Capabilities
docs.text:
• Git repositories
  • Pull requests and reviews
  • Issues and projects
  • GitHub Actions
  • Packages and registries
  • Security and audit capabilities

docs.title: Appliance Architecture
docs.text: GitHub Enterprise Server is delivered as a managed virtual appliance. Administrators manage the platform through the Management Console and enterprise administration interfaces.

docs.title: Supporting Services
docs.text: Common dependencies include DNS, NTP, SMTP, identity providers, backup storage and monitoring systems.

docs.title: Traffic Flow
docs.text: Users access the web interface and Git repositories through HTTPS or SSH. Administrators should document network paths, ports and trust boundaries.

docs.title: Summary

docs.title: Enterprise Hierarchy
docs.text:
Enterprise
└── Organisations
    ├── Teams
    ├── Repositories
    └── Members

docs.title: Organisations
docs.text: Organisations provide collaboration and governance boundaries for departments, products or engineering groups.

docs.title: Teams and Repositories
docs.text: Teams simplify permission management. Repositories contain code, history, issues, pull requests, releases and automation.

docs.title: On-Premises Deployment
docs.text: Suitable where organisations require direct infrastructure control, local data residency or integration with private networks.

docs.title: Cloud Deployment
docs.text: Cloud deployments can provide flexible infrastructure, resilient storage and integration with existing cloud services.

docs.title: Selection Criteria

docs.title: Security Layers
docs.text: Security includes identity verification, permissions, branch policies, secret protection, audit logging, backup protection and monitoring.

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text: Users and administrators should receive only the access required for their responsibilities.

docs.title: Operational Security
docs.text: Keep the appliance updated, protect administrative access, review audit activity and test recovery procedures.

docs.title: Lesson 07 - Planning a GitHub Enterprise Server Installation
Goal
docs.text: Turn the request to install GHES into a buildable infrastructure design.

docs.title: What You Need to Know
docs.text:
• Capture user count, repository growth, GitHub Actions usage, availability target, RPO/RTO and authentication requirements.
  • Identify dependencies before deployment: platform, DNS, TLS, networking, identity, SMTP, backup and monitoring.
  • Assign an accountable owner to every dependency.
  • Define measurable go/no-go criteria before the change window.

docs.title: Installation Workflow
docs.text:
1. Document service and workload requirements.
  2. Select a supported deployment platform for the intended GHES release.
  3. Create an architecture/dependency diagram.
  4. Create a responsibility matrix.
  5. Create a staged build, configuration, validation and handover plan.

docs.title: Hands-On Exercise
docs.text:
1. Design a GHES installation for a fictional 150-user engineering organisation.
  2. Name the platform, hostname, network zone, backup target and identity approach.
  3. Define RPO/RTO and five go/no-go checks.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] Every dependency has an owner.
  • [ ] Recovery objectives are explicit.
  • [ ] Hostname/network/storage decisions are recorded.
  • [ ] Production acceptance criteria are measurable.

docs.title: Common Installation Mistakes
docs.text:
• Starting the VM build before DNS/TLS/storage ownership is agreed.
  • Designing only for first boot and forgetting backup or upgrades.
  • Using vague ownership such as 'the infrastructure team' without a named responsibility.

docs.title: Goal

docs.title: What You Need to Know
docs.text:
• GHES sizing depends on licence/user count and workload.
  • GitHub Actions, packages and code-security workloads can increase resource needs.
  • Root and attached data storage must follow the selected platform guide.
  • Capacity monitoring is part of sizing because estimates change after go-live.

docs.title: Installation Workflow
docs.text:
1. Find the hardware table for the exact GHES release and selected platform.
  2. Record the matching CPU and memory recommendation.
  3. Record root storage, attached data storage and storage-performance requirements.
  4. Add growth headroom.

  2. Record the GitHub sizing reference used.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] Chosen size can be traced to current GitHub guidance.
  • [ ] Storage design includes growth headroom.
  • [ ] Performance assumptions are documented.
  • [ ] Capacity alert thresholds have an owner.

docs.title: Common Installation Mistakes
docs.text:
• Using an old sizing table because it exists in a previous design.
  • Counting repositories but ignoring Actions or package workload.
  • Leaving no storage headroom for growth and maintenance.

docs.title: Next Lesson
docs.text: Continue to Network and DNS Planning.

docs.title: Lesson 09 - Network, DNS and Port Planning
Goal
docs.text: Prove every required network path before appliance configuration.

docs.title: What You Need to Know
docs.text:
• TCP 443 serves the web application and Git over HTTPS.
  • TCP 22 is used for Git over SSH.
  • TCP 8443 is the secure Management Console.
  • TCP 122 is the administrative shell.
  • Additional features can require additional ports, so the full current GitHub port list must be reviewed.

docs.title: Installation Workflow
docs.text:
1. Choose a stable FQDN.
  2. Confirm authoritative DNS ownership and record timing.
  3. Create a source/destination/port matrix.
  4. Separate user-facing access from management access.
  5. Confirm proxy/outbound access for the features you intend to enable.

docs.title: Hands-On Exercise
docs.text:
1. Draw developer and administrator access paths to GHES.
  2. Create firewall rules for user HTTPS/Git and separate admin access.
  3. Explain why TCP 22 and TCP 122 are different services.
  4. Document DNS and TLS dependencies.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] Hostname resolves from intended client networks.
  • [ ] Management interfaces are not broadly exposed.
  • [ ] User web and Git paths can be tested independently.
  • [ ] DNS and firewall ownership are recorded.

docs.title: Common Installation Mistakes
docs.text:
• Opening all documented GHES ports to every network.
  • Confusing Git SSH on 22 with administrative SSH on 122.
  • Choosing a temporary hostname that later becomes embedded in clone URLs.

docs.title: Next Lesson
docs.text: Continue to Storage, Backup and Recovery Planning.

docs.title: Lesson 10 - Storage, Backup and Recovery Planning
Goal
docs.text: Design storage and recovery before production repositories are created.

docs.title: What You Need to Know
docs.text:
• GHES platform data needs supported persistent storage.
  • High availability is not a substitute for an independent backup.
  • Use the backup method supported by the GHES release you operate.
  • Restore testing is the evidence that a backup strategy works.

docs.title: Installation Workflow
docs.text:
1. Record root and data storage design.
  2. Define backup destination outside the appliance failure domain.
  3. Set frequency and retention from the agreed RPO.
  4. Monitor backup success and storage consumption.
  5. Schedule restore exercises and record achieved RTO.

docs.title: Hands-On Exercise
docs.text:
1. Design a backup policy for a four-hour RPO and eight-hour RTO.
  2. Define monitoring for backup failure.
  3. Write the acceptance criteria for a quarterly restore test.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] Backup destination is independent of production.
  • [ ] Backup failures create an actionable alert.
  • [ ] Restore tests have a schedule and owner.
  • [ ] Version compatibility is checked before restore.

docs.title: Common Installation Mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating a replica as the backup.
  • Running backups without monitoring whether they complete.
  • Never performing a restore exercise.

docs.title: Next Lesson
docs.text: Continue to Licensing and Prerequisites.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Ensure every installation-blocking input is ready before the build starts.

docs.title: What You Need to Know
docs.text:
• A valid GitHub Enterprise licence and supported appliance/platform are required.
  • Hostname, DNS, IP addressing, storage and management access should be ready before setup.
  • TLS, identity, SMTP, backup and monitoring need planned ownership.
  • Access to the virtualisation/cloud platform is itself a prerequisite.

docs.title: Installation Workflow
docs.text:
1. Create a prerequisite register.
  2. Assign owner and evidence to every item.
  3. Mark which items block installation and which block production acceptance.
  4. Run the register as a formal readiness check.

docs.title: Hands-On Exercise
docs.text:
1. Build a table with Item, Owner, Status, Evidence and Blocking columns.
  2. Include licence, image, platform, sizing, DNS, TLS, network, storage, backup and monitoring.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] No blocking prerequisite is marked TBC.
  • [ ] Licence and supported platform are verified.
  • [ ] DNS/TLS/network prerequisites have evidence.
  • [ ] Production-readiness dependencies are visible.

docs.title: Common Installation Mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming the licence or certificate will arrive during the change window.
  • Having no named owner for DNS or firewall changes.
  • Discovering after deployment that the chosen platform is unsupported.

docs.title: Next Lesson
docs.text: Continue to Installation Readiness Review.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Turn the design into an executable installation plan and make a formal go/no-go decision.

docs.title: What You Need to Know
docs.text:
• A readiness checklist must contain evidence, not just tick boxes.
  • The change plan needs build, configuration, validation, rollback and handover stages.
  • Go/no-go criteria should be decided before the change begins.
  • Operational readiness belongs in the installation definition of done.

docs.title: Installation Workflow
docs.text:
1. Complete the pre-install checklist.
  2. Review all blocking dependencies.
  3. Write the step-by-step build sequence.
  4. Define rollback/recovery criteria.
  5. Define post-install validation.
  6. Record the readiness decision.

docs.title: Hands-On Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run a mock go/no-go review.
  2. Mark one dependency as failed and explain whether the installation can safely continue.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] All blockers are closed or explicitly accepted.
  • [ ] Rollback/recovery is defined.
  • [ ] Validation covers real user workflows.
  • [ ] Handover activities are included.

docs.title: Common Installation Mistakes
docs.text:
• Using vague checks such as 'network OK'.
  • Deciding rollback criteria after a failure has already occurred.
  • Treating successful VM deployment as completed service delivery.

docs.title: Next Lesson
docs.text: Continue to Building the GitHub Enterprise Server Lab Environment.

docs.title: Module 03 - Build the Lab or Staging Environment
docs.text: Practise the real installation on a supported platform before it becomes a production change.

docs.title: Lesson
docs.text: 1. Building the GitHub Enterprise Server Lab Environment

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: You will have a reproducible environment with documented sizing, storage, DNS, network and admin-access paths.

docs.title: Lesson 13 - Building the GitHub Enterprise Server Lab Environment
Goal
docs.text: Prepare a realistic, isolated environment in which the full installation can be practised.

docs.title: What You Need to Know
docs.text:
• Use a platform supported by the GHES release you are testing.
  • Keep lab DNS, users and credentials separate from production.
  • Record appliance version, VM sizing and storage layout.
  • Restrict management access even in the lab.

docs.title: Installation Workflow
docs.text:
1. Choose the supported platform.
  2. Create the VM/cloud instance from the correct appliance image.
  3. Attach root and required data storage.
  4. Connect the intended network.
  5. Create or reserve DNS.
  6. Validate admin access to 8443 and 122 and user access to 443 and 22.

docs.title: Hands-On Exercise
docs.text:
1. Create a lab build record with version, image, platform, CPU, memory, disks, hostname, IP and admin source network.
  2. Draw the four main access paths: web, Git SSH, Management Console and admin shell.
  3. Document how the lab can be reset for another installation attempt.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] Lab hostname resolves.
  • [ ] Management ports are restricted.
  • [ ] Supported sizing is used.
  • [ ] The installation can be reproduced from the build record.

docs.title: Common Installation Mistakes
docs.text:
• Using an unsupported hypervisor for the main installation exercise.
  • Reusing production credentials.
  • Building a disposable lab that cannot be reproduced.

docs.title: Next Lesson
docs.text: Continue to Installing GitHub Enterprise Server.

docs.title: Module 04 - Install GitHub Enterprise Server
docs.text: This is the core appliance-installation module.

docs.title: Lesson
docs.text: 1. Installing GitHub Enterprise Server

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: You will deploy the appliance, complete Management Console setup and prove normal user and administrator access.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Take the prepared platform from an appliance image to a functioning GHES instance.

docs.title: What You Need to Know
docs.text:
• Deploy the appliance image that matches both the GHES release and supported platform.
  • The secure Management Console is reached over HTTPS on TCP 8443.
  • Normal Git SSH uses TCP 22; the administrative shell uses TCP 122.
  • The final hostname should align with DNS, TLS, clone URLs, identity and documentation.

docs.title: Installation Workflow
docs.text:
1. Deploy or launch the appliance on the selected supported platform.
  2. Attach the storage required by the platform-specific guide.
  3. Power on and validate IP, routing and DNS.
  4. Open the Management Console on HTTPS port 8443.
  5. Upload the GitHub Enterprise licence and set the Management Console password.
  6. Configure the intended hostname and required settings.
  7. Apply configuration and allow the appliance to restart/apply changes as required.
  8. Configure a trusted TLS certificate for production use.
  9. Validate administrative shell access from the approved admin network.
  10. Create the first user/admin context according to the current GitHub setup flow.

docs.title: Hands-On Exercise
docs.text:
1. Create a disposable repository after setup.
  2. Clone it using the intended protocol.
  3. Create a branch and push one commit.
  4. Open a pull request to prove the application workflow.
  5. Record GHES version, install date, platform, sizing, storage, hostname and owners.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] Web interface works on the intended hostname.
  • [ ] TLS is trusted by intended clients.
  • [ ] Management Console is reachable only from intended admin networks.
  • [ ] Administrative shell on 122 is tested.
  • [ ] Git clone and push work.
  • [ ] Installation record is stored.

docs.title: Common Installation Mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating 'VM powered on' as successful installation.
  • Using an IP address as the long-term service identity.
  • Leaving Management Console/admin SSH exposed to broad user networks.
  • Disabling TLS verification instead of fixing certificate trust.
  • Changing appliance internals outside supported GitHub procedures.

docs.title: Next Lesson
docs.text: Continue to Initial Configuration.

docs.title: Module 05 - Complete Initial Configuration
docs.text: A running appliance is not yet a production-ready service.

docs.title: Lessons
docs.text:
1. Initial Configuration
  2. Create the First Organisation and Prove the Platform

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: You will complete the service baseline and prove the first real collaboration workflow.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Move from successful appliance setup to an operational service baseline.

docs.title: What You Need to Know
docs.text:
• DNS and TLS should be stable before wider onboarding.
  • Identity and SMTP should be configured only after their dependencies are understood.
  • Backup and monitoring are part of initial readiness, not later nice-to-have work.
  • Optional services such as Actions should be enabled only when their runner, network and storage requirements are understood.

docs.title: Installation Workflow
docs.text:
1. Confirm final hostname, DNS and TLS.
  2. Confirm administrator access.
  3. Configure SMTP if required.
  4. Configure the intended authentication model.
  5. Review enterprise-level policies.
  6. Configure backup.
  7. Configure monitoring and audit/security integrations.
  8. Enable optional services only when prerequisites are ready.

docs.title: Hands-On Exercise
docs.text:
1. Create an initial-configuration record showing every enabled integration and its owner.
  2. Run the repository Post-Installation Validation checklist.
  3. Record a baseline platform health state before onboarding users.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] Certificate is trusted.
  • [ ] Authentication works for intended users/admins.
  • [ ] Backup is active.
  • [ ] Monitoring can detect service/backup problems.
  • [ ] Enabled integrations have owners.

docs.title: Common Installation Mistakes
docs.text:
• Onboarding users before backup and monitoring exist.
  • Changing identity without a recovery route.
  • Enabling Actions before runner/security ownership is agreed.

docs.title: Next Lesson
docs.text: Continue to Create the First Organisation and Prove the Platform.

docs.title: Lesson 16 - Create the First Organisation and Prove the Platform
Goal
docs.text: Use a complete repository workflow as the installation acceptance test.

docs.title: What You Need to Know
docs.text:
• Organisation ownership should not depend on one person.
  • Teams scale access better than individual repository grants.
  • A real clone/branch/push/pull-request test validates more of the platform than simply loading the homepage.
  • Normal users should not need site-admin permissions.

docs.title: Installation Workflow
docs.text:
1. Create the first lab or production organisation.
  2. Assign accountable organisation owners.
  3. Create initial teams.
  4. Create a disposable validation repository.
  5. Grant team-based access.
  6. Test Git and pull-request workflows using a normal user.

docs.title: Hands-On Exercise
docs.text:
1. Clone the validation repository.
  2. Create a feature branch.
  3. Commit and push a small file.
  4. Open, review and merge a pull request according to the intended policy.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] Repository lives in the intended organisation.
  • [ ] Normal user can work without owner/admin rights.
  • [ ] Git transport works.
  • [ ] Pull-request workflow works.
  • [ ] Team permissions behave as designed.

docs.title: Common Installation Mistakes
docs.text:
• Testing everything with the site-admin account.
  • Granting users directly instead of testing the team model.
  • Calling the install complete without performing a Git operation.

docs.title: Lesson 31 - Backup, Monitoring, Upgrades and Recovery
Goal
docs.text: Create the day-two operating model for the newly installed appliance.

docs.title: What You Need to Know
docs.text:
• Monitor instance health, capacity, backup completion, certificates and integrations.
  • Use the backup method supported by the installed GHES release.
  • Read release notes and supported upgrade paths before every upgrade.
  • Recovery exercises are part of platform assurance.

docs.title: Installation Workflow
docs.text:
1. Define daily/weekly health and capacity checks.
  2. Configure and monitor backups.
  3. Schedule restore testing.
  4. Create an upgrade runbook with pre-checks, backup, maintenance communication and post-change validation.
  5. Create a certificate-renewal procedure.
  6. Create an escalation path for platform incidents.

docs.title: Hands-On Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write a quarterly recovery-test plan.
  2. Write an upgrade checklist that validates login, clone, push, pull requests, integrations and backup after change.
  3. Measure whether the recovery exercise meets RTO/RPO.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• [ ] Backup failures alert an owner.
  • [ ] Restore testing is scheduled.
  • [ ] Upgrade validation covers real user workflows.
  • [ ] Certificate expiry is monitored.
  • [ ] Support/escalation ownership is documented.

docs.title: Common Installation Mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming a successful backup job proves restore will work.
  • Upgrading without reading the version-specific upgrade path.
  • Failing to test Git operations after maintenance.
  • Letting certificate renewal depend on one person's calendar.

docs.title: Lesson 32 - GHES Installation and Handover Project
Scenario
docs.text:
Your organisation has approved a new GitHub Enterprise Server deployment. You are responsible for taking the service from design to installation, validation and operational handover.

Use a supported lab/staging appliance where available. If licensing prevents a live build, produce the same artefacts as a reviewed installation design.

docs.title: Deliverable 1 - Installation Design
docs.text:
Document:

  • target GHES release
  • supported deployment platform
  • workload/user assumptions
  • CPU and memory sizing
  • root/data storage
  • hostname and IP
  • DNS
  • firewall rules
  • TLS
  • identity
  • SMTP where required
  • backup
  • monitoring

docs.title: Deliverable 2 - Readiness Gate
docs.text: Complete the repository Pre-Installation Checklist with no blocking item left as TBC.

docs.title: Deliverable 3 - Appliance Deployment
docs.text:
Document or perform:

  1. deploy appliance image
  2. attach required storage
  3. configure network
  4. access Management Console
  5. upload licence
  6. set Management Console password
  7. configure hostname
  8. configure TLS
  9. apply settings

docs.title: Deliverable 4 - Access Validation
docs.text:
Explain and validate the four primary access paths:

Port Purpose 443 web / Git HTTPS 22 Git SSH 8443 Management Console 122 admin shell

docs.title: Deliverable 5 - Application Validation
docs.text: Create an organisation, team and repository. Then perform clone, branch, commit, push, pull request, review and merge using a non-admin workflow.

docs.title: Deliverable 6 - Production Readiness
docs.text:
Provide evidence for:

  • backup configuration
  • backup monitoring
  • restore-test plan
  • monitoring/alerting
  • certificate renewal ownership
  • upgrade procedure
  • support owner
  • escalation path

docs.title: Deliverable 7 - Handover
docs.text: Complete the repository Post-Installation Validation checklist and package the architecture diagram, installation record and operating runbooks.

docs.title: Acceptance Standard
docs.text:
The installation must be:

  • reproducible
  • validated
  • secured
  • backed up
  • monitored
  • documented
  • recoverable

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A hands-on training course covering Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Promtail, exporters, alerting, security monitoring, capacity planning, and production operations.

The course is designed around a practical Docker-based homelab and includes examples using Node Exporter, cAdvisor, BirdNET metrics, CrowdSec metrics, Grafana dashboards, Loki logs, and alerting.

docs.title: Course Modules
docs.text:
• Module 01 - Observability Fundamentals
  • Module 02 - Prometheus
  • Module 03 - Exporters
  • Module 04 - Grafana
  • Module 05 - Loki And Logging
  • Module 06 - Alerting
  • Module 07 - Security Monitoring
  • Module 08 - Performance And Capacity
  • Module 09 - Production Operations
  • Module 10 - Final Project

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This lesson is part of Module 01 - Observability Fundamentals and explains the principles, architecture, implementation approach, validation methods, and operational considerations for What Is Observability.

The lesson is designed to support practical learning in a Linux and Docker-based homelab environment.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Explain the purpose of What Is Observability
  • Identify the key components and dependencies
  • Implement the technology or workflow in a practical lab
  • Validate that the implementation is working
  • Troubleshoot common problems
  • Document the result using Git and Markdown

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Monitoring and observability should follow a repeatable engineering process:

Define the objective
        |
        v
Collect telemetry
        |
        v
Store and query data
        |
        v
Visualise behaviour
        |
        v
Alert on meaningful conditions
        |
        v
Investigate and improve

The implementation should prioritise:

  • Reliability
  • Clear ownership
  • Secure access
  • Useful labels and metadata
  • Low-noise alerting
  • Repeatable deployment
  • Documented recovery procedures

docs.title: Architecture Considerations
docs.text:
Review:

  • Data sources
  • Network connectivity
  • Authentication
  • Storage requirements
  • Retention
  • Scaling
  • Failure modes
  • Backup and recovery
  • Monitoring of the monitoring platform

docs.title: Practical Exercise
docs.text:
1. Review the lesson objectives.
  2. Prepare the required services or containers.
  3. Implement the configuration.
  4. Validate connectivity and data collection.
  5. Query or visualise the results.
  6. Introduce one controlled failure.
  7. Diagnose and resolve the issue.
  8. Record the commands and findings.
  9. Commit the completed lesson evidence to Git.

docs.title: Validation Checklist
docs.text:
• The service is running
  • Metrics or logs are available
  • Labels are meaningful and consistent
  • Queries return expected data
  • Dashboards show useful information
  • Alerts are actionable
  • Security controls have been considered
  • Recovery steps are documented

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Check:

docker ps
docker logs <container>
curl -s http://localhost:<port>/metrics

Review:

  • Service logs
  • Container networking
  • DNS resolution
  • Firewall rules
  • Target configuration
  • Labels
  • Query syntax
  • Data retention and storage capacity

docs.title: Knowledge Check
docs.text:

  2. Which services or dependencies are required?
  3. How would you validate the implementation?
  4. What are the main security considerations?
  5. How would you troubleshoot missing data?
  6. What operational risks should be documented?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: You have reviewed the architecture, implementation, validation, troubleshooting, and operational considerations for What Is Observability.

docs.title: Lesson 56 - Build a Complete Homelab Observability Platform
Overview
docs.text:
This lesson is part of Module 10 - Final Project and explains the principles, architecture, implementation approach, validation methods, and operational considerations for Build a Complete Homelab Observability Platform.

The lesson is designed to support practical learning in a Linux and Docker-based homelab environment.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Explain the purpose of Build a Complete Homelab Observability Platform
  • Identify the key components and dependencies
  • Implement the technology or workflow in a practical lab
  • Validate that the implementation is working
  • Troubleshoot common problems
  • Document the result using Git and Markdown

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Monitoring and observability should follow a repeatable engineering process:

Define the objective
        |
        v
Collect telemetry
        |
        v
Store and query data
        |
        v
Visualise behaviour
        |
        v
Alert on meaningful conditions
        |
        v
Investigate and improve

The implementation should prioritise:

  • Reliability
  • Clear ownership
  • Secure access
  • Useful labels and metadata
  • Low-noise alerting
  • Repeatable deployment
  • Documented recovery procedures

docs.title: Architecture Considerations
docs.text:
Review:

  • Data sources
  • Network connectivity
  • Authentication
  • Storage requirements
  • Retention
  • Scaling
  • Failure modes
  • Backup and recovery
  • Monitoring of the monitoring platform

docs.text:

  7. Diagnose and resolve the issue.
  8. Record the commands and findings.
  9. Commit the completed lesson evidence to Git.

docs.title: Final Linux Administrator Lab
docs.text:
Estimated time: 4–6 hours

Difficulty: Intermediate

Prerequisites: - Complete Modules 01–10

Objective:

Build, secure, troubleshoot, and document a Linux server using the skills learned throughout this training.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You have been given a new Linux server that will be used to host internal services.

Your task is to prepare the server for production use.

The server must be:

  • Secure
  • Properly configured
  • Monitored
  • Documented
  • Easy to troubleshoot

docs.title: Lab Requirements
docs.text:
Complete the following tasks:

  1. Initial system assessment
  2. User configuration
  3. Storage configuration
  4. Network configuration
  5. Software installation
  6. Service management
  7. Security hardening
  8. Troubleshooting tests
  9. Documentation

docs.title: Lab Validation Script
docs.text:
Once you have completed the final administrator lab, you can use the validation script to check your work.

Download the checker script:

Download check-my-work.sh

Make the script executable:

chmod +x check-my-work.sh

# Task 1 - System Assessment

Collect information about the server.

Commands:

```bash
hostname

uname -a

cat /etc/os-release

uptime

df -h

free -h

Document:

  • Hostname
  • Operating system
  • Kernel version
  • CPU/memory resources
  • Storage availability

docs.title: Task 2 - User Management
docs.text:
Create an administration user.

Requirements:

  • Create a named user
  • Configure sudo access
  • Set a secure password
  • Verify access

Commands:

sudo adduser adminuser

sudo usermod -aG sudo adminuser

id adminuser

docs.title: Task 3 - File Permissions
docs.text:
Create an application directory:

sudo mkdir /opt/application

Create a test file:

sudo touch /opt/application/config.txt

Configure:

  • Correct ownership
  • Secure permissions

Example:

sudo chown adminuser:adminuser /opt/application/config.txt

chmod 640 /opt/application/config.txt

Verify:

ls -l /opt/application

docs.title: Task 4 - Storage Management
docs.text:
Review storage:

lsblk

df -h

du -sh /*

Tasks:

  • Identify mounted filesystems
  • Identify large directories
  • Check available space

docs.title: Task 5 - Networking
docs.text:
Verify network configuration.

Commands:

ip address

ip route

ss -tulnp

Document:

  • IP address
  • Default gateway
  • Listening services

docs.title: Task 6 - Install Software
docs.text:
Install useful administration tools.

Example:

sudo apt update

sudo apt install htop curl wget tree

Verify:

htop --version

curl --version

docs.title: Task 7 - Create a Service
docs.text:
Install a web service:

sudo apt install nginx

Check:

systemctl status nginx

Enable startup:

sudo systemctl enable nginx

Test:

curl localhost

docs.title: Task 8 - Firewall Configuration
docs.text:
Enable firewall protection.

Example:

sudo ufw enable

Allow SSH:

sudo ufw allow ssh

Allow web traffic:

sudo ufw allow http

sudo ufw allow https

Check:

sudo ufw status

docs.title: Task 9 - Security Review
docs.text:
Complete a security review.

Check:

Users:

cat /etc/passwd

Permissions:

find / -type f -perm -002 2>/dev/null

Open ports:

ss -tulnp

Authentication logs:

sudo tail /var/log/auth.log

docs.title: Task 10 - Troubleshooting Exercise
docs.text: The following issues have been introduced.

docs.title: Problem 1
docs.text:
The web service is unavailable.

Investigate:

systemctl status nginx

journalctl -u nginx

Restore service.

docs.title: Problem 2
docs.text:
The disk is reporting low space.

Investigate:

df -h

du -sh /*

Identify the cause.

docs.title: Problem 3
docs.text:
A user cannot access a file.

Investigate:

ls -l filename

Correct:

  • Ownership
  • Permissions

docs.title: Task 11 - Monitoring Script
docs.text:
Create:

nano system-check.sh

Create a script that displays:

  • Hostname
  • Disk usage
  • Memory usage
  • Running services
  • Network ports

Example:

#!/bin/bash

echo "System Health Check"

echo "=================="

hostname

echo ""

df -h /

echo ""

free -h

echo ""

systemctl --failed

echo ""

ss -tulnp

Make executable:

chmod +x system-check.sh

Run:

./system-check.sh

docs.title: Task 12 - Documentation
docs.text:
Create a final report.

Document:

Server Details:

Configuration Changes:

Security Improvements:

Services Installed:

Problems Found:

Solutions Applied:

Lessons Learned:

docs.title: Final Assessment
docs.text: You should now be able to:

docs.title: Linux Administration
docs.text:
• Manage users
  • Manage permissions
  • Manage services
  • Manage software

docs.title: Networking
docs.text:
• Configure networking
  • Troubleshoot connectivity
  • Analyse ports

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
• Understand filesystems
  • Investigate disk usage

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Secure accounts
  • Configure firewalls
  • Harden services

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Gather evidence
  • Identify root causes
  • Apply fixes
  • Document solutions

docs.title: Completion Criteria
docs.text:
The lab is complete when:

  • The server is configured
  • Services are running
  • Security controls are applied
  • Troubleshooting scenarios are resolved
  • Documentation is completed
